News.title: People who work hard KNOW the only winners in Burnham’s Britain will be those on benefits
News.content:
Next

LOOK around Britain today, and you’d be hard-pressed to find any ordinary people who reckon the economy is on the up.

And yet, with just weeks to go before his first Budget, Chancellor John Healey is reportedly claiming he didn’t know how bad things are.



We should all be very worried — but small businesses and the self-employed most of all.

Apparently, two years of weekly cabinet meetings sitting next to then Chancellor Rachel Reeves didn’t do much for him.



Two tax-raising budgets in which he sat on the Labour front bench simply passed him by.

The hundreds of thousands of jobs gone under Labour, the closed businesses, the families hammered by tax rises? John Healey didn’t know.



Of course, I don’t believe him.

But I do believe that he, as was the way with Rachel Reeves, is saying this because he is too weak to tell the truth.

Labour’s problem is that they don’t get business, they won’t cut out-of-control welfare, and so all that they have left is to raise taxes.

Nowhere is that betrayal felt more than among the five million small businesses in this country, and the four million self- employed.



They are the bedrock of our economy — the plumbers, electricians, hairdressers and brickies who get up early every day, show up and get the job done.

Labour ministers could learn something.

But instead of backing these people, it looks like Healey is dead set on hammering them again, with his Budget on October 28.

He’ll do it the same way Reeves did — with lofty words about growth and responsibility while, in truth, snuffing out the last signs of life in our economy.

Because as Conservatives know, you grow an economy from the bottom up, not the top down.



If every small business hired just one extra person, that would be millions of jobs across the country added.

Instead, Labour have taxed those jobs, making that all but impossible.

That attitude is what we should all fear.

No matter the warm words Healey might use in his speeches, or PM Andy Burnham in his TikToks, it doesn’t matter if, in the end, taxes just keep going up.

If everyday life for families just gets even more expensive.



If those who work hard know that the only winners in Burnham’s Britain are the residents of Benefits Street.

Small businesses and the self-employed are already feeling the pinch.

They’re spending 44 hours and £4,500 a year just on working out how to comply with tax rules, before they’ve spent a single penny paying their actual taxes.



One in three small businesses surveyed expects to shrink, sell up or close over the next year.

Over the last year, only a minority increased their revenues, while the majority saw them fall.

In short, it’s a slow-mo disaster. And it’s not getting any better.

Since September 1, HMRC has mandated Making Tax Digital — better known as Making Tax Difficult.

It means the self-employed and landlords will have to file four separate reports to HMRC every year, using expensive software, before they can even file their actual tax return.



That is to say nothing of the chaos the IR35 tax legislation continues to cause for those who choose to work as contractors rather than employees, for entirely legitimate reasons.

In short, small businesses and the self-employed need someone who will back them, not another budget horror show.

We all do.

That’s why, today, I am pledging to put small businesses and the self-employed at the heart of my plans as Shadow Chancellor.

Healey may not care for them, or he may not know they exist, but the next Conservative government will treat them with the respect they deserve.



In the meantime, Healey should make their lives easier.

He owes it to hard-pressed taxpayers to pause Making Tax Difficult and find a better way to digitise the tax system — one that doesn’t cost the self-employed even more time and money.

But he should also end the pain — and we cannot wait until Budget Day.

Healey should promise today that he will not raise taxes on small businesses and the self-employed.

Indeed, he should not raise taxes on anybody.



The Conservatives have already set out billions worth of savings that will allow us to pay down debt, fund defence — and cut taxes.

Because we get it. Britain has paid enough. We are already facing the highest tax burden on record.

Now it’s Westminster’s turn to do their job and make the tough choices needed to bring down spending, borrowing and taxes.

Conservatives are the party of business.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

We didn’t always get it right in the past but we know what it is to run a business, to be self-employed and to make tough choices.



Under Kemi Badenoch’s leadership that is exactly what we will do.

News.title: How Iran-backed Houthi fanatics are sending cost of living in Britain soaring from 3,000 miles away – with WORSE to come
News.content:
Next

THE fanatical Islamist terror group’s holy war is a relentless conflict happening more than 3,000 miles away.

But every British motorist, van driver and trucker filling up today is feeling the pinch, thanks to Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.



And defence experts and motoring groups are warning that more pain is coming, as the Houthis help to tighten Iran’s stranglehold on the global economy.

UK inflation jumped to 3.1 per cent yesterday, driven by more Middle East mayhem as the seven-month war detonated by Donald Trump and Israel drags on.



Petrol and diesel prices here have already leapt by around 4p a litre in the past week as benchmark crude oil prices remain near four-month highs.

Analysts predict that if the Middle East oil crisis continues to a worst-case scenario, unleaded fuel could hit £2.05 a litre and diesel £2.25.

That would push the price of filling up a standard UK diesel family car with a 55-litre tank to a wallet-busting £123.75.

Fuel prices impact not only inflation, but also the cost of distributing goods, as well as driving up interest and mortgage rates.

And it is Houthi hellfire in Saudi Arabia’s oilfields that could push Bank of England bosses into a long-dreaded interest rate rise today.

On top of all that, our household energy bills are currently on a steep upward trajectory, with a confirmed increase this autumn and a massive spike predicted for early winter.



The Ofgem energy price cap has been confirmed to rise by four per cent to £1,723 a year on October 1.

Compounding this, major energy suppliers and analysts are now warning that the price cap is projected to surge by roughly 24 to 25 per cent in January 2027, pushing typical household bills up to around £2,152 a year.

The latest crude oil price hike follows two strategic triumphs by the Houthis.

First, they tightened their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb strait in the Red Sea, part of the crucial trade route leading to the Suez Canal, by capturing a string of key island bases — and cut off a vital 745-mile east-west Saudi pipeline.



It was being used to move billions of barrels of oil away from the Strait of Hormuz — already paralysed by Iranian strikes to the east of the Arabian peninsula.

But it was still offline yesterday as Houthi drones and missiles targeted the Saudis again, hitting the King Khalid Air Base and the vast Aramco refining plants in the port city of Yanbu.

Saudi air force hangars, radar sites, runways and ammunition depots at Khamis Mushait air base were also hit after the capture of Yemen’s Greater and Lesser Hanish islands.

Defence analyst and historian Paul Beaver told The Sun yesterday: “Six months ago Iran was in a very weak position after the US and Israeli attacks decimated their leadership.



“But the mullahs believe they are winning the war now — and it is largely thanks to the Houthis.

“Their allies in Yemen have opened up a whole new front by focusing on Saudi Arabia to choke a second supply route after the Strait of Hormuz was effectively blocked.

“They have control of the Red Sea route to the Suez Canal and have been driving commercial shipping away and increasing costs for months.

“But this week’s successful attack on the Saudi pipeline was, in military terms, a masterstroke.

“It showed they are now a formidable enemy with technical, tactical and intelligence assets and are a force to be reckoned with.”



The Houthis have come a long way since the rebel group was formed from disgruntled tribesmen in the north of Yemen in the 1990s.

Officially named Ansar Allah — or “Supporters of God” — they were founded and first led by religious leader Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi, who inspired their nickname.

The group went on to become a central pillar of Iran’s “Axis of Resistance”, receiving unassembled arms shipments smuggled by a shadow fleet of ­wooden-hulled Arab dhows.



Their charismatic first leader was killed battling Yemeni government forces and was succeeded by his hermit-like brother Abdul-Malik al-Houthi in 2004.

Under his rule the Houthis enforced a barbaric Islamist code in all areas they controlled, laid down in al-Houthi’s pre-recorded speeches smuggled from his secret lair.

Brutally oppressed women wear burkas and are never allowed out without a male chaperone, while political opponents are routinely ­tortured and executed.

Anyone found guilty of the “crimes” of homosexuality or adultery are liable to be crucified or stoned to death in public squares.

Houthi forces, bolstered by child soldiers, have besieged and starved tens of thousands of Yemenis.



After the 2011 Arab Spring revolts, they used Iranian financial, political and military backing to seize control in a power vacuum, capturing the capital, Sanaa, in 2014.

Since then, cargo worth billions has been diverted away from Red Sea shipping routes after Houthi pirates boarded commercial ships and kidnapped crews.

In recent years their medieval savagery has combined with a lust for military power, and they have received training from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp.

With Palestinian nationalist group Hamas and Lebanon’s Hezbollah now weakened by Israel’s huge offensive in the wake of the attacks of October 7, 2023, the Houthis are now Iran’s main proxy warriors.

The group have become expert in assembling missile parts, guidance units, drone engines and explosive warheads smuggled by sea.



With such advances the Houthis’ sphere of influence is no longer confined to Yemen.

They are believed to have teamed up with pro-Iranian comrades based in Iraq to launch the Saudi pipeline attack.

In recent days their actions have directly affected British fuel prices, which suppliers have quickly passed on to drivers.



Western leaders, including Andy Burnham, have been anxious to play down spiralling fuel costs amid fears of panic-buying.

Chancellor John Healey will also have one eye on the conflict when he delivers his “challenging” first Budget next month. In the UK, the cost of filling up a family car’s 55-litre tank has risen to around £92.65 — up £12 to £15 since the Iran War began.

And filling up with diesel now costs around £104.50 — up more than £17 in the same period.

An AA spokesman said: “It is hard to see an end soon to this chaos. I think it is the persistence of this crisis which is most draining on drivers and businesses.”

But President Trump is continuing his “long game” bid to wreck Iran’s economy in a drive to drag them back to the negotiating table.



It seems a long time since Iran’s power base appeared to have been wiped out by the Operation Epic Fury attack which killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in February.

Khamenei’s vengeful son Mojtaba — crippled by the Tehran blast which killed his father — now leads an even more fanatical and resourceful regime which is funding the Houthis, Hamas and Hezbollah and is more entrenched than ever.

And Mr Trump’s options — despite his constant threats and victory claims — are now limited.

Defence analyst Paul Beaver added: “I’m afraid Mr Trump started a war without a plan while the Iranians had a clear strategy.

“And no matter what he decides to do, historians will say that right now, in September 2026, Iran and the Houthis had the upper hand.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Mr Trump has painted himself into a corner and it’s hard to see how he’s going to get out of it.

“But I suspect we will all be paying a price until he does.”

News.title: Unruly passenger duct-taped to seat breaks his silence after ‘abusing plane crew’ during mid-air rampage
News.content:
Next

A RAGING passenger who was duct-taped to his seat after he allegedly exploded into a hate-fuelled rant has spoken out for the first time.

Flyers wrapped Layne Lundeen, 67, in sticky tape before air crew booted him off the flight from Dallas, Texas to Newark, New Jersey nine days ago.



The Arizona realtor allegedly spewed racist and homophobic slurs at his seatmate and cabin crew in a mid-air meltdown on September 5.

Now a court has heard that Lundeen had knocked back two screwdriver cocktails and blacked out the memory of the chaotic incident, as reported by The Banner.



Speaking to District Court Commissioner George Haag, Lundeen said: “I don’t remember any of what happened.”

In audio obtained by the news outlet, the American appeared to be confused about why he was even in court.

“I assaulted a police officer? Is that what it says?” Lundeen said. “I don’t have my glasses.”

Haag then read the allegations to him. “Oh my God. What a mess,” Lundeen said, adding: “I don’t remember any of it.”

Shocking images from the incident show a man strapped tightly to his first-class seat with silver tape coiled around his body – including his head.

Lundeen has since been unmasked as the individual who allegedly hurled the N-word at a flight attendant.



Eyewitnesses said that the realtor “became increasingly unruly”, shouting profanities and waking up a sleeping passenger while asking another if she loved Jesus, cops said.

The allegedly raging man had been sat in first class beside rabbi and author Jonathan Cahn.

Cahn told the Daily Mail that the pair had been debating religion when “in a split second” he flipped.

The rabbi had been telling Lundeen about his experience of God when the realtor “changed”.

“His face changed, his voice changed, and he said… almost in a whisper, he was like, ‘I have something to tell you’ and he said, “Bulls**t””, claimed Cahn.



The author then said the man tried to smash his laptop – before raging against flight attendants.

Cahn alleged that Lundeen threatened: “I’m gonna punch your f****** Jewish face in.”

Police eventually bundled the man off the plane – but not before he allegedly hit an officer in the chest.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Long Realty, the firm for who Lundeen worked, has fired the man following his unbelievable outburst.

The Arizona-based real estate firm ended their “affiliation” with Lundeen after “concerning criminal charges” emerged from the incident.

News.title: Piddington’s independence vote speaks for everyone utterly sick of illegal migration but is anyone in Labour listening?
News.content:
Piddington dare







Next

PIDDINGTON residents yesterday roared on behalf of everyone utterly sick of the consequences of illegal migration.

In voting to symbolically leave the UK, they spoke for those fed up with unvetted young men leaving perfectly safe France to break into our country.



For working families staggered by the £1billion paid to the French while the small boats still come. And for those communities terrified by shocking cases of sexual violence and rape by migrants.

But is anyone in Labour listening?



Yesterday, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy admitted the Government was preparing to spend MORE cash to flood middle-class areas with illegal migrants.

Labour says spreading the migrant housing problem around the country is about fairness — as if the British people have a duty to meekly accept this outrageous assault on their safety.

After more than two years in power, ministers STILL talk as though there is nothing they can do to stop any of this.

It would be whole lot “fairer” on all voters if Labour did something to fix our broken asylum system.

Before villages, towns and cities up and down the land decide they too would like independence from Labour’s Britain.

All at odds

ANDY Burnham supposedly cares about wanting to get kids into work AND revive the high street.



But Labour’s war on fun is destroying both — with working-class communities taking the brunt.

Entain, the owner of Ladbrokes and Coral, has axed 400 jobs following a swingeing tax grab in the last Budget.

Now Burnham is said to be considering even higher taxes on gaming machines in bookies — which would lead to even more jobs being lost, especially young workers in entry-level posts.

It will also deliver another kick in the teeth to racing, which relies on subscriptions paid by high street shops.

Meanwhile, a House of Lords committee of hopelessly out-of-touch peers is pushing for a ban on gambling advertising.



What do they think that will do to struggling lower league football clubs and others who rely on the lifeline?

Such virtue-signalling and economic ignorance is a nailed-on loser.

Fortune teller

MINISTERS and unions have spent days attacking Reform over £72million donated by two cryptocurrency tycoons, claiming democracy should never be for sale.

For its part, Labour’s had £100million from the unions in recent years — all while hiking the minimum wage, imposing burdensome workers’ rights and giving huge public sector pay boosts.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Now TUC leader Paul Nowak has been made a director of the Bank of England, supposedly on the basis he’s “apolitical”!



It must be a different Mr Nowak who led the charge against the Reform donation . . .

News.title: Budget will be ‘challenging’ Burnham admits as Tories warn him NOT to hike taxes
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham has said October’s Budget will be “challenging” as Tories warn him not to hike taxes.

The PM blamed the Iran War for forcing him to make “difficult decisions”.



His admission came as inflation surged 3.1 per cent, driven by higher pump prices and energy bills.

Mr Burnham said: “It is going to be challenging, because the picture around the world is challenging — particularly in the Middle East.



“We won’t take risks with people’s living standards or with the economy.”

Pressure is mounting on Chancellor John Healey over rising borrowing costs, which hit a 19-year high this week.

He may be left with no choice but to hike taxes or cut spending to maintain the Government’s financial cushion, which stood at £24billion at the last Budget.

Experts at Oxford Economics have said he may have to find £11billion just to maintain the same buffer.

MONETARY UNION A MILITANT union boss has been made a director of the Bank of England. TUC General Secretary Paul Nowak was parachuted into the £20,000 job for three days’ work a month by Chancellor John Healey. The left-wing firebrand, one of four new appointments, has called for a banking tax raid. He said he will give his salary to charity. Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said Nowak’s selection is “the last thing our country needs”.

But Mr Burnham was forced to hit back at ally and ex-Bank of England economist Andy Haldane who said there has been an inability so far to cut public spending.

Haldane said “the markets now suspect this is a traditional tax and spend socialist government, with better TikTok videos”.



The PM said: “We are not that.

“Already, I have taken difficult decisions in this job in relation to reprioritising Government spending, putting digital ID on hold for instance.

“So it’s not the case that we aren’t going to take difficult decisions.”

The Tories last night urged the Government not to squeeze households and firms even more ahead of the Budget at the end of next month.

Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said: “Burnham and Healey must rule out tax rises and pledge not to introduce new taxes.”

News.title: We live on HMO Street where a THIRD of homes are houses in multiple occupation – parking’s chaos but landlords love it
News.content:
Next

FURIOUS residents call their road “HMO Street” since almost a third of its homes have become houses in multiple occupation or flats.

Locals on Princes Street in Mansfield, Notts, claim it has brought parking chaos and overflowing bins.



At least 13 out of 42 homes are being converted into HMOs or flats as the Home Office moves asylum seekers from migrant hotels.

Mansfield District Council has approved expanding an existing HMO into a ten-person home.



Martin Radcliffe, 62, who has lived there since 1990, said: “At £100 per person, that’s £1,000 a week the landlord will coin in.”

He added: “HMOs seem to be breaking down the community because no one knows who you’re living next door to anymore”.

The council confirmed three HMOs, three in the licensing process, six homes converted into flats and an assisted living dwelling.

Lorry driver Lonel Tolan, 35, said the situation is so bad he sometimes cannot use his own driveway.

The dad-of-two said: “The parking is hell.

“Sometimes it’s impossible to park on your own drive.”



One woman, who asked not to be named, branded the road “HMO Street”.

She said: “It’s getting to the point where it can go on for too long and there’s no turning back.

“It’s a big problem and the only way to sort it is limiting how many HMOs are on each road to preserve the communities living ther



“It needs to be regulated better.”

News.title: Newts ‘may thwart Piddington migrant camp after Home Office failed to identify protected species on site’
News.content:
Next

NEWTS could stop a migrant camp from being built in Piddington after the Home Office failed to identify the species on the site.

Campaigners in the Oxfordshire village voted to leave the UK in a symbolic referendum over the controversial proposals to house 1,250 male asylum seekers in the hamlet.



Now they have discovered records showing a number of protected wildlife species on the site, the Telegraph reports.

The Home Office didn’t mention the presence of any protected species when submitting their planning application for Bicester Garrison.



Locals have warned they will be free to mount a legal challenge to foil the development unless it repeats an ecological assessment.

If not, the government department could be open to a legal challenge that could stop the plans in their tracks.



Claire Brenner, a resident with a zoology degree, who uncovered the evidence, said: “If the Secretary of State determines this application with this materially incomplete information, that’s open to legal challenge.

“If they proceed to work on the site without a licence, then potentially it’s a wildlife crime.”



She added that the Home Office’s ecological assessment wasn’t “fit for purpose” with its claim that there were no records of five different types of protected wildlife at the proposed site being wrong.

Claire analysed documents at Thames Valley environment records centre where she claims she discovered there was evidence of a breeding population of newts on the site.

She also said there was evidence of 12 different species of bats, nightingales, badgers and an otter.

According to Claire, the Home Office consulted the wrong environment centre.

Newts are a protected species under British law meaning the developer must stop work and conduct surveys if there is any record or evidence of their presence at the site.



If the home office is likely to disturb the site it must get a licence from Natural England, the official government adviser.

It comes as it is revealed that the migrant centre faces further setbacks in the form of a lack of gas and water.

A Home Office assessment reportedly found no viable gas network and limited use of the main water supply at the site – a former military storage space.

6 Credit: Reuters



The existing electricity infrastructure is also reportedly unreliable and would leave the proposed camp requiring generators.

As well as this, the drainage system at the site was identified as being “largely non-operational”, the Times reports.

Piddington, which has a population of 358, voted 285 in favour, 26 against and one spoilt vote in a referendum to become independent.

The women of Piddington say they fear they will be attacked on their doorstep if Home Office proposals to house some 1,250 asylum seekers there go through.

They said that the migrants, almost four times the local population, pose a threat to public safety in the community and will add to pressure on local services.



The hamlet’s symbolic referendum of independence was held on Wednesday in protest against the plans.

Following the referendum jubilant villagers were seen holding up a ‘Principality of Piddington’ sign as they celebrated the result.

Bicester Garrison has been chosen as part Labour’s wider scheme to convert Ministry of Defence facilities into migrant housing and close asylum hotels.

But, in July, 96 per cent of villagers said they wanted a referendum on leaving the UK and slammed the controversial plans for “Site A”.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he understands the “strength of feeling” across the country about migration.



When quizzed on the referendum, he said: “Well, I understand the strength of feeling.

“That’s something that is across the country, but the only thing to do is to get the numbers down, the number of crossings down.

“We also made a commitment to people to end the use of hotels to house refugees and asylum seekers. That commitment needs to be honoured.”

But Joe Marshall, a professional planner who is leading the campaign to oppose the scheme, said: “Andy Burnham is supposed to be a family man so he needs to come here and listen to our concerns now.

“The idea of 1,250 migrant males roaming around a quiet village like Piddington should fill anyone with horror.



“Of course the vast majority of these men will be perfectly fine, but if five per cent are not, that’s more than 60 men causing all sorts of problems.

“To put it bluntly, these men will have needs they can’t suppress and that could lead to attacks on women here. We can’t have that.”

Recently-released documents revealed the centre would potentially house 3,510 asylum seekers, more than double the original proposal of 1,256.

Refugees would be moved into the sprawling site, which is located just yards from the village’s Jubilee Reserve community park.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

All single men from several different countries, they would start arriving in November.



Although free to leave the camp and walk into the village or travel to nearby towns, none would be allowed to work.

News.title: Moment monster 40ft jellyfish with excruciating sting is spotted off UK coast – as beachgoers warned
News.content:
Next

THIS is the moment a monster 40ft jellyfish was spotted off the UK coast with beachgoers warned of its exruciating sting.

A free diver from Pembrokeshire captured stunning footage of the lion’s mane jellyfish off the Welsh coast, saying it was the “length of a bus”.



Swimmer Iestyn Morgan, 21, was stunned at the sight of the lion’s mane jellyfish with 40ft tentacles in the water.

He spotted at least 20 in the shoal as he swam off the coast of Pembrokeshire – and has been assured their sting is “nasty but not life-threatening.”



Morgan filmed the giant moving slowly through the water as it dwarfed nearby fish and its tentacles went “beyond the range of visibility”.

He said: “Three turned to 10, and then to 20. They just kept on coming.

“It must have been the length of a bus or small train. I couldn’t believe how big it was.”

He initially thought it was a compass jellyfish, which are native to UK waters, before realising it was too big.



Morgan said on social media it was “one of the most memorable sights of my life” as “this giant cruised over the shallows”.

Lion’s mane jellyfish gets its name from its long tentacles, and has “all the beauty and bite of a lion”.

They can grow up to nearly 10ft in length, but the tentacles – which are used to catch their prey – can measure as long as 120ft making it one of the longest animals on Earth.

Iestyn was “grateful” they were in the waters near Trefin, West Wales – adding they were not “big scary monsters” as some people may think.

“Your biggest problem is if you swim into them. You don’t want to get stung by a lion’s mane,” he said.



He is creating a conservation project – saying his content has been “very rewarding” as he wanted to make aquatic environments “more accessible” to people.

But he was always conscious that he never wanted to harm the animals as part of his project.

“I don’t want to turn it into something that I’m going out to hunt the animals or anything,” he said.

“I just get in the water, film and swim.”

Marine biologist Dr Cathy Lucas, from the University of Southampton, said Iestyn showed the animal’s incredible length.



“The tentacles are so long and so fine you might not even see them,” she said.

“They still sting after they break off,” she said, adding that while the sting was “nasty” and “the worst in the UK”, it was not dangerous.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The advice is not to touch them and if you get a bit of tentacle on your skin flick it off with a stick and wash in warm water to neutralise,” she said.

Lucas said lion’s manes “occasionally” reach the Welsh coast later in the summer or autumn but their main habitat in the UK was Scotland.

News.title: Body found in search for missing Noah Woods, 3, in Brantham as volunteers weep
News.content:
Police searching for three-year-old Noah Woods, who vanished from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, on Tuesday afternoon, have recovered the body of a child from nearby Decoy Pond

A body has been found in the search for missing three-year-old Noah Woods.

Noah was last seen at Merriam Close Playground in Brantham, Suffolk, at around 2.30pm on Tuesday. The little boy, who was non-verbal and had partial hearing loss, became separated from a relative while visiting the playground.

Hundreds of people from the village and beyond joined the search, hoping to find Noah safe and well. Many volunteers wept as they were told on Wednesday evening that a body had been found.

A specialist dive team from the Metropolitan Police was deployed on Wednesday afternoon to assist with the search of Decoy Pond, a fishing lake about 0.2 miles from Merriam Close Playground. The body of a child was subsequently recovered from the lake.

Suffolk Police previously said officers were keeping an open mind about Noah's disappearance, but said there was "nothing to indicate anything sinister or any element of criminality has taken place".

News.title: 'Doctors told me I was being overdramatic when my toddler was ill - the truth was sinister'
News.content:
'Doctors told me I was being overdramatic when my toddler was ill - the truth was sinister'

Sophie Sparks, 37, claims she was told she was being an "overdramatic first time mum" after taking her daughter to A&E over her daughter Darcey's symptoms - which turned out to be leukaemia

View 3 Images Darcey with her family after battling leukaemia (Image: Sophie Sparks / SWNS)

A mum has told how her daughter was diagnosed with leukaemia after doctors told her she was being an "overdramatic first-time parent" over her mystery symptoms.

‌



Sophie Sparks, 37, spent six weeks desperate for answers after her daughter Darcey was struck down with repeated infections, soaring temperatures and endless coughs and colds.

‌



But she said Darcey was treated for tonsillitis, given throat spray at A&E, and told she was simply picking up common childhood illnesses from nursery.

‌



When her stomach started to swell, doctors suggested she was probably just constipated, her mum said.

It was only when a GP arranged an urgent hospital assessment at Queen's Hospital in Romford, Essex, that medics finally discovered she was seriously ill.

View 3 Images Her family fought for a second opinion when she never fully recovered between illnesses (Image: Sophie Sparks / SWNS)

‌



Elizabeth Line worker grandad killed with single punch by passenger who missed train READ MORE :

Within 24 hours of doing blood tests, Darcey was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) and began chemotherapy at Great Ormond Street Hospital the following day in November 2022.

Mum-of-two Sophie, Rainham, Essex, said: "It started with what seemed like normal coughs and colds, so we didn't think much of it at first.

"The problem was that she never seemed to recover from one illness before the next one started.

‌



"She might have one or two good days, then she'd be poorly again with high temperatures and complete exhaustion. She just wasn't herself.

"Every time we took her to a doctor, we raised concerns about it, but we were repeatedly told it was a minor illness she probably picked up at nursery or constipation.

"Because we could never get an appointment with our own GP, we ended up visiting walk-in centres three times and A&E once.

‌



"Each time, we were told she was simply building her immune system, that she was young, and that these things were normal and we were just being overdramatic first-time parents.

"Eventually we got a GP appointment and as soon as the doctor saw her, he was alarmed. She was extremely pale, almost yellow in complexion. He immediately told us to take her straight to A&E.

"Even then, we spent four hours waiting before anyone saw us. They told us she appeared fine at which point I was beside myself and pushed for tests.

‌



"Once blood tests were done, the nurses face changed and told us Darcy was incredibly anaemic. We were told she needed a blood transfusion and would have to stay overnight.

View 3 Images Darcey on her fifth birthday (Image: Sophie Sparks / SWNS)

"At around 1am a doctor came to see us and said they'd reviewed her blood results. They didn't know exactly what was wrong, but they believed she had leukaemia. Within a single day, our whole world had changed.

‌



"Within 48 hours we were at Great Ormond Street Hospital and Darcy was starting chemotherapy."

After two years of gruelling chemotherapy and treatment, the battling youngster, now aged five, was eventually told she was cancer free in December 2024, and rang a bell to mark the milestone.

Sophie, an aviation insurance claims manager, added: "Looking back, it's hard not to question why it took six weeks to reach that diagnosis.

‌



"I don't blame individual doctors, but I do think the bigger picture was missed.

"Doctors see lots of coughs, colds and infections, and I understand that. But they should also listen to parents.

"We kept saying that Darcy didn't look right, that her stomach was swollen, that she was unusually pale and exhausted. Parents know when their child has changed.

‌



"But once we entered the NHS cancer system, the care was incredible. The teams at Queens and Great Ormond Street were absolutely outstanding."

Darcey started school in September last year and is said to be doing "brilliantly" and is loving life as a big sister to one-year-old Harry.

Sophie, who is married to husband Jon, 37, a carpenter, added that seeing Sophie walk into her first day at school reception was "one of the proudest and most emotional moments of our lives" - and revealed that she has already told them she wants to be a doctor.

‌



"That was incredibly special to hear and she is loving being a big sister, the novelty certainly hasn't worn off and they love each other."

The mum now wants other parents to be more aware of the symptoms of chemotherapy, and said: "Trust your instincts. You know your child better than anyone.

"If they're unusually tired, pale, developing swellings, or simply don't seem themselves, keep pushing for answers. Childhood cancer can develop quickly, and early diagnosis saves lives.

Article continues below

"Even if it turns out to be nothing serious, it's always worth getting concerns checked. Knowing the signs and symptoms, and trusting your gut as a parent, could make all the difference."

News.title: Flight to Manchester declares mid-air medical emergency after entering UK airspace
News.content:
Flight to Manchester declares mid-air medical emergency after entering UK airspace

A Pakistan International Airlines flight from Islamabad to Manchester declared a mid-air emergency on Wednesday due to a medical issue on board

View 3 Images Pakistan International Airlines flight PK701 declared a mid-air emergency on Wednesday (file image) (Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)

A Pakistan International Airlines flight from Islamabad to Manchester declared a mid-air emergency after a medical issue was reported on board.

‌



Flight PK701 departed the Pakistani capital at around 12.15pm local time (8.15am BST) and continued its journey through Asia and Europe as normal for around eight hours, according to flight-tracking data.

‌



The flight crew transmitted a 7700 squawk code - the international signal for a general emergency - over the North Sea shortly after entering British airspace, Manchester Evening News reports.

‌



The Boeing 777-240LR landed safely at Manchester Airport at around 4.30pm - approximately 30 minutes ahead of its scheduled arrival time of 5pm.

View 3 Images A Manchester Airport spokesperson said the aircraft was met by ambulance services on the tarmac (Image: Teamjackson via Getty Images)

Plane crashes in Swiss Alps as police confirm everyone on board is dead READ MORE :

A spokesperson for Manchester Airport said a "medical emergency" had been reported on board and that ambulance services met the aircraft on the tarmac.

‌



An RAF spokesperson confirmed there was no RAF aircraft activity involved in the incident, following speculation online that the plane had been escorted by two Typhoon fighter jets.

The Mirror has contacted Pakistan International Airlines for comment.

Pakistan's national flag carrier primarily operates Boeing 777, Airbus A320 and ATR aircraft.

‌



It comes after a Jet2 flight from London to Bulgaria was diverted to Germany following a medical incident on board.

View 3 Images A Pakistan International Airlines aircraft at Islamabad International Airport (file image) (Image: Xinhua News Agency/PA Images)

Flight LS1413, which was travelling from London Stansted to Burgas Airport in south-east Bulgaria, landed at Frankfurt Airport at 5.43pm local time (4.43pm BST) on Monday.

‌



Jet2 said the diversion was "due to a medical incident on board" and that the aircraft would refuel in Frankfurt before continuing to its destination.

The Airbus A321 eventually touched down at Burgas at 10.27pm local time (8.27pm BST) - around one hour and 45 minutes after its scheduled arrival time of 8.40pm local time.

In a customer notice on its website, Jet2 said: "Due to a medical incident on board, we wanted to let you know that flight LS1413 London Stansted to Bourgas will need to make a fuel stop in Frankfurt.

Article continues below

"Once the plane has refuelled, it will then continue to Bourgas Airport. This is an unscheduled change, so we're doing everything we can to minimise any disruption to your onward journey.

"Thanks in advance for your understanding and patience during this time - we'll have you on your way as quickly as we can."

News.title: Lewis Hamilton weighs in as message sent to Macklemore after Ed Sheeran row
News.content:
Lewis Hamilton weighs in as message sent to Macklemore after Ed Sheeran row

Macklemore was dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour after making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage, and Lewis Hamilton is among the celebrities who have shown solidarity with the rapper

View 2 Images Lewis Hamilton has backed Macklemore (Image: NurPhoto, NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Lewis Hamilton has thrown his weight behind rapper Macklemore, after the artist was axed from Ed Sheeran's tour following pro-Palestinian comments made on stage. Macklemore called for a 'free Palestine ' while supporting Sheeran in the United States and displayed footage of Gaza during performances in New Jersey.

‌



Macklemore's public stance caused controversy, as the musician came under criticism from figures such as Pink. She criticised the artist for standing in "front of a stadium full of music-loving families, with violent images from a war on the screens... then took the mic to tell all of the Jews in the stadium that it wasn't about them".

‌



Robert Kraft, owner of the NFL's New England Patriots, prohibited Macklemore from appearing at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts. It is alleged that the businessman, who had previously booked Sheeran to perform at his wedding, mobilised other stadium owners to issue an ultimatum that if Macklemore remained on tour, Sheeran would be barred from performing at their venues.

‌



Kraft stated his venue would not 'provide a platform for hate speech' and accused Macklemore of "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric". This is a claim the rapper has denied.

F1 news: George Russell admits resignation as Max Verstappen reveals quit thoughts READ MORE :

Lewis Hamilton stunned after Spanish GP retirement and furious Max Verstappen clash READ MORE :

Sheeran said he engaged with venues all week to try and build a bridge, but 'the venue's and promoter's decision was final'. Consequently, Macklemore was removed from the tour, though numerous supporters have rallied behind him.

Sheeran's remaining opening acts and backing band have withdrawn, while Formula 1 star Hamilton has also voiced his backing.

‌



"Thank you for using your voice, standing with you," the Ferrari star said on an Instagram post where Macklemore explained he had been taken off the tour.

View 2 Images Macklemore has often spoken about Palestine but has now been dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour (Image: Kieran Frost, Redfernsvia Getty Images)

Hamilton wasn't the only one. Activist Greta Thunberg declared: "Full solidarity and free Palestine. Artists' very active silence in the face of injustice and genocide will not be forgotten."

‌



Controversial rap group Kneecap added: "Free Palestine. They can never silence the truth".

Pop star Paloma Faith said: "You are a rare and important voice ... thank you for existing.... This is so articulate and so powerful. You are a hero."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Swedish singer-songwriter Zara Larsson threw her support behind the post with a string of heart emojis.

In his statement confirming he had been removed from Sheeran's tour, Macklemore was keen to point out that neither he, Sheeran, nor outspoken critic Pink were the real victims. "The victims are the Palestinian people," he said.

"The men, women and children who have been killed, starved, displaced and forced to live through unimaginable violence. More than 20,000 children have been killed in Gaza alone. People are being killed today, and people will be killed tomorrow. I want to make sure that as I tell this story, we don't lose sight of that."

‌



The rapper also opened up about his close bond with Sheeran, acknowledging the awkward position his friend had been placed in.

"Ed is my friend. I've known him for 13 years," Macklemore explained. "We've shared late nights, studio sessions and stages. He has this infectious magic about him that I've grown to love. I consider him a brother. And because of that, we've had some difficult conversations this past week.

"The type of talks rooted in love and respect for one another that still end in a place of fundamental disagreement. Nothing I'm writing here is out of spite or because I want to tear down his character. But as I told Ed multiple times on the phone, our friendship can't change my responsibility to tell the truth about what happened."

‌



He continued: "His typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it never had been before. He told me that the words "Free Palestine" and the image of the Palestinian flag were hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with. I told him that if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and where I stood. But he couldn't get past his public-facing, 'I don't take sides.'".

Macklemore feels he was singled out because of the exposure touring alongside Sheeran gave him, arguing the 'stage becomes resistance'. He maintains that claims of antisemitism were being used as a weapon to suppress his views.

Regardless of the controversy, the rapper hinted this might still rank as his most triumphant tour to date.

Article continues below

"I didn't need 10 shows from Ed," he stated. "I needed 2. Two chances to stand in front of 90,000 people and say the words that somehow became too dangerous to say.

"Free Palestine. But if those words cost me the stage, while turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've ever been on."

News.title: Elizabeth Line worker grandad killed with single punch by passenger who missed train
News.content:
Elizabeth Line worker grandad killed with single punch by passenger who missed train

Grandfather-of-five Jorge Ortega, 61, died after being punched by 29-year-old passenger Ayodele Jamgbadi, who had lashed out after missing his train

View 2 Images Jorge Ortega, 61, died after being punched by an angry passenger (Image: British Transport Police/PA Wire)

A man who missed his train and threw a fatal punch at an Elizabeth Line worker has been told he will be detained in hospital indefinitely.

‌



Grandfather-of-five Jorge Ortega, 61, hit his head on the concrete platform at Ilford station, East London, after being punched in the face by passenger Ayodele Jamgbadi in December 2024.

‌



He died two days later of a severe traumatic brain injury. Jamgbadi, a 29-year-old from Ilford, was charged with murder but was deemed unfit to stand trial due to significant mental health issues.

‌



On Wednesday, a jury sitting as part of a trial of issue at Inner London Crown Court unanimously agreed that Jamgbadi's attack led to Mr Ortega’s death.

'Murder' arrest after LA bus collision and NBC helicopter crash which killed 5 READ MORE :

View 2 Images The incident unfolded at Ilford Elizabeth Line station (Image: Network Rail)

Jamgbadi was handed a strict hospital order with restrictions aimed at ensuring he gets appropriate treatment and to protect the public, British Transport Police (BTP) said.

‌



Under the order, Jamgbadi will be detained in hospital for treatment and cannot be discharged, transferred or granted leave without the approval of the Secretary of State for Justice, or the direction of a Mental Health Tribunal.

It was heard how, on the day of the incident, Mr Ortega and two other Transport for London employees had stepped out of an office to try and calm Jamgbadi, who was kicking an advertising frame after missing a train when he lashed out at Mr Ortega.

Jamgbadi was arrested on December 5 2024, a day after the attack. Prosecutor Patrick Dennis had told the court: “The defendant stated to the police at that point, ‘What are you going to do about it?’ “’I punched him in the face. I literally punched him in the face. Are you going to nick me then?’” Mr Ortega’s co-worker, Mohammed Alim, said the man “seemed a bit disturbed, a bit angry and just said ‘who’s got a problem?’”.

‌



Mr Alim told the court: “Within a split second, he swung a punch on Jorge’s left-hand side. The attacker used his right hand. It struck Jorge near the temple area. The impact of the punch was with so much force that I saw something fly out of his mouth.

“He was floored. He hit the back of his head.”

Pathologist Dr Michael Parsons, who carried out the post-mortem examination, concluded: “Jorge Ortega died as the result of a severe blunt force head injury, the pattern of which is characteristic of a heavy impact to the back of the head. He had also sustained soft tissue injuries around the right eye that would support a heavy punch to the face being the event that precipitated an accelerated fall to the ground and setting in motion the sequence of clinical events that resulted in death.”

‌



In a tribute after the finding, Mr Ortega’s family remembered him as “a loving husband, a devoted father and a wonderful grandfather” in a tribute released via the police. They said: “We miss Jorge every single day. As a family, we wish he were here to see everything that has happened since he left us, and to share in the moments, both big and small, that we wish we could have experienced together.

“We want Jorge to be remembered for the life he lived, not for the way he was taken from us. He was a loving husband, a devoted father and a wonderful grandfather. He was hardworking, kind, generous, caring, funny, wise and incredibly talented.

He had a gift for art and drawing, and his creativity and attention to detail were a special part of who he was. The artwork he created is something we proudly display in our homes, and it will always be a part of him that we can hold on to.”

Article continues below

After the sentencing, BTP detective chief inspector Paul Attwell said: “I would like to pay tribute to the dignity, strength and courage shown by Mr Ortega’s family following his untimely loss.

“I recognise that their grief has been compounded by the length of time it has taken to reach this stage. I am grateful for the patience, support and understanding they have demonstrated throughout the investigation and the proceedings that have followed.

“Mr Ortega was a kind and hardworking man who was carrying out his duties as usual that evening, when he became the victim of a wholly unacceptable act of violence. Nobody should be subjected to abuse, intimidation or violence whilst travelling or working on the rail network.”

News.title: 'Baroness Chakrabarti is correct — the law must not have a blind spot on the right'
News.content:
'Baroness Chakrabarti is correct — the law must not have a blind spot on the right'

Baroness Shami Chakrabarti had said Shabana Mahmood should consider outlawing far-right group Patriot Platform under terrorism laws, such as Palestine Action

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Nothing will corrode public faith in the law faster than the belief that ministers look the other way when intimidation comes from the “wrong” side. Baroness Shami Chakrabarti has raised a question the Government cannot simply brush aside: where exactly is the line between protest, intimidation and conduct serious enough to justify a ban? Palestine Action was proscribed in July 2025. Patriot Platform, meanwhile, has brought masked protesters onto the streets of Dover and Portsmouth and talked of blockading sites housing asylum seekers. These are different organisations with different records, and proscription is an exceptional step carrying grave consequences. That makes consistency all the more important. People must be able to trust that the law is enforced according to conduct, rather than which cause happens to be involved. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood now faces a serious test. The Government must clearly explain where that threshold lies, examine the Patriot Platform against it, and act without fear or favour. Public confidence depends on one standard applying to everyone.

‌



Yes we Nissan

Nissan has been building cars in Sunderland for 40 years. Its decision to invest another £170 million and bring production of the Kicks hybrid to Wearside shows exactly why. Twelve million cars have rolled off those production lines since the first Bluebird in 1986, powered by the skill, graft and expertise of generations of North East workers. In a world where manufacturers can choose almost anywhere to invest, Nissan has chosen Sunderland again. That is a tremendous vote of confidence in British workers and British manufacturing, and the rest of the country should take heart from it. Britain can still build things brilliantly. Give communities skilled jobs, investment and the chance to compete, and they will deliver. Sunderland has proved it for four decades. Britain should believe in itself just as strongly.

Fitting tribute

Just two days after losing his father to dementia, Andy Burnham is back at work, carrying a grief millions of families will understand. He says his dad would have wanted him “back out there”, pursuing the changes he always urged him to make. Few tributes could be more fitting than turning loss into action.

News.title: 'Ban Danny Tommo's Patriot Platform like Palestine Action under terror laws'
News.content:
'Ban Danny Tommo's Patriot Platform like Palestine Action under terror laws'

In a speech to peers, Baroness Shami Chakrabarti has called for the government to consider proscribing Patriot Platform as a terror group in the same way as Palestine Action

View 3 Images Supporters of far-right Patriot Platform blocked access to the Port of Dover earlier this month (Image: @Ay_audits/YouTube)

Shabana Mahmood should consider outlawing far-right group Patriot Platform under terrorism laws like Palestine Action, peers have been told.

‌



Baroness Shami Chakrabarti said there is a risk of perceived double standards if similar action is not taken against the anti-migrant group led by Danny "Tommo" Thomas.

‌



Balaclava-clad followers have brought chaos to Dover and Portsmouth this month, and Thomas has spoken about blockading sites housing asylum seekers. Labour peer Baroness Chakrabarti said in a Lord Speaker's lecture that the government must look at proscribing the group as a terror organisation.

‌



Piddington village in Oxfordshire votes to leave UK over asylum seeker plans READ MORE :

View 3 Images Baroness Shami Chakrabarti called on the Home Secretary to consider proscribing the group as a terror organisation (Image: PA)

Hundreds of Palestine Action supporters have been arrested after the same action was taken against it in July 2025. Baroness Chakrabarti, a barrister and human rights activist who served as shadow attorney general from 2016 to 2020, said: “I maintain my view that the proscription of Palestine Action was a disproportionate and counterproductive mistake, given the breadth of that movement and the possibility of prosecuting the violent few rather than the peaceful many.

"That issue is of course pending before the Supreme Court. Still, I wonder whether it isn’t time to at least give consideration to the proscription of the so-called Patriot Platform after recent events on our south coast. That is if we, as legislators, are not to lose the public over inaction in the face of rising threats, and perceived double standards.”

‌



Patriot Platform sparked alarm earlier this month when a large group of masked men blocked the Port of Dover, claiming to be stopping small boat crossings. Thomas has indicated more such demonstrations are likely in the coming weeks and months, saying in an interview with fellow rabble rouser Tommy Robinson, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon: "I predict in the next six months, the Patriot Platform, with one message through a secure app, will be able to bring five to 10,000 people to a location within a matter of hours."

And he hinted that Piddington in Oxfordshire could be targeted, with men camping for days around a former MoD site set to house more than 1,200 male asylum seekers.

View 3 Images Hundreds have been arrested since Palestine Action was proscribed (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The group's actions have sparked calls for a blanket ban on face coverings. Under current law police can arrest people who wear coverings in a designated area during protests.

Baroness Chakrabarti said: “To be clear, I have spoken against the blanket banning of face coverings at protests. We must protect the immune compromised and those who reasonably fear repercussions when protesting outside the embassy of a repressive state or office of an abusive employer.

"Nonetheless, political uniforms in public were understandably banned by section 1 of the Public Order Act 1936. The year is pertinent."

Article continues below

More than 3,000 people are believed to have been arrested for showing support for Palestine Action since it was proscribed. At one protest in April the Met Police arrested 523 aged between 16 and 87.

In June the Court of Appeal ruled that the government's decision to proscribe Palestine Action as a terror organisatin was legal. Co-founder Huda Ammori has appealed the ruling to the Supreme Court.

The Home Office declined to comment.

News.title: 'Murder' arrest after LA bus collision and NBC helicopter crash which killed 5
News.content:
'Murder' arrest after LA bus collision and NBC helicopter crash which killed 5

A woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a bus crash in Chatsworth, Los Angeles, killed two people, in a prelude to a second deadly tragedy

View 3 Images An NBC Los Angeles helicopter crashed in the city's suburbs on Tuesday while reporting on a deadly bus crash (Image: CHRIS TORRES/EPA/Shutterstock)

A woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder after an SUV crashed into a city bus in Los Angeles on Tuesday, killing two people. About two hours later, a news helicopter covering the crash went down nearby, killing three more people.

‌



Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, of Simi Valley, is being held at a Los Angeles jail on $4million bail, police said.

‌



Authorities said Rios slammed her SUV into a city bus on Nordhoff Street in Chatsworth at about 5pm local time on Tuesday (1am BST on Wednesday). Two bus passengers, Gage Weida, 31, and Daniel Castillo, 46, were killed. Six other people were injured.

‌



An NBC Los Angeles helicopter covering the bus crash went down near the scene in Chatsworth shortly before 7pm local time (3am BST on Wednesday). Reporter Eliana Moreno, 38, and pilot George Marciniw, 70, were killed, along with Edy Gutierrez Mejia, 29, who was on the ground.

View 3 Images Reporter Eliana Moreno, 38, and pilot George Marciniw, 70, were killed in the helicopter crash (Image: Facebook)

Plane passengers scream in horror as ceiling collapses on flight from hell READ MORE :

Private jet carrying singer and 7 others crash-lands in Brazil and bursts into flames READ MORE :

There were no immediate details about what caused the crash of the Eurocopter AS350, which also operated for Telemundo 52.

‌



An alarm can be heard sounding in the cockpit as the aircraft loses altitude in the final seconds of footage broadcast by the crew.

Shortly after the alarm begins, a woman can be heard saying "uh oh". The helicopter then moves away from the bus crash site and begins to lose altitude.

The woman asks: "You can't pull up?" before the footage ends as the helicopter nears the ground.

‌



The helicopter went down near a large storage facility. At least four cars and two storage containers burned after the helicopter caught fire.

View 3 Images The aftermath of the helicopter crash (Image: KABC-TV via AP)

NBC4 reporter Robert Kovacik, who had been at the scene of the bus crash, said he saw black smoke before rushing to the helicopter crash site.

‌



NBC4 identified the helicopter victims as Moreno, a familiar voice during NBC4 and Telemundo 52's aerial coverage, and Marciniw. Both worked for Angel City Air, which operated the helicopter for the station.

Moreno, who was born in Orange County, joined Angel City Air in 2010 after graduating from Chapman University with a degree in broadcast journalism and political science.

She had previously reported for several news outlets and began flying with Marciniw in 2023, according to NBC4.

Article continues below

Marciniw grew up in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School in 1974.

Mejia was identified by the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner's Office.

News.title: Body found in search for missing three-year-old Noah Woods
News.content:
Supt Pearse said formal identification had yet to take place, but Noah's family had been informed.

"Our thoughts are with Noah's family and all those who knew him," he said.

"We have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support and people putting on their boots to help."

Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had helped in the search for the missing boy, who was non-verbal and partially deaf.

People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire had turned up to help.

Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the estuary of the River Stour on the Essex border.

Volunteer efforts had been co-ordinated from Brantham Leisure Centre and the village hall, which ran out of hi-vis vests due to the number of volunteers.

Those looking for Noah had been told he would not respond to shouting.

News.title: 'Grief can colour memory': Palace responds after Earl Spencer's claim in Diana book
News.content:
Buckingham Palace has responded after a claim by Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, that King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" days after her death.

Earl Spencer alleged the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to walk in her funeral procession.

The claim was made in an extract from his upcoming memoir, published by the Daily Mail.

A Palace spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. BBC News has not seen the book in full.

In the first extract, external from it to be made public, Earl Spencer claims to have been informed by a senior Palace aide that the young princes would walk alongside Princess Diana's coffin, which he objected to.

He claims to have received a phone call from Charles shortly after.

Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."

Earl Spencer's book about his sister seems set to open a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family.

The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, in a car crash in 1997, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood.

Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's untimely death.

Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do".

In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.

Earlier on Wednesday, it emerged that copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book had been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands.

BBC News understands four copies of the Dutch language edition were taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher's printers to their warehouse.

News.title: 'Putney pusher' suspect found dead at home
News.content:
The man suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge in west London in 2017, has been found dead at his home.

Nicholas Brandram, 44, was under investigation in the so-called "Putney pusher" case, after CCTV went viral showing just how close the woman came to being run over by the 430 bus, in a seemingly unprovoked attack.

He was arrested in June this year on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Last week, the Metropolitan Police confirmed he had been released under investigation.

The banker was found dead in his home on Tuesday evening. The Met said his death was being treated as "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious".

News.title: Watch: BBC crew catch thieves in act while filming shoplifting report
News.content:
A BBC team who came to a Greggs to talk to staff and customers about shoplifting were confronted by thieves openly stealing in front of them.

Two men with rucksacks did not bother to hide their faces as they ransacked the fridge for more, swearing angrily at a female worker who tried to stop them, at the outlet in Bearwood, near Birmingham.

Workers told the BBC the brazen 55-second raid was all in a day's work, with offenders targeting the outlet multiple times every day.

Greggs says it takes the industry-wide problem of shoplifting "extremely seriously", has enhanced security measures across its outlets and works closely with police.

News.title: How being music's Mr Nice Guy contributed to biggest crisis of Ed Sheeran's career
News.content:
Singer Ed Sheeran is facing the biggest controversy of his career after a storm over a decision to drop support act Macklemore from his US stadium tour following the rapper's on-stage pro-Palestinian comments.

Sheeran is one of the most successful songwriters of all time. He has sold more than 120 million records and spent more than 1,000 weeks on the US album charts.

Part of his appeal - apart from those insidiously catchy songs - is his everyman persona. He looks and dresses like a fan on the train home from Glastonbury, rather than one of the festival's headliners.

He has carefully cultivated a non-threatening, everyone welcome public image. In 2014, he donated his entire wardrobe to charity shops. The same year, he adopted a one-month-old kitten, saving it from euthanasia, and named it Graham. Today, he runs a charity providing music lessons to under-18s in his home county of Suffolk.

He tries to stay out of politics - usually only getting involved to campaign for issues like copyright protection and ticket touting, or to raise concerns over the impact of Brexit on touring musicians.

But like most artists, he leans left. In 2017, he said he supported then-Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, despite not endorsing him at the stump.

"People thought that, because I didn't put myself behind him, I wasn't a Corbyn supporter," Sheeran told the Sunday Times. "If you knew me as a person, and listened to my music, you would be able to make a pretty educated guess that he would be the kind of person I really dig."

When it comes to non-musical issues, Sheeran prefers to remain circumspect. His reasoning, he says, is that music should unite. He views his concerts as a "place of safety and sanctuary" built on shared humanity.

This week, that argument has come crumbling down - creating a crisis for his reputation and career.

News.title: Two Britons among three killed in Swiss Alps light aircraft crash
News.content:
Two Britons are among three people killed in a plane crash in the Swiss Alps.

The light aircraft crashed high in the mountains near the town of Leukerbad in the southern canton of Valais on Tuesday.

The authorities said the Cirrus SR22T took off from Sion airport in the RhÃ´ne Valley and, for unknown reasons, collided with a mountain slope about 10 minutes later.

Witnesses reported seeing a fire and smoke.

Emergency teams from the Valais Rescue Organisation, police and firefighters were sent to the scene along with three helicopters.

The Swiss Transportation Safety Board has started an investigation.

And the Valais Police and the Office of the Attorney General have launched a inquiry.

Formal identification of the victims is under way.

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was "providing support to the families of two British nationals who died in Switzerland".

It said officials were in contact with the local authorities.

"Our thoughts remain with the families during this difficult time," it added.

News.title: 'Let's go, let's go' - inside catastrophic Manchester derby VAR mistake
News.content:
Pro Ref has placed a huge level of training and resources into VAR in an attempt to make it as efficient and accurate as possible.

But when an error of this magnitude happens, no amount of investment can mask the failure.

There have been calls to appoint VAR specialists, yet this is exactly what Donohue is - in the Premier League's definition.

Three seasons ago, Pro Ref asked for candidates interested in becoming video officials.

All those who applied were put through aptitude tests. About 15 made it through to the final stages of training, of which 10 have officiated games in the Premier League.

One of those is Donohue, who on Sunday was the video official for the 65th time.

Such as been Donohue's development that he is now on the international list, appointed to Uefa club competition qualifying ties over the summer.

Donohue has made mistakes, in fact very few do not. It shows how difficult the role is.

The only two VARs to have a clear record over the last two seasons are Nick Hopton and Neil Davies, both graduates from the same accelerated programme.

Persuading referees to hang up their whistles and spend their professional lives in the VAR room is not easy, nor does it guarantee success.

Lee Mason and Mike Dean, the Premier League's only full-time VARs appointed after retirement, were both dismissed by Webb just a few months into his tenure because of a catalogue of errors.

One of the only leagues which has a full team of officials who only act as VARs and never go out on the pitch is Spain's La Liga and second division - yet one glance at the headlines there will tell you the controversy is no different to that in England.

At the start of last season the VAR completely missed that a player who scored a goal was in an offside position when the ball was played.

Pro Ref will have questions to answer over its processes and why a VAR is rushing so desperately over a review in one of the biggest games of the season.

That did not happen when West Ham's stoppage-time equaliser against Arsenal was ruled out last season. It took over four minutes - but the VAR came to the correct outcome.

The obsession with speed threatens to undermine all the work behind the scenes.

But that feels like a football problem and not one caused solely by the actions of the VAR.

News.title: British soldier who died in Ukraine road accident named by MoD
News.content:
The member of the UK armed forces who died in a road traffic accident in Ukraine last week has been named as Major Paul Wilks.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) described the 40-year-old as a "gifted leader who earned the admiration and respect of all those fortunate enough to have served alongside him".

The incident on Saturday was not the result of hostile action, the BBC understands, with the MoD stating that the accident happened "away from the front lines".

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Major Wilks served this country with pride and dedication. His loss will be deeply felt by those around him."

He said: "The tributes paid by those who worked with Paul illustrate his exceptional talent and ability, underscored by genuine warmth, compassion and a desire to support others.

"His loss is a poignant reminder of the enormous sacrifice that our armed forces and their families make in the service of our country."

Major Wilks, described by the MoD as a "proud family man", is survived by his wife and two sons.

He joined the Intelligence Corps in 2012 and was deployed on multiple operational tours, including to Afghanistan.

Major Wilks was the recipient of two operational service medals and a long service and good conduct medal.

His commanding officer praised Major Wilks as "a man of great intellect, yet he remained a mate to those he served with".

They added: "He spoke often of his love for his wife and two sons, expressing his deep gratitude for the support they provided, which allowed him to serve with such distinction.

"It is because of that foundation that he was able to meet the challenges of his role, and it is in the course of his devotion to duty that he made the ultimate sacrifice."

News.title: Schools in England get extra £500m in bid to avoid teachers' pay strike
News.content:
Schools in England are to get around Â£500 million in extra funding towards the teachers' pay award this school year, reducing the risk of a strike ballot by the largest education union.

Schools had been expected to fund some of the 3.5% teachers pay increase for the current school year out of their existing budgets, which National Education Union (NEU) leaders had strongly objected to.

Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the NEU, said the offer of more funding was a "significant" step in negotiations.

In a letter to the union on Wednesday, which has been seen by the BBC, the government said the increase would be funded by savings in employers' contributions to the local government pension scheme.

The letter said the 4.9 percentage point drop in what employers are expected to contribute will deliver "significant savings" on the pay bill for support staff, which will not be clawed back by central government.

The National Education Union said it expected the extra money to be around Â£500m, which schools can now use towards teachers' pay this year.

In July, ministers accepted the recommendation of the independent pay review body for teachers and agreed a 3.5% increase from September 2026 would be followed by 3% the following year.

The pay increase had been partly funded by an additional Â£700m for 2026-27 and Â£1.1bn for the following year.

Independent economists at the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said that left schools facing a shortfall of around 1% between rising costs and funding this year.

Luke Sibieta, IFS research fellow, said the extra money would mean the pay increase this year was fully funded - and on top of other funding increases, schools would be Â£1.6bn better off by next year than they had expected this summer.

The additional money could potentially bring the uplift for this year into line with next year.

Kebede said schools has been "running on empty" and the funding signalled "a welcome return to reality, and a message of hope for the entire school community".

Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the National Association of Headteachers, said the decision is "certainly welcome", putting schools in a "better position".

He said his union would look carefully at the detail "to determine whether this means the pay uplift is genuinely fully funded" for schools.

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said he was "pleased" at the announcement of additional funding but "the wider pressure on school and college budgets remains intense".

Similarly, the NASUWT union welcomed the news. General secretary Matt Wrack added schools needed "a sustainable, long-term injection of extra funding" to meet the needs of young people.

In an indicative ballot by the NEU in April, 90% of teachers who voted said they would be prepared to take industrial action over funding and pay, on a turnout of 48%.

A formal ballot was due to begin on 3 October and close 15 December, raising the prospects of teachers pay strikes early in 2027.

The national executive of the NEU will meet on 24 September to consider whether to call that off following the additional funding on offer from the government.

A spokesperson for Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government was "confident schools can now meet the costs of the award at a national level".

"The Secretary of State has been clear from day one that supporting teacher recruitment, retention and wellbeing, and rebuilding the relationship with the profession, are among her top priorities."

Laura Trott, shadow education secretary, said it was "not at all clear this is new money for schools", and questioned whether schools were "simply being given funding to replace savings they had already built into their budgets".

Liberal Democrat schools spokesperson Caroline Voaden said she was "glad the government has seen sense, but schools shouldn't have gone through the stress of working out where the money would come from".

News.title: Village votes to leave UK over asylum housing plan in symbolic referendum
News.content:
Residents of an Oxfordshire village have voted to become independent from the UK in a symbolic referendum held in protest at plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at a former military base.

Villagers in Piddington, near Bicester, voted on Tuesday over Home Office proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at nearby MoD Bicester.

The referendum was organised by the parish council and out of 312 votes cast, 285 voted to leave, 26 voted no, and one ballot paper was spoiled.

The culture secretary told BBC Breakfast the government would not reconsider the migrant housing proposal.

Piddington's 350 residents were invited to cast their ballot in a small box outside the village hall.

Delivering the result, parish council vice chair Susannah Parden said: "We are Piddington the village that roars."

Parish council chair Tim McNally added: "This is an example of democracy in operation.

"We went into this village hall as the underdogs - we had a plucky idea. We have given a message to the world."

News.title: Police officer guilty of series of rapes and sex attacks over 17 years
News.content:
A former Police Scotland officer has been convicted of a catalogue of sex crimes, including two counts of rape, over a 17-year period.

Campbell Petrie, 50, was found guilty of nine charges at the High Court in Glasgow, which took place between 2006 and 2023.

Petrie was a serving officer at the time of the offences, which included indecent assault, assault with intent to rape and assault to injury and danger of life.

The force confirmed he was arrested, charged and suspended from duty in December 2023. He retired from the force in December last year.

Petrie was remanded in custody and is due to be sentenced next month.

News.title: Ex-BBC presenter questions role of Royal Family in new documentary
News.content:
Veteran broadcaster John Humphrys has said the people of the United Kingdom should "be able to choose our leaders" as he releases a documentary exploring the role of the Royal Family.

Humphrys, who for decades was one of the most prominent faces on the BBC, is presenting a new Channel 4 documentary called The Royals: Time to Go?

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, the Cardiff-born presenter said he "admires" King Charles III in many ways, but said it was a "matter of choice".

Buckingham Palace has been approached for comment.

In the documentary, Humphrys speaks to both critics and supporters of the monarchy, and makes the case for electing a president as the head of state.

He recalled seeing the late Queen Elizabeth II visiting Cardiff when he was growing up, watching her being driven down Newport Road.

"My father didn't attend and said he would never bend the knee to anyone. I guess that rubbed off on me," he said.

Humphrys asked why it was seen as such a taboo to call for an alternative to the Royal Family, saying that "we can because it's a democracy".

"I know the monarch is not a political leader, but he is our leader, and we need to bow our knee to him.

"That's what I object to. Shouldn't we get a choice?"

He met the Queen throughout his career, including at Buckingham Palace where he said he spoke to her "and the corgis of course".
