Humphrys, who presented the Nine O'Clock News, the Today programme and Mastermind throughout a decades-long career with the corporation, said he took the opportunity to ask her for an interview.

"When I'd finished, she looked up at me and said just one word 'no' and I thought I could build on that," he said.

News.title: More than £2m spent by government on influencers since July 2024
News.content:
While the figures cover Labour's time in office under Sir Keir Starmer, his successor Andy Burnham has continued to use influencers to get the government's message out.

On his first day as prime minister, Burnham was already posting videos on TikTok of him running with Sir Mo Farah and appearing on influencer Max Klymenko's "career ladder" podcast.

Prof Andrew Chadwick, an expert in political communication at Loughborough University, said working with influencers "chimes with the change of direction since Burnham took over", with the PM using his following on TikTok and Instagram to engage directly with the public.

He argued using influencers could be an effective way of telling the public about things like how to file their taxes, or counter health misinformation on social media.

Governments have traditionally paid for advertising through newspapers, TV, radio and social media.

But Prof Chadwick says paying content creators is increasingly used on top of this.

At a time when more people - especially younger age groups - are switching off from traditional media, he said influencers could act as a trusted source of information.

"It's taken a while to get to this stage, but I'm surprised in a sense at how little has been spent by these departments," he added.

However, Prof Chadwick said there were also risks, as the government had less control over what posts could appear alongside, which could damage credibility.

He added that it was difficult to predict what the public response would be to a collaboration.

"The comments are there, they're underneath the post, and you'll get these kind of backlash moments," he said.

"That undermines the purpose of the original campaign."

Earlier this year, the Department for Education faced criticism over its collaboration with reality TV star Gemma Collins to promote post-16 education.

The department said Collins was not paid for the content.

Defending the campaign, then-education secretary Bridget Phillipson said Collins could reach people politicians could not, suggesting some of the criticism was driven by "snobbery".

Government guidelines for influencer marketing have existed since 2023.

Under the government's influencer due diligence policy, external, departments must consider the size and demographics of an influencer's following, as well as whether they have previously posted about political issues which could undermine the effectiveness of a campaign.

Spending by government departments on social media influencers since July 2024:

Department for Education: Â£718,971 (from 2024/25 to July 2026)

HMRC: Â£591,200 (excludes agency fees)

Department for Transport: Â£302,873.83

Department for Work and Pensions: Â£212,425

Ministry of Justice: Â£206,140

Department for Energy Security and Net Zero: Â£176,100

Ministry of Defence: Â£123,173

Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government: Â£114,831.95

Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade: Â£39,700

Departments including the Treasury and the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs said they did not spend any money on social media influencers during the period.

Some departments, such as the Home Office and Foreign Office, said they did not hold information on payments to influencers centrally.

News.title: Call to raise tax thresholds among union demands ahead of Budget
News.content:
Unions who donate to Labour will meet John Healey on Thursday to press home their demands ahead of next month's Budget.

Unite, the UK's second biggest union, has called for a reversal of the freezing of tax thresholds, that see the lowest paid drawn into paying tax.

The union's leader, Sharon Graham, said she told Andy Burnham that the cut to the winter fuel allowance, carried out under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, was a "disgrace", adding: "What to you need to do is winter fuel in reverse - something that says to everyday people I am on your side."

The call is one of a number of policy proposals unions are taking to the chancellor, including increased taxes on tech companies.

Unions say they believe Healey's first budget will define Andy Burnham's direction of travel as prime minister.

Unite took legal action against Sir Keir's government when the winter fuel payment was restricted to the poorest pensioners, and Graham believed this policy - which was not in Labour's manifesto - was politically poisonous.

Burnham said the freezing of tax thresholds had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to return to Westminster as MP for Makerfield.

In her last Budget, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves froze tax thresholds until 2031. The basic rate of 20% is paid on annual earnings between Â£12,571 and Â£50,270. The higher rate of 40% is paid on earnings between Â£50,271 and Â£125,140.

By not uprating those rates in line with inflation, more lower paid people have paid tax for the first time and more better-off workers, including public service workers such as senior nurses, police officers and teachers, are now paying tax at the higher rate.

Graham said: "We must see things happen immediately. I told him [Burnham] that you have to make working class people believe their best days are in front of them.

"That tax threshold of around Â£12,500 - if that hadn't been frozen for the past few years it would have moved up to over Â£16,000 now. People at the lower end are paying eye-watering amounts of tax."

News.title: Ex-officer jailed over 'toxic' WhatsApp culture
News.content:
An ex-police sergeant who asked to share a female suspect's sex video with "the lads from footy" has been jailed for four years.

Former Cambridgeshire Police officer Paul Street, 41, engaged in "salacious gossip" with former PC Josh Williams after he found intimate pictures and footage on the woman's personal phone.

The Old Bailey heard how Street, of Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, created a "toxic" WhatsApp culture at work. He was found guilty of two charges of misconduct in a public office.

Judge Mark Lucraft KC said: "The public should expect to be able to trust police officers to act fairly in the execution of their powers to prevent, detect and solve crime."

On Wednesday, the woman told of her "overwhelming sense of shock, violation, anger and humiliation" as Street was sentenced.

The court also heard Street encouraged colleagues in WhatsApp messages to "bully" a teenage detainee.

News.title: British-American author and critic Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
News.content:
British-American author and cultural commentator Bonnie Greer has died at the age of 77 after a brief illness, her husband has said.

In a statement delivered with "profound sadness", Greer's widower David Hutchins noted how the acclaimed playwright and critic had made "an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life" with her "intelligence, courage and distinctive voice".

He added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her."

Hutchins continued: "Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together."

Almost 600 climate scientists, health professionals and conservationists have issued a fresh plea urging Prime Minister Andy Burnham to decline licence applications for the Rosebank oil field in the North Sea.

It comes ahead of Mr Burnham’s meeting with Donald Trump, which is expected to take place in New York next week.

Mr Trump has made calls for the UK to start drilling in the North Sea, saying it would become “a really rich country” as a result.

But in a letter dispatched to Mr Burnham and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, the 575 experts warned that sanctioning the project would defy climate science and lead to the UK breaching both its national and international climate obligations.

The intervention follows reports that the UK Government intends to greenlight new North Sea drilling, beginning with the Jackdaw gas field, located 150 miles east of Aberdeen, potentially as early as this month.

open image in gallery More than 100 projects in the North Sea could be ‘unlocked’ if the current tax regime on the sector was reformed, it has been claimed (Jane Barlow/PA) ( Jane Barlow/PA )

According to the BBC and The Guardian, Ms Fahnbulleh is also expected to grant approval in the coming months for Rosebank – the largest untapped oil field in the North Sea, situated roughly 80 miles north-west of Shetland.

Deciding whether to authorise these ventures will pose a major environmental test for Mr Burnham.

He has been under pressure from climate campaigners to "stick to the spirit of Labour’s manifesto commitment" and withhold permission since assuming office as Prime Minister in July.

In their letter on Thursday, the group of experts said: “We believe that approval of Rosebank would be ignoring the warnings of scientific research on climate change and would be the wrong decision for the UK, sending a dangerous message on the international stage.”

It comes as Rosebank’s resubmitted application says the field would produce more than 250 million tonnes of planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions – equivalent to 70% of UK annual emissions.

The experts cited a recent report that said the estimated cost of the damage caused by the fossil fuels produced at Rosebank would be between £119 billion and £336 billion over the coming decades, compared with £28.7 billion in value to the UK estimated by Adura – the developer behind Rosebank.

open image in gallery Burnham is expected to meet Trump next week ( Getty/AP )

The letter read: “Our conclusions are that Rosebank is not compatible with the UK Government’s national and international obligations to protect communities from the adverse effects of climate change.”

The experts pointed to how the past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this summer brought record-breaking heatwaves, devastating wildfires and widespread drought to the UK, and that this extreme weather is estimated to have cost the UK more than £4.4 billion.

They also warned that Rosebank would not lower bills or meaningfully impact UK energy security, with most of the fossil fuels extracted planned for export.

“Communities are already facing rising costs because of drought, excess deaths because of heatwaves, and loss of land due to wildfires,” the experts said.

“This is a matter of national security and approving Rosebank would be adding fuel to the fire.

“A Government’s first responsibility is to prioritise above all else the best interests of the people it serves and protects – approving Rosebank would be completely going against this principle, by knowingly triggering more devastation on the people of the UK.”

open image in gallery Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh ( Getty )

Emeritus Professor Joanna Haigh from Imperial College London; Professor Elizabeth Robinson, director of Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change; and Professor Paul Behrens from the University of Oxford are among the signatories.

Prof Haigh said: “The science is clear. If we are to meet our international and national targets on the climate and nature emergency, we cannot allow any additional oil and gas extraction.

“Rejecting Rosebank gives the UK an opportunity to once again show global leadership and be a positive example for other nations to follow.”

Prof Robinson said: “This summer, thousands of people died prematurely. British households faced rising costs and communities had to suffer severe heatwaves, wildfires and now drought – all because of human-induced climate change.

“Approving Rosebank would only lock communities into that same cycle.”

In a separate letter last month, a group of 150 climate scientists argued the Government should at the very least require fossil fuel firms to remove some of the carbon emitted by burning oil and gas extracted from the North Sea as a condition of new drilling licences.

An Energy Department (Desnz) spokesperson said: “We do not comment on speculation. The North Sea remains a vital national asset and oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come – alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.

“Any decision will take into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received during the consultation process.”

Health officials have advised that people seeking cosmetic procedures ought to be screened for body dysmorphic disorder (BDD).

If a patient is likely to have BDD then healthcare workers should not carry out a procedure and refer the patient to a specialist, according to new draft guidance aimed to improve identification of BDD and obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD).

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) guidance further recommends that medical staff consider evaluating patients presenting with anxiety and depression for both OCD and BDD.

Those with autism or ADHD may also need to be assessed.

OCD is a mental health condition where a person has obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours.

And BDD, also known as body dysmorphia, is a mental health condition where a person spends a lot of time worrying about flaws in their appearance.

Nice said that healthcare professionals “do not routinely ask about or explore whether people have intrusive thoughts, images, urges, impulses, doubts, or worries about appearance” as it called for more to be done to help identify cases.

People with these symptoms may not disclose them unless specifically asked, Nice said.

Its new draft guideline calls on healthcare workers to consider assessing for the condition among those who are at higher risk.

open image in gallery And BDD, also known as body dysmorphia, is a mental health condition where a person spends a lot of time worrying about flaws in their appearance ( Getty Images )

Nice said health workers who provide cosmetic procedures should ask patients structured questions about appearance-related concerns before carrying out a cosmetic procedure.

If the responses indicate a person may have BDD they should be referred for specialist assessment before proceeding with the procedure.

“If BDD is suspected, they should not perform the procedure because it may reinforce or worsen BDD-related distress and behaviours,” the guidance states.

Nice said that there is an “under-recognition” of OCD and BDD.

It called on healthcare workers to normalise people’s experiences “as much as possible” highlighting how many people can experience “stigma shame and fear of judgment”.

It if hoped that the new guideline will help people be identified sooner before their symptoms become more severe.

OCD is estimated to affect about 1.2% of people while BDD affects about 2% of the population.

Eric Power, interim director of the Centre for Guidelines at Nice, said: “People with obsessive compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder can experience symptoms for a long time before they receive the right diagnosis and support.

“These conditions are often misunderstood, and many people find them difficult to talk about because of embarrassment, shame or fear of being judged.

“Our draft recommendations aim to help healthcare professionals recognise symptoms earlier, ask the right questions and support people to access appropriate treatment sooner.

“Earlier identification can help ensure people receive care that reflects their needs, preferences and circumstances, rather than waiting until symptoms become more severe or reach crisis point.”

An existing antioxidant and anti-inflammatory medicine may slow down progression of multiple sclerosis (MS), a world-first trial has found.

The MS Society, which is funding the trial, said the findings showed that ”treatments to slow or stop MS progression have never been more within our reach”.

Researchers said alpha-lipoic acid, also known as ALA, has moved to the second stage of the Octopus trial after showing early promise as a potential treatment to slow progression.

Another drug, diabetes medicine metformin, meanwhile, has been removed after it failed to demonstrate positive findings.

More than 850 people have been recruited at hospitals across the UK and Australia for the study, with more patients being urged to sign up.

Researchers from the Queen Square MS Centre and the innovative clinical trials unit at University College London (UCL) are running the trial.

They believe high-dose ALA could have the potential to become the first neuroprotective treatment in MS.

However, they said people should not attempt to acquire the drug outside of a clinical trial, as further research is needed to fully understand its safety and dosage.

More than 850 people were recruited at hospitals across the UK and Australia ( PA )

UCL neurologist, Professor Jeremy Chataway, who is leading the study, said: “This is very exciting and proves not only that the Octopus trial design works, but that a new way of protecting nerves could be on the horizon.

“Of course, learning that metformin will be discontinued is disappointing. But finding treatments for progressive MS is extremely difficult, and we’re so pleased to be taking alpha-lipoic acid into the second stage of the trial.

“We’re now looking forward not only to seeing what the final results are, but also to adding in new ‘arms’ to Octopus next year.

“In the meantime, we do need to remind people with MS to not try to source unproven drugs outside the safety of a clinical trial.”

MS symptoms range from chronic fatigue and bladder and bowel problems to issues with mobility.

There are over a dozen treatments for people living with relapsing MS (where symptoms can come and go), but people with the progressive form need new treatments to slow or stop the nerve damage that causes disability.

Dr Emma Gray, director of research at the MS Society, said: “We are so proud to be funding the first ever multi-arm multi-stage (MAMs) trial for people with progressive MS.

“MS can be debilitating, exhausting and unpredictable but today’s results are a huge step forward and show treatments to slow or stop MS progression have never been more within our reach.

“Octopus was made possible entirely by public donations and our Stop MS Appeal. We’re continuing to seek funding from our generous supporters for the future delivery of the trial to build a future where no-one needs to worry about MS getting worse.”

Symptoms of multiple sclerosis (MS) NHS Some of the most common symptoms include: feeling extremely tired (fatigue)

problems with your eyes or your vision, such as blurred vision or eye pain

numbness or a tingling feeling in different parts of the body

feeling off balance, dizzy or clumsy (uncoordinated)

muscle cramps, spasms and stiffness

needing to pee more often or not being able to control when you pee

problems with memory or concentration

sexual problems, including a dry vagina or erection problems

Ailsa Guidi, 50, from Surrey, was one of the first participants on the Octopus trial.

She was diagnosed with relapsing MS in 1999 when she was 24 but in 2023 was told her MS had progressed to secondary progressive MS.

She said: “Being on the trial has been such a positive experience because you’re thinking about MS in positive terms.

“Often I have to talk to medical professionals about getting help to deal with the challenges of MS, but this is different – it’s about working with researchers to find something that can really help thousands of people living with progressive MS.”

Professor Max Parmar, from UCL, said the trial design, also used for prostate cancer, works to accelerate “the evaluation of promising therapies” and deliver benefits to patients “years, and in some cases decades, sooner than would have been possible with conventional approaches”.

He added: “The potential to evaluate treatments more efficiently and accelerate progress for people living with MS is incredibly exciting.”

More than 150,000 people live with MS in the UK.

Anyone who has primary or secondary progressive MS and is aged between 25 to 70 in the UK can register their interest in the trial via the UK MS Register.

They can visit www.ukmsregister.org/octopus

Breast cancer patients have said they are "thrilled" after the health spending watchdog approved a life-extending drug for NHS use.

However, campaigners said that some patients living with incurable breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body have "died waiting" for Enhertu.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) announced it has reversed an earlier decision rejecting the treatment for widespread NHS use in England.

In 2024, it previously stated that the treatment was "not cost effective".

It has now confirmed the drug will be provided "from today" for roughly 1,000 women with HER2-low advanced breast cancer, after a "commercial solution has now been agreed".

The therapy has been available to patients in Scotland for more than two years.

It is the first licensed targeted treatment for patients with HER2-low breast cancer that cannot be removed surgically or that has spread to other parts of the body, also known as metastatic breast cancer.

Clinical trials have found that women with breast cancer who took the drug survived for around two years, compared with 17.5 months for those who had chemotherapy.

Paula Van Santen, who was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer in July 2022, said that the announcement has given her a “new sense of hope”.

Mother-of-three Ms Van Santen, 51, from Banbury, said: “Today is a day I never thought I’d see.

open image in gallery Paula Van Santen was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer in July 2022 ( PA )

“After years of waiting and hoping, there aren’t enough words to express how thrilled I am to see Enhertu finally approved for use on the NHS.

“Having access to this life-extending treatment brings a new sense of hope.

“It gives me the chance of seeing my daughter graduate from university, become a grandparent for the first time and simply be a mum to my children for longer as they continue to grow.

“These are life’s simple privileges that many of us take for granted, but which mean everything to me and thousands of others living with incurable metastatic breast cancer. That’s the difference a decision like this can make.”

Patient Kathryn Hulland, 48, said the decision would give her more time with her nine-year-old daughter Grace.

Ms Hulland, from Devon, was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer in 2022.

She said: “I may still be here to support my nine-year-old daughter into high school.

“When I was first diagnosed, I was told I’d be lucky to see 12 months.

“Three years later I know how important every extra month is. It’s another chance at more time with my daughter, another chance to make memories together, another month to be her mum and see her grow.

“And that’s the hope this life-extending treatment now brings, it means everything.”

open image in gallery Patient Kathryn Hulland, 48, said the decision would give her more time with her nine-year-old daughter Grace ( PA )

Charity Breast Cancer Now hailed the announcement as “momentous”.

Claire Rowney, chief executive, said: “After more than two years of relentless campaigning, Enhertu has been recommended by Nice for use on the NHS in England for people with HER2-low metastatic breast cancer.

“This is a momentous day for thousands of people who will now have access to a drug that will give them the opportunity to gain precious extra time with loved ones. More ordinary days that become extraordinary because they were there.

“This milestone victory belongs to every person who refused to accept that access to a life-extending treatment was out of reach. For people in England, the wait for Enhertu is finally over. We must now also see Wales and Northern Ireland make Enhertu available for use on the NHS for those who need more time to live.”

She added: “Since 2024 when it was first rejected for use, thousands of people have missed out on access to Enhertu and tragically many have died. We remember with deep gratitude the women who stood alongside us and fought for this very moment.”

Nice said that a commercial solution has now been agreed for Enhertu, also know as trastuzumab deruxtecan made by Daiichi Sankyo and Astra Zeneca, following changes made to its methods as part of the UK/US Pharmaceutical Pricing Agreement.

Helen Knight, director of medicines evaluation at Nice, said: “I’m pleased that a commercial solution, alongside recent changes to Nice’s cost-effectiveness thresholds and the use of new methods for assessing quality-of-life, has meant this treatment can now be provided on the NHS.

“However, we know this decision comes too late for many families, and our thoughts are with them today. Our role is important in ensuring NHS spending on new medicines reflects the benefits they deliver while protecting valuable health resources for other essential patient services.”

Dr Anne Rigg, consultant medical oncologist and NHS England’s national specialty adviser for chemotherapy, said: “This is hugely positive news for women with secondary breast cancer who will now be offered this life-extending treatment on the NHS, giving them the opportunity for more time with their loved ones.”

Tom Keith-Roach, UK country president for AstraZeneca, said: “Today’s announcement marks a vital milestone for women in England living with HER2 low metastatic breast cancer. It brings access into line with Scotland and 26 other European countries, offering renewed hope to more than 1,000 women living with this particularly aggressive form of the disease.”

A key enforcer for Henry VIII secretly saved a Catholic book he was tasked with destroying, a study has found.

Sir John Gage, portrayed in Hilary Mantel’s Wolf Hall trilogy as a dependable figure while serving as Constable of the Tower and Privy Counsellor, was a key agent in the dissolution of the monasteries.

However, research reveals that Gage, who remained a Catholic throughout the Reformation, shielded a manuscript of Nicholas Love’s early 15th-century Mirror Of The Blessed Life Of Jesus Christ.

Academics from the universities of Cambridge and Sussex identified a six-page fragment stored at The Keep Archive in Brighton as belonging to a manuscript held at Yale University in the US.

The fragment was contained within 46 boxes of documents deposited on loan by Gage’s family with the Sussex Archaeological Society in 1929.

It is believed the pages became detached after Gage acquired the text and before it was rebound in the 19th century.

Researchers confirmed the link by matching the scribe’s handwriting and filling a gap in Yale's digitised manuscript.

open image in gallery Henry VIII ( Getty Images )

The Yale manuscript was bought at a Christie’s sale of properties belonging to John Gage’s descendant Viscount Gage of Firle in 1970 by a collector in Tokyo, Japan – Professor Toshiyuki Takamiya.

It was transferred in 2017 to Yale University where it remains.

The final page of the Yale manuscript has the signature of John Gage, among a list of names of likely owners including those of two religious women.

Dr Katie Walter, of the University of Sussex, said: “The fact two possible owners before Gage were religious women suggests the manuscript might have been in a monastic house before it came into his possession.

“The dissolution of the monasteries led to the destruction of many books but others were taken and then circulated through informal networks.

“Considering Gage’s active role in the dissolution, it’s very possible he acquired the book during this chaos.”

She continued: “We often associate this period with book burning and destruction, so this manuscript’s story goes a bit against that grain.

open image in gallery The manuscript might have been in a monastic house before it came into Gage’s possession, Dr Katie Walter said ( PA )

“It reminds us that people were also rescuing, valuing and caring for books.”

She said that “by keeping this book on his shelf, John Gage and his family were part of a much bigger secret effort to preserve Catholic literature and knowledge”.

Dr James Wade, of Cambridge University’s Girton College, said: “One possibility is that John Gage went to a monastic library and brought it home.

“Another is that someone else smuggled it out, and it briefly circulated from hand to hand until Gage acquired it.

“The key thing is – he kept it safe when he was meant to destroy books precisely like this one.”

He said that 65 copies of Love’s text survive today.

“That’s a lot for a 15th-century manuscript but so many could have been destroyed in the Reformation,” said Dr Wade.

“It shows how popular it was, but it also shows how a work that became suspicious and dangerous for some could also be valued and preserved by others.”

The study is published in the journal Notes And Queries.

Major employers ought to be legally mandated to evaluate their internal pay structures every three years to ensure female staff receive equal treatment, a trade union has urged.

Unison stated that findings from its research indicate the existing equal pay framework is no longer fit for purpose. It argued the system depends excessively on employees undertaking lengthy, complicated legal proceedings against organisations suspected of breaching legislation.

To stop unwarranted disparities emerging, companies should be compelled to assess wage systems on a routine basis and resolve unfair pay gaps, according to the union.

Unison highlighted that local authorities, NHS bodies and education providers have paid out substantial back-pay settlements to low-paid female employees in recent years—claims that could have been avoided if employers had conducted timely reviews of their pay setups.

open image in gallery Cambridge professor Catherine Barnard said the current system ‘fails to deliver for many women’ ( University of Cambridge )

Unison general secretary Andrea Egan said: "Women shouldn’t be spending years fighting through the courts for money they were due long ago.

"It’s time to end this injustice.

"Equal pay laws have existed for more than half a century, yet major cases involving councils and other public bodies show the system still isn’t working as it should.

"Employers should be identifying and fixing problems before workers are forced to take legal action.

"Regular compulsory audits would expose unjustified differences and help stop discrimination becoming embedded in pay structures."

Professor Catherine Barnard of the University of Cambridge, who helped with the research, said: "The current system of pay, dating back to 1970, fails to deliver for many women.

"They’re currently dependent on expensive and stressful litigation, often funded by unions, to get equal pay.

"Our report proposes a proactive approach requiring employers to consider their pay scales on a regular basis.

"This will deliver not just equal pay but fair pay."

News.title: Passenger fatally punched Elizabeth line worker after missing his train
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

A train passenger who missed his train and threw a fatal punch to the face of an Elizabeth line worker has been told he will be detained in hospital indefinitely.

Transport for London (TfL) worker Jorge Ortega, 61, hit his head on the concrete platform at Ilford station, east London, after being struck by a single blow from Ayodele Jamgbadi in December 2024, Inner London Crown Court heard.

The grandfather-of-five died two days later of a severe traumatic brain injury.

Jamgbadi, of Kingston Road, Ilford, was charged with murder but was deemed unfit to stand trial due to significant mental health issues.

On Wednesday, a jury, sitting as part of a trial of issue at the court, unanimously agreed that Jamgbadi did the act that led to Mr Ortega’s death.

The British Transport Police (BTP) also said Jamgbadi was handed a strict hospital order with restrictions aimed at ensuring he gets appropriate treatment and to protect the public.

open image in gallery Jorge Ortega died of a severe traumatic brain injury ( BTP/PA )

Under the order, Jamgbadi remains detained in hospital for treatment and cannot be discharged, transferred or granted leave without the approval of the Secretary of State for Justice, or a direction of the Mental Health Tribunal.

Mr Ortega and two other Transport for London employees had stepped out of an office to try and calm Jamgbadi, who was kicking an advertising frame when he hit out at Mr Ortega.

BTP said Jamgbadi had apparently missed a train and began kicking a wall on platform three.

After the finding, Mr Ortega’s family remembered him as “a loving husband, a devoted father and a wonderful grandfather” in a tribute released via the police.

They said: “We miss Jorge every single day. As a family, we wish he were here to see everything that has happened since he left us, and to share in the moments, both big and small, that we wish we could have experienced together.

open image in gallery Ayodele Jamgbadi was charged with murder but was deemed unfit to stand trial due to significant mental health issues ( Yui Mok/PA )

“We want Jorge to be remembered for the life he lived, not for the way he was taken from us. He was a loving husband, a devoted father and a wonderful grandfather. He was hardworking, kind, generous, caring, funny, wise and incredibly talented.

He had a gift for art and drawing, and his creativity and attention to detail were a special part of who he was. The artwork he created is something we proudly display in our homes, and it will always be a part of him that we can hold on to.”

After the sentencing, BTP detective chief inspector Paul Attwell said: “I would like to pay tribute to the dignity, strength and courage shown by Mr Ortega’s family following his untimely loss.

“I recognise that their grief has been compounded by the length of time it has taken to reach this stage.

“I am grateful for the patience, support and understanding they have demonstrated throughout the investigation and the proceedings that have followed.

“Mr Ortega was a kind and hardworking man who was carrying out his duties as usual that evening, when he became the victim of a wholly unacceptable act of violence.

“Nobody should be subjected to abuse, intimidation or violence whilst travelling or working on the rail network.”

Jamgbadi was arrested on December 5 2024, a day after the attack.

Prosecutor Patrick Dennis had told the court: “The defendant stated to the police at that point, ‘What are you going to do about it?’

“’I punched him in the face. I literally punched him in the face. Are you going to nick me then?’”

Mr Ortega’s co-worker, Mohammed Alim, said the man “seemed a bit disturbed, a bit angry and just said ‘who’s got a problem?’”.

Mr Alim told the court: “Within a split second, he swung a punch on Jorge’s left-hand side. The attacker used his right hand.

“It struck Jorge near the temple area. The impact of the punch was with so much force that I saw something fly out of his mouth.

“He was floored. He hit the back of his head.”

Pathologist Dr Michael Parsons, who carried out the post-mortem examination, concluded: “Jorge Ortega died as the result of a severe blunt force head injury, the pattern of which is characteristic of a heavy impact to the back of the head.

“He had also sustained soft tissue injuries around the right eye that would support a heavy punch to the face being the event that precipitated an accelerated fall to the ground and setting in motion the sequence of clinical events that resulted in death.”

News.content:

Peter Max, whose colorful, psychedelic pop art expressed the optimism of the “flower power” movement of the 1960s and graced everything from postage stamps to a cruise ship, has died at 88, his son said in a written statement Wednesday.

Max died on Monday, the statement said. No cause was given.

Max began his career in graphic design in the 1960s, and his swirly, colorful, instantly recognizable designs epitomized the era’s “flower power” art. But thanks to his prolific output and fun, accessible style, Max’s work remained well known and popular well into the 21st century.

Max was the official artist for the Olympics, the Super Bowl, the Indianapolis 500, the World Cup, the World Series and many other events. His art appeared on a Boeing 777 airplane and a Norwegian Cruise Line ship. His portrait subjects ranged from U.S. presidents to Taylor Swift.

But in his first flush of success in the late 1960s and early 1970s, his murallike tableaus of flowers, the cosmos and cartoonish figures — all in vivid colors like turquoise, orange and neon green — seemed to be everywhere. Dorm room walls were plastered with his posters. Household furnishings like clocks and bedspreads sported his designs.

He even created covers for the Manhattan Yellow Pages, a business phone directory distributed to millions of people. Max himself was featured on the cover of Life magazine in 1969, his trademark dark, bushy mustache framing a hearty grin.

“We will remember his extraordinary creativity, his warmth, his curiosity, and the way he saw beauty and possibility everywhere,” his son Adam Max said in the statement announcing the death. “His art became part of American culture, but the man behind that art — the father we knew and loved — is the person we will miss most.”

Family fled Nazi Germany

Max was born Peter Max Finkelstein in 1937 to a Jewish family in Berlin. They fled Nazi Germany for Shanghai when he was a baby and later spent time in Tibet, Israel and Paris before settling in New York City when Max was 16. By then, he said in an interview, he was already “a huge fan of American culture”: comics, movies and “all the jazz music.”

Max studied in New York at the Art Students League, the School of Visual Arts and Pratt Institute. In 1961, he opened a graphic design studio with friends. His bold, unique style was an immediate hit with ad agencies, publications, the corporate world and in pop culture.

That led to a booming commercial business. "My work was really, I would say, almost exploited," he said. "It was on mugs, it was on bedsheets, it was on dresses, it was on silks and scarves and ties — 70 product lines."

But what “bothered” him about all that success, he said, was that he “wasn't painting anymore.” So he shut the business down for a time in the early 1970s to reconnect with his art. One of his biggest projects after returning to public life was a series of portraits of the Statue of Liberty, painted at the White House at the invitation of first lady Nancy Reagan in 1981.

Max weathered various controversies in his personal and professional life. He pleaded guilty to tax fraud in 1997 after the IRS alleged he concealed more than $1 million in income from his art. He was originally sentenced to two months in prison but ultimately was allowed instead to serve the time in a work-release program, pay the back taxes and a $30,000 fine, and perform 800 hours of community service teaching art in Harlem schools.

In 2015, his family life became tabloid fodder in a back-and-forth between his second wife Mary and Adam, his son from a previous marriage. The son and a guardian alleged that Mary Max had depleted his finances and browbeat him. She in turn claimed that they had kept him from her against his will and stolen paintings that belonged to her. Accounts of court appearances described him as frail.

His art had a bright, happy vibe

Those dark allegations contrasted with the relentlessly bright, happy vibe that infused his work. "The colors are strong, sometimes loud, sometimes raw and sometimes harmonious, but always powerful, and the images are always on the side of the peaceful nature,” he said. “I don't discuss in my paintings negative things, I don't dwell on it in my mind and don't dwell on it in my canvasses."

In another interview, he summed it up like this: "I see everything through rainbow eyes."

Although accounts of Max’s career sometimes lament that he was not taken seriously by the art establishment, in fact his work has been featured in dozens of museum exhibitions around the world. New York’s Museum of Modern Art owns seven of his works.

The art for the Beatles’ “Yellow Submarine” is sometimes mistakenly attributed to Max, but the design for the album cover and “Yellow Submarine” movie are officially credited to the late Heinz Edelmann. Max claimed in a 2012 interview he did the original “Yellow Submarine” design before handing it off to Edelmann. But the website for New York’s Park West gallery, a longtime dealer of Max’s art, described Max’s involvement in “Yellow Submarine” as “early consulting work.”

Max was, however, friends with the Beatles and many other celebrities. He also had a deep interest in Eastern spirituality. He brought “Swami” Satchidananda Sariswati to the U.S., and helped him popularize yoga here.

Max’s first marriage to Elizabeth Nance ended in divorce. In addition to his second wife, Mary Max, and his son Adam Cosmo, he is survived by a daughter, Libra Astro.

News.title: Manchester United booed after being dumped out of League Cup by Brighton
News.content:
After a humiliating defeat to Grimsby Town in their previous League Cup campaign, Manchester United found a different way to exit the competition this time around. The jeers heard at the full-time whistle after throwing away a two-goal lead pointed to more worrying times a year on from Blundell Park.

For the first time in half a century, United lost a game at Old Trafford having led 2-0, highlighting the defensive problems Michael Carrick needs to solve after turning results around last season.

“What the f---ing hell was that?” chanted the home fans, in a chant that may have been aimed at the referee but equally applied to United players, who led through Shea Lacey and Mason Mount’s early goals.

Brighton cut through Carrick’s defence several times before staging their comeback with goals from Charalampos Kostoulas, Pascal Gross and Maxim De Cuyper. All three goals will have Carrick and his analysts rewatching the footage in horror at how they conceded.

“I totally understand the feelings of the supporters,” said Carrick. “We have to accept it. I totally accept it. It’s on me ultimately: as a team what we look like, how we play and what results you get. I take that. I’ll take the praise, I’ll take the criticism and the upset.”

Erik ten Hag used the domestic cups to taste success while struggling in the Premier League, but one of those opportunities is now lost to Carrick, who must be careful not to spiral from a poor start to the campaign into crisis. Saturday’s trip to Fulham before the international break now feels like a big game for United and Carrick.

News.title: Spurs finally score... but still lose
News.content:
“But that is why we cannot say it does not work for anyone. There are players who play every three days with no issues. They are very robust, their performances do not change too much. There are other players where the risk is bigger and the performances are different. I have to learn who is ready to play games every three days and who needs a rest so their performance level is not affected. I thought I had it quite clear in my mind with some, but with others, it is new, even for them, because they have not played as many games. We are learning.”

Liverpool were knocked out in the fourth round of this competition last season, losing 3-0 at home against Crystal Palace. Joe Gomez returns to the squad for the hosts tonight after an injury early in pre-season but Giovanni Leoni, Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Federico Chiesa remain out.

Tottenham are still without a league win or goal this season. Their 0-0 draw at home against Everton Saturday means they sit just above the relegation zone. Tottenham overcame Charlton in the second round, convincingly winning 5-1 at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium last month.

“I think we are working well,” Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi said. “We played 30 minutes, 25 minutes very well [against Everton]. In that moment we could score two goals. Then we lost maybe the confidence because we did not score. For sure we have to improve. For sure I have big confidence in my players, they are very good players.

“We have to improve, yes. We can say the coach has responsibility if we do not score, yes, I accept, no problem. We did not win any game so far, yes. We are disappointed, sorry for that. But we have other positive things, like I said we did not [concede goals] in the last two games and the things we have to improve, we start our work. Nothing changed in my project and my idea.”

News.title: England cruise to victory led by ‘absolute freak’ Brook
News.content:
Whatever his returns, there has been an extra focus to Brook’s approach this summer, possibly because he has learnt from a grievous indiscretion in Wellington last winter. While others chase the Indian Premier League, he is totally committed to England, taking his break while that tournament is on and playing every match in all formats for his country.

Brook had come to the crease at the fall of the first wicket and, while it is early days, England appear to have added another arrow to their quiver. They handed a debut to opener Aneurin Donald, with his cap presented in the pre-match huddle by Pietersen, the new “specialist mentor”.

Donald has been selected as an “intent merchant”, charged with going extremely hard from the first over, aping Phil Salt, who is missing with a quad injury. He did what he was asked to do, smearing his first ball for two, then pulling six to leg and hammering four through the offside before the first over was out. Another big shot, off Wellalage, in the second saw him well caught in the deep, but 12 off five had kickstarted the innings.

News.title: Max Dowman-mania could make League Cup hottest ticket in town
News.content:
At this rate, Arsenal supporters will be looking forward to Carabao Cup matches as eagerly as any Premier League or Champions League game, simply because it will be a chance to watch Dowman again. The forward’s age and inexperience means he is still used sparingly in those high-priority competitions. The League Cup, by contrast, may prove to be his domain over the coming months.

Dowman’s double at Portman Road made him just the second 16-year-old to score two goals in a game for a Premier League side. The first was Wayne Rooney, for Everton against Wrexham in 2002.

The two goals underlined why there is so much excitement around Dowman. The first was a demonstration of his prodigious dribbling ability, as he weaved through Ipswich’s defence and buried his shot with the weaker right foot. The second showed his composure: a slotted finish, rolled in with ease.

News.title: UK borrowing costs hit 19-year high as global bond rout intensifies
News.content:
The cost of UK government borrowing hit its highest level since 2007 in a fresh global debt sell-off.

The yield on 10-year gilts, a benchmark for what the Treasury pays to borrow money, rose from 5.37pc to a fresh 19-year high of 5.41pc on Tuesday as rising oil prices risk reigniting inflation.

Mortgage experts have warned that residential and buy-to-let mortgage rates are set to climb towards 5pc, as market turmoil threatens to filter through to household finances.

Short-term debt costs have also jumped, with the yield on two-year UK bonds surpassing 4.9pc for the first time in three years.

The bond chaos came as Andy Haldane, a former Bank of England chief economist, warned that Labour risked becoming “just a traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok videos”.

He told LBC that John Healey’s original plan for a “low drama budget” had been “torpedoed” by higher borrowing costs and “events over the last couple of weeks”.

He said: “I think that [the bond market turmoil] will mean some hard choices next month at the Budget.”

“Few hard choices so far, but one is looming on the horizon, how any hole to the budget headroom is made good on. Is that a question of tax rises, or is it a question of taking the knife to public spending.”

Mr Haldane has been advising Labour since Andy Burnham took power.

It comes as the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of England face pressure to raise interest rates this week to combat rising prices.

Anthony Brinkman, a portfolio manager at Principal Asset Management, said: “The recent gilt market movements seem to be intent on showing central banks they are out of time – the market is expecting action.”

Borrowing costs around the world are rising after a 20pc surge in oil prices so far this month.

Brent crude tipped above $109 a barrel this week after Houthi rebels in Yemen, considered a proxy for Iran’s forces, seized control of a key port in the Red Sea, threatening shipping.

The US Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates on Wednesday in the face of the inflation threat.

As a result, the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds has surged above 5pc for the first time since 2007.

News.title: AI could transform global inequalities or ‘widen the gap’, warns Bill Gates
News.content:
“AI could be a great equaliser, or [it could] widen the gap”, says Mr Gates. “This is not a long-range prediction. It’s a present-tense choice”.

“We can harness AI for good. But it won’t happen by accident. After all, the market is an extraordinary engine of innovation, but a terrible guarantor of equal opportunity.

“With AI, the gap could grow even faster … That is what makes this moment so urgent. Things are changing rapidly, and the window to shape who benefits from AI, and how soon, is short”.

The key issue holding back the deployment of AI in the developing world revolves around the availability of local data and, in turn, the ability for the technology to scale in environments very different from where it is currently being created.

An app that is trained on billions of hours of American English, will struggle at first with British English (see your spell check) but is next to useless if your local language is Swahili or Chichewa.

More profoundly, an AI tool that allows a farmer in Hampshire to control his combine harvester remotely, will offer little to a smallholder in South Sudan who works the land by hand and faces a completely different array of pests, weather conditions and costs.

The same is true for health. “A community health worker in Rwanda examining a baby with a fever faces different questions than a clinician in a well-resourced hospital - and the AI supporting her needs to reflect that”, says Mr Gates.

He adds: “Most of the world is invisible to today’s AI models. These AI systems were trained primarily on what exists on the internet – and the internet reflects a deeply unequal world. More than 90 percent of the data used to train early, large language models came from English-language sources. The communities that stand the most to gain from AI are largely absent from the knowledge base these tools are built on. They are not just underserved. They are not in the picture at all”.

The new investment aims to help correct that. Mark Suzman, CEO of the Gates Foundation, says investments are already being made with companies including Microsoft and Google to build databases of a much wider range of languages, for instance.

Africa alone has more than 2,000 languages, and for AI’s to be effective there they have to understand what and how people actually speak - “their dialects, accents, and slang, too”.

The investments, he says, are being made on the condition that the intelligence and knowledge they accumulate are made freely available for others to use.

Languages for AI “are true public goods, almost definitional public goods. They need to be freely available to everybody. Once they’re created, they are public goods that can be uploaded onto any AI,” said Mr Suzman.

News.title: Reynolds refuses four times to rule out tax raid on state pensioners
News.content:
The Business Secretary refused four times to rule out retirees paying tax on the state pension from next year.

Jonathan Reynolds declined to reassure pensioners that they would not pay income tax on the benefit for the first time, saying it was a question for the Chancellor.

The comments on Tuesday raised concern for millions of retired people expecting to see their state pension surpass £13,000 from April, forcing them to pay income tax.

However, pensions minister Torsten Bell later insisted Labour would not put up taxes on people who rely on the state pension.

It is still unclear how this will be implemented given the complexity of separating the tax arrangements of different groups of pensioners.

The rise under the triple lock guarantee would drag many pensioners into paying income tax for the first time because their state income would surpass the personal allowance of £12,570.

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, said last year that people solely reliant on the state pension would not have to pay the tax.

However, Mr Reynolds was repeatedly asked on BBC Breakfast whether Labour would honour this commitment after the next increase in the state pension in April. He declined to answer four times.

He said: “I’m sorry, that is for the Chancellor and for a Budget.

“The majority of pensioners in this country don’t just rely on the state pensions. Some do, I accept that, but the majority don’t.

“Sometimes when this is looked at, we’re focusing just on the state pension side of this. You’ve got to consider the full range of income retired people in the UK have.”

However Mr Bell, the pensions minister, walked back from Mr Reynolds comments.

He said: “In line with the commitment made at Budget 2025, pensioners who only just exceed the personal allowance will not have the administrative burden of paying small amounts of tax in this Parliament.

“The Chancellor will set out further details on how that commitment will be delivered at the Budget.”

Former pensions minister Sir Steve Webb said only one in 16 pensioners would benefit from this policy.

He said: “Those on the new state pension can expect to see an increase of nearly £500 per year next April.

“But the sting in the tail is that this will take the standard rate of the new state pension above the tax threshold.”

The comments came after official figures on Tuesday indicated the triple lock will rise by 3.9pc from April.

Under the triple lock, the state pension rises each April in line with inflation, average wages or 2.5pc, whichever is highest.

Total pay, including bonuses, rose by 3.9pc in the three months to July, down from 4.2pc in the three months to June.

Pensioners may yet receive a bigger increase if September’s inflation figure is higher than 3.9pc. That will be revealed next month but a higher figure is thought to be unlikely.

Sports.title: Sunderland 1 AZ Alkmaar 0: Enzo Le Fee the hero as Black Cats win on return to Europe after 53-YEAR absence
Sports.content:

ENZO LE FEE wrote his name into Wearside folklore as Sunderland returned to European football with a bang.

The Frenchman had a penalty saved four days earlier against Arsenal. But he was the coolest man in the North East as his spot-kick secured this 1-0 Europa League win over AZ Alkmaar from the spot.



It may not have been spectacular. It still meant everything to the Mackems.

William Hughes, Dennis Tueart, Robert Kerr and Micky Horswill have enjoyed the fame of being the only players in the club’s history to score in Europe for over half a century.



Now Le Fee has ensured it will be his name being spoken about by future generations.

Five years ago this week Sunderland had just hosted Accrington Stanley before travelling to Fleetwood Town in League One.



Now they have trips to Portugal, Poland, Belgium and Italy’s legendary San Siro to come.

It has been doom to boom since Swiss-French billionaire Kyril Louis-Dreyfus bought the club in 2021.

Two promotions in three years and a top seven finish on their Premier League return is the stuff of dreams for long-suffering supporters.

Of course, this is not the Black Cats’ first foray into European competition.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Not many fans that saw the famous 1973 FA Cup win over Leeds United are still around.

Even less can say they were there at Roker Park to see their side face Hungarian outfit Vasas SC in the resulting Uefa Cup Winners’ Cup campaign.

A decision by greedy club chiefs to double ticket prices backfired. Fuming Mackems voted with their feet as under 23,000 watched them win their first-ever Euro game on Wearside.

Knocked out by Sporting Lisbon in the next round, it has taken 53 years for Sunderland to get back.

And nobody wanted to miss out this time. There was not a spare seat in the Stadium of Light for the start of this new adventure.



The sky was lit up first red and then white pre-game by spectacular searchlights, not used since 2003 and long forgotten about.

The players entered to deafening noise and a huge flag of a ship down the Roker End declared: ‘New shores to conquer!’

Moments later you could hear a pin drop as Enzo Le Fee passed straight to Kees Smit, who sent Mexx Meerdink clear only for Robin Roefs to come to the rescue.

AZ Alkmaar are no mugs. Dutch Cup holders, undefeated and sitting second in Eredivisie and Europa Conference League quarter finalists last term.

But it is now 12 games on the spin they have failed to beat English opposition as Sunderland responded to that scare in style.



Le Fee nearly made amends as Jari De Busser parried away his shot up the other end while the Frenchman’s drive back across the box was missed by both Trai Hume and Wilson Isidor.

Kevin Danso, a winner of competition with Tottenham in 2025, had De Busser working again before Le Fee’s first-time shot from Isidor’s cutback smashed off the post.

Sunderland’s French winger was on a mission and smashed another into the side-netting as the half ended all-square.



Smit’s shimmy round Nordi Mukiele and shot past the far post had Mackem hearts in mouths again before the hosts swung back.

Isidor wildly lashed high into the stand before De Busser’s legs denied Trai Hume.

Finally, just after the hour, Sunderland had lift-off.

A counter-attack found man of the match Le Fee, he cut inside Wouter Goes and went to pull the trigger before being clipped by Weslley Patati.

Penalty. Unlike Arsenal’s David Raya, De Busser guessed wrong as Le Fee slotted home to spark wild celebrations.



Mukiele lifted the scorer high into the air with glee. He was furious moments later when his run into the box was abruptly ended by Mateo Chavez’s bodycheck with no penalty this time.

It was backs to the wall late on as Regis Le Bris men clung on to what they had.

Dan Ballard and then Reinildo threw their bodies in front of two fierce strikes before Dutch goalie Roefs brilliantly denied Mexx Meerdink.

Nilson Angulo could have ended all of the agony late on but somehow had a shot blocked on the line by Elijah Dijkstra with the goal gaping.

Fortunately, it did not matter. Sunderland are off and running in Europe.

Sports.title: Man Utd player ratings: Lacey a shining light on dark evening as Heaven and Yoro ripped apart in Carabao Cup KO
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED suffered a humiliating Carabao Cup exit at Old Trafford as Brighton came from two goals down to reach the last 16.

It is the first time in 50 years that United have held a 2-0 lead at Old Trafford and lost the game.



The Red Devils were in dreamland after early goals from Shea Lacey and Mason Mount, before the Seagulls took control and mounted a stunning comeback.

United have not won a domestic cup match since beating Leicester in the FA Cup in February 2025 and again crashed out at first attempt of the Carabao Cup following last season’s horror show at Grimsby.



Michael Carrick is feeling the heat after goals Charalampos Kostoulas, Pascal Gross and Maxim De Cuyper ended one of two potential trophy hopes this season.

Here’s how SunSport’s Katherine Walsh rated the United players from Old Trafford, as Brighton picked up a fifth straight victory in M16...



Karl Darlow – 4

Shipped three goals in an unconvincing club debut. Hardly evoked confidence as he flapped to Kostoulas’ shot.

The back-up goalkeeper started well with several commanding punches but the equaliser would not have gone down well with supporters.

Was less at fault for the other two goals.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Diogo Dalot – 4

After a disaster against City, Dalot’s awful clearance was headed back by Luka Vuskovic in the lead up to 2-2. He hardly stood out before then, which was probably a good thing.



Ayden Heaven – 3

Handed his first minutes since a disappointing showing in the embarrassing 2-0 defeat at Hull, Heaven failed to inspire confidence again.

The 20-year-old was far to casual when he tried to shield a ball out of play only for Matt O’Riley to take advantage of his dallying in the first half.

Leny Yoro – 4

The Frenchman won a first start of the season, but was as shaky as his young centre-back partner before it all resulted in being skinned by Pascal Gross.

Yoro was guilty of wayward passing, poor positional play and weak tackling as United played themselves into trouble after taking a 2-0 lead.

Noussair Mazraoui – 4

The Moroccan should have played himself into the left back position for Fulham on Sunday, given Patrick Dorgu‘s mistake in the lead up to Erling Haaland‘s goal in the derby defeat.



But he was just as unconvincing as the Danish wing back. Torn apart for the third goal.

Andrey Santos – 6

The £48m summer signing started for the first time since the Hull debacle and was better defensively. However the midfielder struggled on the ball at times.

The Belgium skipper was vocal in his captain duties for the rested Bruno Fernandes. Tielemans kept United ticking at times when his teammates were dodgy at the back before the system fell apart.



Mason Mount – 5

The midfielder returned from injury and carried off from where he left off during a strong pre-season with a sweet volley to notch his first goal in nine months.

Tried to lob Jason Steele from 50 yards, which did not go down well with Carrick. Did not offer enough going forward as United’s No10 for the evening.

Shea Lacey – 7

It had to be him. The patient academy graduate provided the feel good story in a fraught week for United as he fired in an opener in the eighth minute of his full club debut.

The 19-year-old kissed the badge in perhaps a pointed message to academy star JJ Gabriel, who asked to leave.

Rashford chased every ball down, but should have done better when he was one-on-one with Steele for a potential leveller.

The £74m striker needed to get hold of the ball more and make it stick. He was, however, starved of service and nobody can knock his workrate.

Not strong enough.

Sports.title: Man Utd 2 Brighton 3: United’s epic 42-YEAR record broken after throwing away half-time lead to be dumped out of cup
Sports.content:
Next

A SHOCKING Carabao Cup exit plunged Manchester United into crisis mode — and ramped up pressure on Michael Carrick.

Their old nemesis did a number on them again as Brighton now boast wins at Old Trafford in five successive seasons.



It was the first time since 1984 – 42 years ago – that United lost a home match when leading at half-time.

They had led at the break on 550 occasions in that time – winning 498, drawing 52 and never losing. Until today.



The result also ended a 50-year run of never losing when leading by two goals at Old Trafford.

And since Sir Alex Ferguson headed upstairs 13 years ago, United had won 143 games and drawn two at their home having been ahead by at least two goals. Then bogey team Brighton rocked up.



And this third-round collapse — having led 2-0 after just ten minutes — leaves head coach Michael Carrick now possibly past a point of no return.

Two defeats from four in the Prem, including Sunday’s derby loss to ten-man City, was bad enough before 15-year-old academy superkid JJ Gabriel notified the club he intended to quit.

But this result smacked of complacency. Carrick made eight changes, with Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven starting together for the first time at centre-half.

Touted as United’s future, they may have to be consigned to the past after this farce.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Rookie full debutant Shea Lacey, 19, gave the hosts a dream start after eight minutes as he lashed an unstoppable shot past Jason Steele at his near post.

The roar was loud enough on a night where some season-ticket holders could not give their tickets away.

And Lacey earned another cheer when he patted the crest and kissed it in front of the old Scoreboard End.

He almost got on the end of the rebound that Mason Mount converted two minutes later as the Red Devils made a flying start.



Marcus Rashford danced into the area, only to have his effort parried by Steele, and Mount volleyed the ball into the net before Lacey could connect.

That marked Mount’s first goal since Wolves away in December.

Carrick would have been pleased not just with United’s breakneck start, but the identity of the scorers.

Midfielder Mount had looked in good nick during pre-season and was poised to start the competitive campaign, until a foot injury against Paris Saint-Germain in early August sidelined him again.

It was Noussair Mazraoui’s turn in the Red Devils’ problem position of left-back, yet he required treatment midway through the first half.



Man Utd ratings vs Brighton: Lacey a shining light on dark evening as Heaven and Yoro ripped apart MANCHESTER UNITED suffered a humiliating Carabao Cup exit at Old Trafford as Brighton came from two goals down to reach the last 16. Nineteen-year-old Harry Amass was instructed to warm up, and briefly returned, only to be sent back down the touchline by Carrick’s assistant Steve Holland. Yet Mazraoui soldiered on.

Brighton, with a tiny following sheltering from the drizzle, did not initially seem enthusiastic about salvaging the tie, until they belatedly realised just how gettable United’s defence was.



Goalkeeping debutant Karl Darlow flapped at a corner while the raw centre-halves Yoro, 20, and 19-year-old Heaven were both guilty of dozy moments on their first start together.

Malick Yalcouye was sprung through for a one-on-one and opened up his body, but he skewed his attempt well wide of Darlow’s left-hand upright.

Pascal Gross, scorer of seven goals against United during his first spell with Brighton, skied a presentable shot into the Stretford End in the 41st minute as the visitors upped their dominance.

A goal is always coming against this Carrick team and Darlow inexplicably stayed near his goal-line as a long hopeful ball bounced into the path of Charalampos Kostoulas to bundle in on the stroke of half-time.

Heaven misjudged the flight of Jaouen Hadjam’s hoik but Darlow seemed stuck in cement.



Rashford was in crowd-pleasing form but is still yet to register his first United goal since December 1, 2024.



Just as Carrick was preparing to send on Kobbie Mainoo, Bryan Mbeumo and Joshua Zirkzee, the sloppy hosts played themselves into more trouble and Gross got his customary goal against them.

After United’s back four dilly-dallied from left to right, Benjamin Sesko was on his heels from Dalot’s panicky clearance.

The ball travelled all the way back to onside German ace Gross, who controlled and slotted in on 65 minutes to leave Old Trafford stunned.

Carrick’s bid to introduce seniority with his triple change did not work.

Four minutes after the Seagulls levelled, Heaven and Mazraoui ended up in each other’s positions, Kostoulas ran to the byline and squared for sub Maxim De Cuyper to scoop the ball in for 3-2.



Even as late as the 82nd minute and with Brighton ahead, Heaven overhit a pass for Youri Tielemans inside his own area to widespread groans from the crowd. United fans immediately booed.

They were not aimed at the officials — or Brighton.

Bruno Fernandes soon arrived for the salvage operation and prodded the ball through for Rashford.

He, too, was denied by Steele, who stretched every sinew to deflect the ball with his right boot.

Rashford’s race was run now and he made way for Matheus Cunha in the 80th minute.

MANCHESTER UNITED fans savagely booed Michael Carrick’s players after surrendering a two-goal lead to Brighton and crashing out from the Carabao Cup.

United scored twice within two minutes – less than ten minutes into the match – but the soaring Seagulls came back to seal a dramatic 3-2 win in the third round at Old Trafford.

SHEA LACEY appeared to aim a cryptic swipe at Manchester United wonderkid JJ Gabriel after the 15-year-old asked to leave Old Trafford.

The highly-rated winger posted a picture of himself wearing United colours on X on Tuesday night alongside a simple red heart emoji.

Sports.title: Do Carabao Cup 3rd round ties go to extra time or straight to penalties if it ends as a draw after 90 minutes?
Sports.content:
Next

ENGLISH football’s biggest sides begin their Carabao Cup campaigns in the third round.

Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City and Aston Villa are all playing in the Champions League this season, which is why they start later in the competition.



CARABAO CUP FOURTH ROUND DRAW LIVE COVERAGE

Some third round ties look too close to call and could still be level at the end of normal time.



If the match ends all square, the question at the front of everyone’s mind is whether there is extra time and penalties.

SunSport brings you all the information you need.

Do Carabao Cup 3rd round ties go to extra time or straight to penalties if it ends as a draw after 90 minutes?

Carabao Cup third round ties go straight to penalties if the score is level after 90 minutes.

Ahead of the 2018/19 season, organisers scrapped extra time to reduce “additional fatigue issues” following a vote by English Football League clubs.

Extra time is used only in the Carabao Cup in the second leg of the semi-finals (if the aggregate score is level) and in the final.

What happened in last year’s Carabao Cup final?

Manchester City are the Carabao Cup holders after they beat Arsenal 2-0 in last year’s final.



Nico O’Reilly scored twice in four second-half minutes to fire his side to Wembley glory.

City’s triumph meant that Pep Guardiola became the first manager to win the League Cup a whopping five times.

The legendary gaffer left his post at the Etihad at the end of last season.

Sports.title: Horror own goal sees Fleetwood shock Sheff Utd and book Arsenal tie
Sports.content:
Rhys Norrington-Davies' horror own goal sent Fleetwood into the last 16 of the Carabao Cup for the first time as the League Two side stunned Championship Sheffield United 1-0 at Highbury.

Norrington-Davies nodded a Danny Andrew cross into his own net from close range in the 57th minute to earn Fleetwood a bumper home draw against Arsenal.

Matt Lawlor's side, unbeaten now in nine games in all competitions, had another Andrew effort ruled out for offside and twice hit the woodwork in a dominant second-half display.

Tom Cannon did put the ball in the net for Chris Wilder's visitors, who lined up with only four starting survivors from last Friday's 1-0 league defeat by Wolves, but an offside flag was raised before the striker slid the ball into the net.

United had started positively and Ollie Arblaster had a goalbound effort blocked after only 36 seconds.

But Mark Helm forced Blades goalkeeper Cooper into a seventh-minute save before former United star Ched Evans put his follow-up header narrowly wide.

Jay Lynch denied Joe Rothwell as the visitors attacked again but Cooper was the busier, saving from Lewis McCann and Crispin McLean.

Helm's dipping right-foot effort from 18 yards grazed the top netting as Fleetwood finished the first half in the ascendancy, and they deserved their break from Norrington-Davies' own goal.

United finally came to life in the last 10 minutes with Lynch brilliantly denying Sydie Peck and Ben Brereton Diaz while Cannon saw a goalbound strike superbly blocked.

But the equaliser proved elusive as the away fans made their displeasure known at the whistle.

Sports.title: Abraham double helps Villa cruise past Coventry into fourth round
Sports.content:
Tammy Abraham scored twice as Aston Villa won 3-1 at Coventry City to book their place in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.

Abraham raced through on goal to give Unai Emery's side an early lead, just their second domestic goal of the season, but it was quickly cancelled out by Victor Torp's stunning free-kick into the top right corner.

The lead was restored just before the break through Ross Barkley's glancing header from Ibrahim Mbaye's corner, with the 18-year-old winger impressing throughout on his first start for the club since his £47m move from Paris Saint-Germain this summer.

Abraham, who had offers to leave before Deadline Day but stayed to fight for his place, helped himself to a second with a simple finish from close range as Villa brushed aside their goalscoring woes to tee up a meeting with Bournemouth in the next round.

When is the fourth round of the Carabao Cup? The fourth round of the Carabao Cup will take place in the week commencing October 26.

The fixture marked the first meeting between the two sides since the 3-2 win for Villa in 2001, which relegated the Sky Blues from the Premier League, and now compounds a tough start to the season for Frank Lampard's side.

They have just one win across their opening five games and will now prepare to face Nottingham Forest, live on Saturday Night Football, in search of their first Premier League goal after returning to the top flight.

Emery: We deserved to win

Aston Villa boss Unai Emery speaking to Sky Sports:

"Very good how the players respond on the field. The plan, they followed it and we got the commitment we needed to recover our way.

"This competition, our objective is a trophy, and it is a way to Europe.

"We wanted to play comfortably and get confidence. More or less, we did it. The experienced players like Tyrone [Mings] and John [McGinn] responded well.

'We have to be better,' says Lampard

Coventry City boss Frank Lampard speaking to Sky Sports:

"They started well, better than us, and they get a goal which is poor.

"Our reaction was great. Getting the equaliser and the stadium felt great, but the two goals - we have to be better.

"The critical game from then was set pieces. You cannot win games at this level against Premier League opposition when you give away two easy ones like that.

"It is frustrating; at 1-1 we were pushing but we lacked conviction. It is not an excuse; it is the reality of the game and we need to be better on.

"We have had a tough start and we need to improve. We have to approach in the right way."

Sports.title: Man Utd collapse from 2-0 up to exit Carabao Cup to Brighton
Sports.content:
Manchester United hit a new low under Michael Carrick as they threw away a two-goal lead to lose 3-2 to Brighton - and exit the Carabao Cup at the first hurdle for a second straight year.

It is the first time in 50 years that United have held a 2-0 lead at Old Trafford and lost the game. They had won 143 out of the 145 previous times they had raced into such an advantage.

Yet it was all going to plan for Carrick's side as they looked to respond to the Manchester derby defeat, as talented teen Shea Lacey and Mason Mount put them in control after 10 minutes.

But United began sleepwalking towards defeat - failing to register another shot on target until the 76th minute - and Brighton, who made six changes for this cup tie, took advantage.

After Charalampos Kostoulas pulled one back on the stroke of half-time after questionable goalkeeping from Karl Darlow, the Seagulls struck twice in four second-half minutes through Pascal Gross and substitute Maxim De Cuyper to stun Old Trafford into silence.

Image: Brighton's Pascal Gross, right, celebrates after scoring his side's second goal

Bruno Fernandes was then brought on as an emergency substitute, before Marcus Rashford missed a one-on-one chance to level the cup tie.

Boos rang out at Old Trafford at full-time, with United fans singing: "What the f****** hell was that?" to their team.

This was not quite the second-round embarrassment at Grimsby that Ruben Amorim suffered last season, but Carrick now has a lot of questions coming his way as one of United's realistic trophy hopes disappears for another year.

WATCH: How Brighton fought back!
