World.title: EU rolls out red carpet to Canada to become its first 'associate member'
World.content:
EU rolls out red carpet to Canada to become its first 'associate member'

toggle caption Jean-Christophe-Verhaegen/AFP

BRUSSELS — The European Union is proposing a new kind of relationship with Canada, one that could make it the EU's first-ever "associate member" — a model that does not currently exist.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made the proposal Wednesday during her annual State of the Union address, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney sitting in the European Parliament as her special guest.

"Dear Mark," von der Leyen said, "Europe and Canada believe in democracy, that power does not belong to the strongest, richest and loudest, but to all of us."

And adding the key phrase to her prepared remarks, seen by NPR, which did not include it, von der Leyen went on: "I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union."

Sponsor Message

The announcement drew a standing ovation from lawmakers and dignitaries in the chamber, as von der Leyen and Carney exchanged kisses on the cheeks.

The moment comes as the EU and Canada look to strengthen their partnership amid increasingly difficult relations with Washington under President Trump.

Von der Leyen stressed that the proposed relationship was not "against anyone." But the very fact she felt she had to emphasize that made the context even more obvious.

For many Europeans, Carney has become a prominent voice for closer cooperation among U.S. partners he calls "middle powers", speaking more forcefully than they themselves dare. At the World Economic Forum in January, Carney warned that "recently, great powers have begun using economic integration as weapons, tariffs as leverage, financial infrastructure as coercion, supply chains as vulnerabilities to be exploited."

"He said it out loud," said Rem Korteweg of the Dutch Clingendael Institute, who says Carney's message has resonated across Europe even as Canada itself has come under intense pressure from the Trump administration.

"All of a sudden Mark Carney is bombarded as almost this honorary hero of what Europeans are actually saying to themselves behind closed doors," Korteweg explained. "Across Europe there is this realization, well, perhaps we need to keep Canada closer to us."

Sponsor Message

But von der Leyen's proposal also raises a fundamental question: What exactly would associate membership mean?

"This is where things become tricky," Korteweg said.

Carney has made clear that Canada does not want to fully integrate with the EU's single market. Canada and the EU already have a free-trade agreement, although Carney is expected to press the 10 EU countries that have not yet ratified it.

The two sides have also been expanding cooperation in security and defense. They signed an agreement deepening security cooperation in 2025, and Canada this year became the only non-European country allowed to participate in the EU's 150-billion-euro fund for joint defense purchases.

So what would a new political status add?

For Jason Wiseman, a Canadian working in the European Parliament, the proposal reflects the opportunity created by Canada's worsening relationship with Washington."The main thing is that we have momentum now," Wiseman said. He sees opportunities for Canada and Europe to build more resilient supply chains and cooperate in strategically important industries.

"Across all of the main sectors that matter the most to the EU and Canada right now, to have the kind of resilient supply chains that would include third-country like-minded partners like Canada," Wiseman says. "Things like critical raw materials. We've got a wealth of small-medium enterprises making mission-critical software…emerging disruptive technologies, especially drones."

The proposal, however, was not preceded by a detailed public negotiation, raising questions inside the EU about how the announcement came about.

Wiseman says he hasn't met anyone in the European Parliament who's against the associate membership idea. But there are reports that some EU governments were furious they were not consulted before von der Leyen's offer, suggesting there may be more resistance in EU capitals whose unanimous support will be needed to create any new partnership.

The proposal is also prompting political questions in Canada, particularly over what an associate membership would actually mean and what closer ties with the EU could require from Canada.

Sponsor Message

Aaron Gasch Burnett, an analyst with the Centre for Strategic Statecraft in Canada, says both Carney's political supporters and opponents have seized on it.

"There's a lot of excitement about what associate membership means when it does not in fact exist … among people who would support closer ties to the EU," Burnett says. "This is also becoming a partisan issue in Canada, with the opposition now saying, 'well, please explain what powers you're willing to give up to Brussels and what you would get in return.'"

On Thursday, Mark Carney will get a chance to do that, when it is his turn to address the European Parliament and explain where he thinks this political romance is headed.

World.title: Congress is under pressure to act on AI — here's what that could look like
World.content:
Congress is under pressure to act on AI — here's what that could look like

toggle caption BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP

This week, some in Congress seemed to discover a new urgency to act on the complicated task of AI regulation after a slew of grim warnings from industry leaders. The only issue: Most of them leave town this week until after the November election.

And they are not just short on time — they're short on consensus on whether regulation is even a task for Congress to tackle. Take, for example, the leaders of the parties in the House of Representatives.

Sponsor Message

Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-La., said Tuesday that "AI is serious. We do need to make sure that it's done safely but let's again let's apply common sense." He then called on the leaders of frontier AI labs to self-regulate.

"They don't need the government to tell them to slow it down. If they want to slow it down, they should," Johnson said. "But we cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI. Okay? Because then we will lose our edge to China and that has serious national security implications."

Democratic Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has taken a different tack.

"It requires decisive congressional action immediately in a manner consistent with what some of the leading AI voices in the country are now saying needs to happen as it relates to slowing things down to protect the health, the safety, and the well-being of the American people," Jeffries said Monday.

The issue also cuts across party lines. Steve Bannon, a key adviser to President Trump, and Vermont progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders spoke separately at an event Tuesday in Washington, calling for the technology to be restricted.

Quick action is unlikely, but lawmakers are not starting from scratch

OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the leading American AI companies, are often at odds on what regulation is necessary. But leaders from both companies recently expressed support for independent watchdogs being able to assess the development process.

Sponsor Message

Though the issue boiled over this week, AI regulation efforts have been simmering on the Hill for years. A bipartisan House task force released a report in 2024. Earlier this year, Representatives Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., released a comprehensive bipartisan proposal.

Those efforts, along with a number of others, were greeted with a shrug by leaders from both parties.

Republicans lack consensus within their on party on the right approach, Democrats appear ready to wait for now, as they anticipate their party will control of one or both chambers of Congress come January.

A fight over who should do the regulating

If and when regulation efforts do, eventually, begin in earnest, one of the key details lawmakers will have to decide is whether states will be allowed to impose their own regulations or whether their statutes will be preempted by federal rules, as desired by the Trump administration.

"The preemption issue is going to be one of the most difficult things that we navigate," Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., said at an Axios event in March. "Companies are not going to be able to have a framework for 50 different states and really survive."

While the GOP has typically supported having states lead on most regulation, House Republican leaders, including Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana, have expressed support for broad bans on states' ability to regulate AI. Many Democrats and states' rights-minded GOP lawmakers oppose them.

"What we've seen over and over again is that while Congress has essentially fiddled under the influence of big tech lobbyists, states like Texas and Florida and Utah, red states in particular," said Daniel Cochrane, "have been leading the charge to hold these companies accountable."

Cochrane, who spoke to NPR in June, is a senior fellow for the Family First Tech initiative at the Institute for Family Studies, a research and advocacy group that works to strengthen marriage, family life and the welfare of children. He worries that a broad federal ban on state AI regulation would result in inaction.

"Almost everyone in Washington agrees AI is transformative and requires some kind of policy response," Nicole Alvarez, a senior tech policy analyst at the Center for American Progress, told NPR this summer.

Sponsor Message

"The real fight," she said, "is what governance looks like."

She worries that, even if a federal framework does move forward, states will be limited if they want to place further restrictions in areas like consumer safety and protections.

While Congress sorts out its approach, Adam Kovacevich, the founder and CEO of center-left tech industry policy group Chamber of Progress worries the patchwork landscape of state regulations is imposing a muddled, de facto national standard.

"Unfortunately we're seeing a creep of blue state laws" on frontier models, fairness and algorithmic discrimination, Kovacevich told NPR in June, "but that's not the best way to regulate AI."

He thinks AI should be regulated largely at the federal level but "there seems to be little energy being spent on actually writing those standards before this year's midterm elections."

It is tough to see beyond the fight about how to regulate to the specifics what rules Congress might agree on. Protections for children appear to be one possible area of common ground.

"Some uses of AI are so structurally dangerous or misaligned with basic social values that they shouldn't just be regulated, they should be prohibited outright," Alvarez said. "For example, banning AI systems from generating child sexual abuse material."

Cochrane points to a proposal from Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., the GUARD Act, which he says "would impose restrictions on AI companions for children and impose criminal liability on anyone who makes a sexually explicit chatbot."

Kovacevich wants to see investments in competitiveness.

"We are in an AI race against China and the Chinese government is viewing AI as an existential race to win," he said. "They're making all sorts of government investments and policies to win that race. We're just not treating the race with the same level of seriousness."

World.title: DOJ charges Russian agents with plotting attacks, including in US
World.content:
DOJ charges Russian agents with plotting attacks, including in the U.S.

toggle caption Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

The Justice Department has brought charges against five suspected Russian intelligence operatives for allegedly plotting attacks against the Kremlin's perceived enemies around the world, including the murder-for-hire of at least one prominent dissident in the U.S.

The indictment, which was unsealed in federal court in Manhattan, says the defendants belong to a network that "is one arm of the Russian Federation's apparatus used to carry out external attacks, including murder, around the world." The network also allegedly conducted operations against civilian and military targets in European allies of Ukraine.

Sponsor Message

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the two countries have been locked in a bloody war since then. Several European allies of Ukraine, including Poland, Germany and Czechia, have accused Russia of conducting sabotage attacks on their soil in recent years. Now, the U.S. is making similar allegations in a criminal indictment against specific, alleged Russian operatives.

"It is our job to stop America's adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil," Attorney General Todd Blanche said. "And that's precisely what we are doing thanks to the work of the FBI and our Justice Department prosecutors."

Court papers identify two of the defendants as Yuri Khrameev, a former colonel in the Russian intelligence service, and his son, Kirill Khrameev, who is a suspected officer in Russia's FSB intelligence agency.

The other defendants are Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, both from Cuba, and Angel Eduardo Castro, who is from Venezuela. Prosecutors say all three men live in Russia.

The five defendants are charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism, while Yuri Khrameev, Suarez and Castro also face one count of murder-for-hire conspiracy. Officials say all of the defendants remain at large.

Venezuelan alleged to seek murder of Russian dissident

The indictment paints a detailed picture of the defendants' alleged efforts since 2024 to recruit and carry out a series of targeted killings and acts of sabotage on behalf of the Russian government.

Sponsor Message

One of the alleged plots took place between July and August 2026, when prosecutors say the network recruited a Venezuelan citizen, identified only as U.S. Resident 1, living in Brooklyn to surveil and murder a prominent Russian dissident in the U.S. The dissident is not named in court papers.

Prosecutors say Castro and Suarez used an encrypted messaging app to communicate with U.S. Resident 1, and gave him two addresses to surveil that were associated with the dissident. They also provided detailed instructions on how to take photos and videos of the locations.

Suarez allegedly stated the addresses were associated with someone they "want to eliminate they want to disappear," and offered $40,000 "for whoever does the work."

U.S. Resident 1 said he was willing to take photos and videos but not commit murder.

The indictment says Suarez then asked U.S. Resident 1 if he knew "someone who wants to do construction," which prosecutors say was code for "carrying out the murder."

Suarez allegedly stated that he was under pressure from his boss to get the job done. He also said that he had a team in Mexico who could do it but that they weren't immediately available.

U.S. citizen allegedly recruited in Lithuania

The indictment also chronicles a separate alleged plot in Europe in 2025 involving efforts to recruit a U.S. citizen to surveil and murder a Kremlin critic believed to be living in Vilnius, Lithuania.

In late June 2025, prosecutors say, the American met with Kirill Khrameev at the Estonia-Russia border, where Khrameev offered to pay the American, who is not named, to take photos of an address in Vilnius.

The American then kept in touch via an encrypted messaging app with Yuri Khrameev, who told him he needed to send photos or videos of the target's residence every two to three days, according to the indictment.

Court papers say Yuri Khrameev told the American that the individual was being targeted for "spreading dirt" about Russia and "telling the media and the common people that the Russians are the aggressors."

The indictment says the American was offered $25,000 to carry out the murder, which Khrameev said could be conducted by "throwing a bottle of gasoline" or "sticking a knife" in the victim, but the American declined, fearing he would easily be caught.

Sponsor Message

Yuri Khrameev then offered him a "simpler job," such as setting fire to a warehouse or electrical substation, according to prosecutors.

"I am interested in all the countries that are helping Ukraine," Khrameev allegedly wrote the American, adding that he was interested in targeting "military facilities and dual-use facilities… located in the countries of the NATO military bloc."

"Serious money for serious work"

"I'm offering serious money for serious work," he allegedly added.

The indictment appears to include details related to some other countries' allegations of Russian sabotage.

It says that Durruthy, one of the Cubans, played a role in coordinating travel and payment for terrorist acts, including in Prague.

The indictment says he transferred more than $1,000 in cryptocurrency to a "criminal associate" and booked hotels in the Czech Republic and in Poland for the associate. The indictment includes a photo pulled from an online account associated with Durruthy that prosecutors say appears to show potential attack sites in the Polish capital.

World.title: Trump signs memorandum to identify and remove Canadian products from U.S. federal procurement
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President ‌Donald Trump ​signed a presidential ​memorandum on ​Wednesday to ⁠identify ⁠Canadian-origin goods ‌in federal ⁠civil government procurement ‌and take steps ​to remove ⁠them, ⁠the ⁠White ⁠House ​said.

The move came a week after Trump banned the import of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and various other products into the U.S. in an escalation of the trade war.

In the memo, Trump directs the U.S. Trade Representative and the Office of Management and Budget to "take steps" to identify items of Canadian origin that could be "removed or made non-available for purchase" from the federal government's procurement system.

The memo does not appear to order an immediate ban on government agencies purchasing Canadian products but could open the door to restrictions in the future.

The White House did not immediately respond to a CBC News query about what value of goods could be affected by the move.

The U.S. government has procured on average about $1.6 billion US worth of Canadian products annually since 2021, says Canada-U.S. trade expert Eric Miller, based on his analysis of published spending data.

Miller, president of Rideau Potomac Strategy Group, says Trump's memo appears to be a reaction to some Canadian provinces putting some limits on U.S. companies bidding on government contracts.

"The U.S. would argue that this is levelling the playing field with the restrictions that Canadian provinces have put on," Miller told CBC News.

WATCH | A lopsided trade war: Can Canada actually win a trade war with the U.S.? | About That | Duration 9:14 How can Canada win a trade war with the U.S. when leverage isn't equal? Andrew Chang explains how Canada is retaliating against massive tariffs levied by a neighbour 13 times its economic size. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

The memorandum also directs the U.S. trade representative to monitor Canada's treatment of U.S. origin goods in Canadian government procurement.

The latest round of U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods took effect just after midnight Tuesday, adding 50 per cent levies to more than 100 products, including specific cheeses, motorboats, all-terrain vehicles (ATVs) and furniture.

WATCH | Canada hit with new tariffs and bans: Trump hits Canada with new tariffs and product import bans | Duration 4:34 U.S. President Donald Trump hit back at Canada's counter-tariffs with stiff new tariffs on billions of dollars in some products, and outright bans on others, including alcohol.

The ongoing trade war ramped up in recent weeks after the U.S. and Canada failed to reach a trade agreement in August.

On Aug. 22, the U.S. followed through on a threat of 50 per cent tariffs on a wide swath of Canadian goods. Canada retaliated with its own tariffs on nearly 700 categories of U.S. goods, which came into effect on Sept. 8.

World.title: Republican senator warns Carney against tightening Canada's links to European Union
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A long-serving Republican senator from a border state is warning Prime Minister Mark Carney against strengthening Canada's economic and political ties to the European Union.

Sen. Susan Collins of Maine — facing a re-election battle in November's midterms in a state highly dependent on cross-border trade — says it's unfortunate that Canada is turning toward the EU in response to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs.

"That doesn't help rebuild the good relationship that we once had and that I want us to have again," Collins told CBC News correspondent Katie Simpson at the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday.

In a speech earlier Wednesday in Strasbourg, France, with Carney present, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Europe wants to open the door for Canada to become an "associate member" of the EU.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: Is Canada more like Europe than the United States? What’s at stake for you if Canada builds closer relations with the EU?

Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show

(It's not clear what that would mean, as "associate member" is not currently a legal designation in the EU. Although Canada's ambassador to the EU says the two sides are "a ways away" from formalizing anything, Carney has said he wants a "unique alliance" with Europe.)

Collins says she believes Canada deepening its ties with Europe could make it harder for the Carney government to reach a deal with the Trump administration to end the escalating trade war.

"I believe that both Canada and the United States should return to the bargaining table. I do not support this tariff war," Collins said.

WATCH | What Europe's top official has in mind for Canada: EU chief opens door to Canada becoming associate member | Duration 4:41 European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed opening a path for Canada to become the European Union's first associate member, a status that doesn't currently exist.

Collins has long tried to distance herself from Trump's tariff policies, in part because Canada accounts for roughly two-thirds of Maine's imports and about 40 per cent of its exports.

She claimed credit last week when the Trump administration announced it was exempting cement and road salt — two products Maine imports from Canada in significant quantities — from its list of Canadian goods facing new tariffs of 50 per cent.

'Not in the interest of our country'

Collins's comments come amid growing signs of unease among some Republicans in the U.S. Congress over Trump's trade tactics toward Canada, particularly as the Nov. 3 midterm elections grow nearer.

The Republicans hold narrow majorities in both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate and stand to lose control of Congress if the Democrats can flip a handful of districts or states.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana who has occasionally broken with Trump on policies, told CBC News he's opposed to the trade war.

"I think it is wrong to have a trade war with Canada. It is not in the interest of our country to have a trade war with Canada," Cassidy said.

U.S. Sen. Chris Coons, a Democrat from Delaware is pictured at the U.S. Capitol on May 19. Coons told CBC News on Wednesday that he is organizing a 'bipartisan trip to Canada' for his fellow lawmakers. (J. Scott Applewhite/The Associated Press)

Meanwhile, Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware says it will be "a tall order" to halt Trump's trade war on Canada even if the Democrats win the midterms.

"We won't be able to reverse his direction immediately, but at least with a new majority in Congress, should we be successful in the November elections, Canadians will begin to recognize their neighbours again," Coons told CBC News.

Coons says he has spoken with "personal friends" in Carney's cabinet about action that he and other members of Congress could take to win back allies in Canada.

He says he's working on "a bipartisan trip to Canada by American lawmakers to say, we hear you, we get it, we're acting."

Coons declined to say who in the Canadian cabinet he was speaking with, and his office had no further details about which lawmakers are interested in the trip or when it's likely to happen.

His initiative is part of a movement among Democrats to try to seize on the concerns of many Americans that Trump's tariffs are driving up the cost of living, which polls suggest is a top issue in the midterms.

This week, Senate Democrats formally introduced a bill that seeks to repeal and refund all tariffs the Trump administration has levied under Section 338 of the Tariff Act, including the 50 per cent duties imposed on Canadian products in August.

The bill, first tabled in the House by congressman Brad Schneider of Illinois, is called the BAD DEAL Act, an acronym for Banning Antiquated Duties and Delivering Equitable American Levies.

What's not clear is whether any such Democrat bill has any chance of becoming law with Trump in the White House for another two-plus years.

Even if the Democrats win control of both the House and the Senate, the U.S. president holds veto power over legislation unless it's approved by a two-thirds majority of both houses.

World.title: U.S. Federal Reserve raises interest rates for 1st time in 3 years
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate Wednesday for the first time since 2023 in an effort to quell stubbornly high inflation, a move that could spur a sharp response from the White House.

The quarter-point increase lifts the Fed's key rate to about 3.9 per cent and, over time, could result in higher borrowing costs for American mortgages, auto loans, and credit cards. In a set of quarterly projections, the Fed also signalled that its rate-setting committee expects to hike rates a second time later this year, to 4.1 per cent.

"Today's policy action will support a timelier return" to the central bank's two per cent inflation goal, the Fed said in a statement.

The move comes as Americans are already struggling with high costs for groceries, gas and housing. Affordability has taken on a leading role in the upcoming midterm elections, just seven weeks away.

In a press conference following the Fed's announcement, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that while the job market remains resilient, inflation has stubbornly remained above the Fed two per cent target for years.

"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," Warsh said.

The rate hike is a surprising turnaround for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who was appointed by U.S. President Donald Trump and took over the top job in May. While under consideration by Trump last year, Warsh often suggested the Fed could reduce its key rate, echoing the president's call for lower borrowing costs.

And in April, when Warsh's nomination was under consideration by the Senate Banking Committee, Trump said in a television interview that he would be disappointed if Warsh didn't cut rates. On the same day, however, Warsh told the committee he had not promised Trump he would cut rates and said he would be "an independent actor" as Fed chair.

WATCH | Will Bessent's bond market intervention make U.S. inflation worse?: Will Bessent's bond market intervention make U.S. inflation worse? | About That | Duration 4:38 U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's recent intervention in the bond market is setting off alarm bells for many investors and analysts. Avneet Dhillon breaks down concerns that Bessent’s attempt to calm the markets and decrease the cost of borrowing may actually worsen inflation. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Yet the ongoing disruptions from the Iran war, which have pushed up average gas prices more than seven per cent from just a month ago, threaten to spread through the economy and keep broader inflation stubbornly high. An inflation report last week showed core prices, which exclude food and energy, accelerated slightly in August.

According to the Fed's preferred measure, inflation was 3.7 per cent in July compared with a year earlier.

Earlier Wednesday, the government said retail sales jumped 1.2 per cent in August from the previous month, a sign consumers are still spending at healthy levels despite sentiment surveys indicating Americans remain gloomy about the economy. Strong spending is a sign that interest rates at current levels aren't necessarily restricting the economy enough to cool inflation.

"While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient," the Fed said, likely referring to ongoing consumer spending and strong investment in AI data centres by large technology companies.

Kevin Hassett, Trump's top economic adviser, was asked in an interview with Fox News on Sunday how Trump might react to a rate hike.

"I'm sure he's not going to be super happy about it, but he will defend the independence of Kevin Warsh above all," Hassett said.

More hikes are also possible. Wall Street investors have forecast three hikes in total, with additional increases in December and March.

WATCH | Why inflation is still a problem: Inflation is still a problem | Mind Your Business | Duration 2:03 Statistics Canada data published Monday shows the annual inflation rate edged up to 3.2 per cent in May — the sharpest increase in more than two years. CBC’s senior business correspondent Peter Armstrong explains what’s happening and where prices could go next.

Bank of Canada not facing same pressure: economist

The rate hike south of the border doesn't necessarily signal similar moves in Canada any time soon, according to economists.

The Canadian and U.S. central banks sometimes change interest rates in similar ways because the two economies tend to face the same challenges, explains Paul Beaudry, a professor at UBC's Vancouver School of Economics and a former deputy governor at the Bank of Canada.

Right now, Canada is also facing rising inflation driven by rising energy prices because of the war in Iran. The pace of inflation held steady at three per cent in August — above the Bank of Canada's two per cent target.

But Beaudry says the inflation problem in the U.S. is worse. Core measures of inflation that strip out volatile items like energy and food are at about 2.4 per cent in the U.S., compared with closer to two per cent in Canada.

"There's more inflation underlying in the U.S. So the U.S. has more to do to try to bring it back … to two per cent," Beaudry said.

Canada's economy is also weaker by comparison, Beaudry points out, partly because tariffs and higher unemployment. All things considered, that means Canada doesn't face the same pressure to raise rates.

A recent RBC Economics forecast update made the same case, saying Canada and the U.S. were both facing inflation pressures and rising bond yields, but were "entering these shocks from different starting points."

For that reason, they predicted the U.S. would raise rates in September but does not expect the Bank of Canada to raise rates until 2027.

World.title: Diver injured in great white shark attack off Quebec's Gaspé coast
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A diver was transported to hospital after being injured by a great white shark in Percé, Que., in the province’s Gaspé region.

According to the Canadian Coast Guard, the incident occurred shortly before 10:30 a.m. on Wednesday.

“Emergency response measures were initiated immediately,” Plongée Percé, a commercial diving firm, said in a Facebook post Wednesday.

“The individual involved received first aid on site before being quickly transported to hospital for further evaluation. We have confirmation that their life is not in danger.”

The Canadian Coast Guard confirms the victim was aboard the vessel Yoda, a Canadian Coast Guard Auxiliary dive boat. As of Wednesday afternoon, the organization was unable to confirm the nature of the victim’s injuries.

On Facebook, Plongée Percé thanked those who helped with the rescue and said it was suspending diving activities for the rest of the season.

Increase in great white sightings

Over the summer, great white shark sightings became more frequent in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and off the coasts of the Gaspé Peninsula and the Magdalen Islands.

Four of these sharks — Webster, Ernst, Bella and Nori — are being tracked by Ocearch, a global non-profit organization that helps scientists study sharks. Nori was spotted south of Anticosti Island, while Ernst and Bella are swimming northeast of the Magdalen Islands.

The organization told CBC News in August that the sighting of Webster off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador was a sign of a healing ocean. Webster is a 12-foot shark weighing just over 1,000 pounds.

Ocearch founder Chris Fischer said the population of great white sharks was nearly decimated from the 1970s to the 1990s. He said only around nine per cent of the global population remained before efforts were made to protect the remaining population.

Having sharks in the region is a good sign for local fisheries, he said, as sharks instinctively put pressure on seals and ultimately protect fish stocks.

Caroline Miri, a marine biologist with Fisheries and Oceans Canada, said sharks play a key role at the top of the marine food chain.

“They're very important to the health and stability of our oceans and marine ecosystems because these sharks help keep in check some populations of invasive species, and they also control competing fish species lower down on the food chain,” Miri said.

Fischer said Ocearch has tagged around 115 sharks across the Atlantic, from Florida to Newfoundland and Labrador.

According to the St. Lawrence Shark Observatory, the recent increase in sightings of great white sharks in the gulf is mainly due to better documentation and a recovery of the species, which was considered endangered in Canadian waters.

According to the Canadian Shark Attack Registry, 15 confirmed shark-related incidents have been recorded in Canada over more than 330 years.

World.title: Diana Fox Carney appointed as Canada's ocean envoy, chair of Our Ocean Conference
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Diana Fox Carney — Prime Minister Mark Carney's wife — is stepping into an unpaid role focused on ocean conservation.

As the country's ocean envoy, Fox Carney will "advance Canada's leadership by connecting ocean conservation, climate action, Indigenous leadership, economic resilience and maritime security," according to a news release.

Fox Carney will also chair the 12th annual Our Ocean Conference, an international gathering that convenes governments, organizations and academics to address modern ocean issues.

The conference will take place in Halifax next year.

"Canada has an opportunity to showcase its leadership in ocean conservation, sustainable fisheries, ocean science and Indigenous-led stewardship" at the 2027 conference, Minister of Fisheries Joanne Thompson said in a statement.

WATCH | Halifax hosting Our Ocean Conference in 2027: Ocean issues will get global attention in Halifax in 2027 | Duration 2:21 Atlantic Canada will play host to the Our Ocean Conference in 2027, which will explore issues of environment, economy and culture — with an eye to protecting 30 per cent of the world’s oceans by 2030. The CBC’s Leila Beaudoin reports.

"I look forward to working with Diana Fox Carney on this important conference for Canada."

The announcement said the upcoming conference is an important step toward Ottawa's commitment to protect 30 per cent of Canada's marine and coastal areas by 2030.

"The conference will provide an opportunity to deepen co-operation, share knowledge and experience and secure commitments to ensure healthy and sustainable oceans for future generations," Fox Carney said in a statement.

Career in economics, environment

Until now, Fox Carney's role largely remained on the periphery of her husband's first 18 months as Canada's 24th prime minister.

Having originally drawn Carney's attention by skating circles around her hockey opponents at the University of Oxford — where they were both students and where the now prime minister played goalie on the men's team — Fox Carney has built a notable career as an economist and environmentalist in her own right.

Fox Carney holds master's degrees in agricultural economics from Oxford and international relations from the University of Pennsylvania.

Throughout her career, Fox Carney has served on the boards of a number of not-for-profit organizations and has held senior roles at prominent think-tanks in both Canada and the U.K., championing environmental issues and income equality among other issues.

In 2013, she drew controversy over a paper she contributed to the Canada 2020 think-tank looking to reignite discussions on carbon pricing in Canada.

WATCH | Diana Fox Carney on CBC's Power & Politics in 2013: Putting a price on carbon | Duration 13:03 Experts debate why carbon tax is such a polarized political topic

In 2021, Fox Carney started a new role as senior adviser at the Eurasia Group, a political research and consulting firm which offers advice to businesses and politicians around the world.

World.title: Gordie Howe bridge vehicle traffic tops 340,000 in first full month of operation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Traffic at the new Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Windsor, Ont., and Detroit topped 340,000 in its first full month of operation, according to new data.

There were 343,507 crossings at the bridge in August, the first full month it was open, per fresh figures from the Bridge and Tunnel Operators Association.

It was nearly the same as traffic at the nearby Ambassador Bridge, which saw 345,445 crossings last month.

But the composition of the traffic on the competing spans was different. The majority of crossings at the Gordie Howe bridge were passenger vehicles: Nearly 270,000 vs. roughly 74,000 trucks.

At the Ambassador, truck traffic was around 150,000, compared to 196,000 passenger cars.

Jason Miller, a supply chain management professor at Michigan State University, says he believes many trucking companies have toll price contracts with the Ambassador Bridge.

"So what's happening is they are probably locked in for this year," he told Windsor Morning on Wednesday. "So it does not make as much sense for them to shift trucks over to Gordie Howe until they would have some type of renegotiated contract or they themselves have a contractual price with Gordie Howe."

LISTEN | Gordie Howe bridge attracts more cars than trucks in first full month of operation: Windsor Morning 6:52 Gordie Howe Bridge attracts more cars than trucks in first full month of operation Gordie Howe Bridge traffic is already neck and neck with the Ambassador.We take a look at the numbers for August with a supply chain expert next.

The Windsor-Detroit Tunnel still had the highest volume of passenger vehicles, with approximately 280,000 crossings in August.

StatsCan data offers different look

Recently released numbers from Statistics Canada offer a more detailed look at the origin of the people crossing the various ports of entry in the Windsor-Detroit corridor.

"In August, the Gordie Howe International Bridge was used for 134,900 Canadian-resident return trips from the United States by automobile, 56.7 per cent of which were same-day," the federal agency said Friday. "It was also used as a port of entry for 101,000 US-resident trips to Canada by automobile, 52.2 per cent of which were same-day.

Statistics Canada graph showing August 2026 crossing data for ports of entry in the Windsor-Detroit corridor. (Statistics Canada)

"During the same period, 348,000 Canadian and US residents entered Canada by automobile at Windsor's Ambassador Bridge and the Windsor-Detroit Tunnel, down 35.4 per cent from August 2025."

The agency also said that 34,800 commercial transport trucks entered Canada using the Gordie Howe Bridge last month.

"Commercial transport truck entries at Windsor's other ports increased by 0.4 per cent from the same period one year earlier to total 87,400," it added.

The Ambassador Bridge, seen here on July 28, 2026, the day after the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge opened, ending nearly a century of private monopoly over bridge traffic between Windsor, Ont., and Detroit. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Miller said traffic volumes at the three crossings are likely to shift in the months ahead as the "novelty effect" of taking the brand new Gordie Howe bridge wears off.

In any case, he said the traffic volumes at the new span being nearly as high as those at the Ambassador Bridge show "the need for that second crossing."

"What I'm really curious to see is if there's any information [to] come out about the wait times at either bridge, because that that to me is the most important thing beyond just the crossings, is just that smoother flow of commerce," he added.

World.title: These documentarians got a standing ovation in Venice, but their fellow Israelis are furious
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On the streets of Jerusalem, there's no debating whether the directors of the documentary film NAZA, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, are truth-tellers or traitors.

They should be "in jail for betraying the country, betraying the army, betraying Jewish [people] all over the world," said Revital Hershko.

Hershko, like many in Israel, has been watching media coverage about the film, which got a special jury prize and a 25-minute standing ovation when it premiered at the Venice International Film Festival last week.

Over roughly an hour and a half, NAZA details Israeli war tactics used in Gaza, including AI systems that, by design, target wanted individuals in civilian spaces, such as apartment buildings, leading to the deaths of average Palestinians.

Abraham and Szor are Israeli, prompting many inside Israel to label them as lying traitors even before they had seen the film.

"I think they make a very bad damage to our country," said Dalia Shemtov, a resident of Netanya who was out with friends in Jerusalem when she overheard CBC News asking locals about the film and what they've heard.

"It's not true what they said. They lie. All the soldiers, they didn't do anything."

While many of the people CBC spoke with are furious about the film, no one had seen it, since it's still only on the festival circuit.

WATCH | Uproar in Israel: Why the film NAZA is causing uproar in Israel | Duration 2:00 A documentary that premiered at the Venice film festival is facing intense scrutiny in Israel, with calls to strip its filmmakers of their citizenships. NAZA examines alleged IDF targeting strategies, including the use of AI systems to identify locations for strikes, sometimes with hundreds of civilians inside.

Producers vow to 'robustly defend' filmmakers

It's grabbing headlines because of the people featured — not Palestinians talking about the tens of thousands of people killed in Gaza after nearly three years of Israel's war with Hamas, but because of 24 Israeli military and intelligence personnel.

They describe, albeit anonymously, how attacks are approved, and their statements counter official lines coming from the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) that it goes to great lengths to reduce the number of civilian casualties.

The IDF has rejected the film's allegations, saying because only anonymous sources are used there is no way to verify if they have had any direct knowledge of Israeli military operations.

It has also labelled one claim from the trailer as "completely false" — in which a man says he was aware of approval for an airstrike to kill 500 people. Although he does say he does not know exactly how many died because there was no official count.

Lt.-Gen Eyal Zamir, the IDF's chief of general staff, on Monday instructed military lawyers to explore legal options against the filmmakers.

Palestinians pray over bodies in a mass grave, in Khan Younis, Gaza, on Nov. 22, 2023. Israel says it goes to great lengths to reduce the number of civilian casualties in its war with Hamas, which has killed more than 73,000 people in Gaza, according to officials there. (Mohammed Dahman/The Associated Press)

The film was produced by the British newspaper the Guardian, which in a statement said it "will robustly defend" NAZA and its team "from any attacks or attempts at censorship."

Abraham says he and Szor felt a responsibility as Israelis to use their position and abilities to bring insider testimony to light.

"There is a direct correlation between the silence or between the denial of the crimes and their ability to persist,” he said at a news event in Venice.

Fellow Israeli filmmaker Uri Rosenwaks has created an online petition in support of the film, calling on those "still fighting for freedom of expression" to sign.

Netanyahu weighs in

But the criticisms keep coming. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a video released by his Likud Party, called the film "shocking" and said it's "intolerable" that Israel must "fight antisemitic incitement" both globally and within.

Eliya Cohen, who was held hostage in Gaza for 505 days, is escorted by Hamas militants upon his release, in Nuseirat, Gaza, on Feb. 22, 2025. (Ramadan Abed/Reuters)

And a man who was held captive in Gaza for 505 days said on Instagram: "I'm angry on a level I can't describe."

Eliya Cohen was among the 251 people kidnapped in the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, when militants crossed into Israel — killing 1,200 Israelis and foreign workers and igniting Israel's war on Hamas, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza, according to officials there.

In his video, translated for CBC News, Cohen says he wants to see pictures of Abraham and Szor posted outside and "across every possible media platform, so that when they walk down the street … they should feel ashamed."

North American audiences will get to reach their own conclusions when NAZA plays at the New York Film Festival, which begins Sept. 25.

World.title: L.A. driver arrested on murder charges after crashing SUV into bus, followed by fatal helicopter crash
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A news helicopter crashed in a Los Angeles neighbourhood on Tuesday and burst into flames, killing at least three people. Reporters were covering the fatal collision of an SUV and a city bus, officials and the news outlet said.

A motorist was arrested on murder charges after authorities say she slammed her SUV into a city bus in Los Angeles, killing at least two people in that incident and injuring six others in a prelude to a second deadly tragedy: the fiery crash of a TV news helicopter that was covering the collision.

Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, of Simi Valley, was arrested Monday night and is being held at a Los Angeles jail with bail set at $4 million US, police said. The case is being forwarded to the district attorney's office, which will decide whether to file the charges in court or pursue different ones.

Information on a lawyer who could speak on her behalf was not immediately available.

The helicopter, which was used by NBC and Telemundo, crashed about two hours after police say Rios drove her 2004 Ford Expedition the wrong way down a busy avenue, ran a red light and struck a vehicle before hitting the bus. One passenger was fully ejected from the bus and another was partially ejected, police said.

Flowers are placed at the scene of the news helicopter crash in L.A. Wednesday. (Ethan Swope/The Associated Press)

News crew killed

Colleen Williams, an NBC4 Los Angeles anchor, confirmed during live broadcasts that two people on board the chopper were killed when the helicopter went down. At least one other person was killed on the ground, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department said.

"We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, process it," Williams said, her voice shaking with emotion. Moments later the coverage cut off.

Williams and the station's website identified those killed aboard the helicopter as Eliana Moreno, a familiar voice for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 during the station's aerial coverage, and pilot George Marciniw. Both were employees of Angel City Air, which operated the chopper.

This still image provided by KABC-TV shows the scene of the helicopter crash. (KABC-TV/The Associated Press)

The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating the helicopter crash and said Wednesday that video from around the crash scene and from on board will be crucial parts of its work.

"The video that was actually taken while the reporter was doing a live coverage," NTSB investigator Fabian Salazar told reporters at a briefing. "That video is probably the most important evidence that we have discovered so far."

Salazar said sounds heard on that video were consistent with the helicopter's engine changing speed, as well as what he said were likely advisory tones for the pilot.

Moreno, born in Orange County, joined the Angel City Air helicopter team in 2010, the same year she earned a broadcast journalism and political science degree from Chapman University. She reported for several Southern California news outlets and began flying with Marciniw in 2023, the NBC4 website said.

Marciniw grew up in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School in 1974.

"Losing five Angelenos is very painful," Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said. "And I know this community of Chatsworth, hit hard, will be grieving for some time."

At least four cars and two storage containers on the ground burned after the helicopter caught fire, which was quickly put out, according to officials.

"The helicopter itself, it's pretty well destroyed," fire spokesperson Capt. Branden Silverman said.

Two people were brought to a hospital, said Rico A. Gross, a fire department battalion chief. Their conditions were not immediately released.

NBC4 and Telemundo 52 Los Angeles said in a statement they "are deeply saddened" and extended "heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives."

California Gov. Gavin Newsom thanked the emergency crews responding to both crashes and said in a post on X that "our hearts are with the victims and families."

The helicopter crashed in the same Los Angeles neighbourhood where news crews were covering a bus crash that killed two people and injured six. (Ronaldo Bolanos /Los Angeles Times/Getty Images)

The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said personnel will arrive Wednesday to begin an investigation into the cause of the helicopter crash.

There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the U.S. since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news accounts.

Some have occurred during live broadcasts, including a midair collision of helicopters in Phoenix in 2007, and a deadly accident involving a Seattle news helicopter in 2000.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: Colombia’s statistics chief sacked for claiming Petro did not manipulate statistics
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked his statistics chief because he claimed he found no anomalies in labor statistics presented by the administration of former President Gustavo Petro.

In a press statement, De la Espriella’s press secretary said that DANE director Ricardo Valencia was sacked for claiming “that he had not found any anomalies in the DANE indicators for the month of July, figures compiled during the final month of the previous administration.”

Valencia made that claim “without any in-depth audits having been conducted beforehand,” according to the press secretary.

It is essential for the National Government to conduct a rigorous review of the information received and to ensure that the data on which strategic decisions for the country are based fully reflect the economic and social reality of Colombians. President’s Office

The former DANE director was sacked days after the President’s Office canceled another statistics press conference that are common because of the agency’s regular updates on the state of the Colombian economy

July’s labor statistics confirmed claims by the previous government that unemployment dropped to record lows after Petro raised the minimum wage.

De la Espriella has insisted that the country’s economy is in crisis contrary to evidence, which indicated Petro increased economic growth in his last half year in office.

World.title: Colombia’s social organizations and labor unions announce national strike in November
World.content:
Some 1,500 representatives of social organizations and labor unions agreed to begin organizing an anti-government national strike that should take place throughout Colombia either on November 11 or on November 20.

The organizations agreed to the mass mobilization during the National Gathering for the Defense of Life, Dignity, Democracy, Peace, Sovereignty, and Social Reforms that had been organized by labor unions in the capital Bogota.

The first and fundamental decision of the Meeting is to declare the most radical opposition to the illegitimate government of Abelardo de la Espriella because of the course it has imposed on the country—one of subordination to the interests of U.S. imperialism and alignment with the agenda of the international far right—which constitutes a direct threat to national sovereignty, democracy, and the rights won by the Colombian people, and an undeniable shift toward fascism. Social organizations and labor unions

In a statement, the organizations said that the national strike will be preceded by regional protests on October 10 and 14 that will seek to generate momentum for the national strike.

Indigenous organizations will additionally organize a Day of Indigenous, Afro and Popular Resistance on October 12.

A final date for the national strike has yet to be defined.

The organizations decided to call a strike to protest the government’s security and defense policy, the ending of peace processes with illegal armed groups and in defense of social reforms that had been implemented by former President Gustavo Petro.

The protests additionally seek to express solidarity with the people of Palestine, western Sahara, Iran, Bolivia and Venezuela, and reject US imperialism in the Americas.

We must categorically reject the interference of U.S. government officials in the formulation of domestic policies under the guise of so-called friendly aid, which in reality masks the ambition to intensify overexploitation, extractivism, territorial control, and the presence of foreign troops on our soil. Social organizations and labor unions

The organizations agreed to “prepare, through the most intense and massive agitation and propaganda campaign, a national strike.”

World.title: Judge suspends Colombia’s aerial fumigation pilot
World.content:
A Putumayo from the southern Putumayo province suspended the government’s announced resumption of the aerial spraying of coca, ordering information that would allow “a sufficiently informed decision on the merits.”

Earlier this week, the National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine, “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

The National Police subsequently said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo, a province inside the Amazon forest.

These announcements triggered a local foundation to sue the administration, claiming that the plans to do a pilot were in violation of the 2015 ban on aerial fumigation and threatened both locals and the environment.

The judge agreed and ordered the administration of President Abelardo de la Espriella to provide information on the environmental and health risk involved in the aerial spraying with glufosinate ammonium.

The potential implementation of the pilot plan before gathering and analyzing the studies, documents, and technical evidence cited by the administration itself as the basis for the decision could render the requested constitutional protection ineffective and jeopardize the possibility of reaching a sufficiently informed decision on the merits; Indeed, the combination of the announced imminence of the measure, the current lack of essential information needed to understand its territorial, social, and environmental scope, and the particular ecological sensitivity of the department of Putumayo necessitates preventive action aimed at preserving the effectiveness of this constitutional action. Putumayo court

The suspension of the aerial spraying comes days after De la Espriella promised US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he would resume aerial fumigation, a notoriously ineffective way to get rid of coca.

World.title: Colombia announces new aerial fumigation pilot program
World.content:
Colombia’s National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine.

In a resolution, the CNE ordered “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

In a public statement, the National Police’s counternarcotics unit said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo and would not affect indigenous and afro-descendant communities, who would need to be asked permission.

The exclusion of environmental protection zones and protected areas, zones associated with bodies of water, rivers, and other environmentally sensitive areas is contemplated, as well as those territories that, in accordance with current regulations and the corresponding technical studies, must be excluded. National Police Counternarcotics

The purpose of the pilot program is to “evaluate the effectiveness of aerial spraying, as well as its application under the established technical and operational conditions, said the police.

The police stressed that “this experimental phase does not constitute the resumption, adoption, or definitive authorization of a widespread or nationwide aerial spraying program,” which was banned by the Constitutional Court in 2015.

In order to resume aerial fumigation, health and environmental authorities must sign off on the program and the police would only be allowed to use airplanes with the approval of the court and local communities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella vowed to resume aerial spraying more than 330,000 hectares while on campaign and after taking office last month as part of his hardline approach to organized crime.

Former President Ivan Duque also vowed to resume aerial spraying, but failed to comply with the norms established by the court.

World.title: Court orders Colombia’s government to remove images of slain “narcoterrorists”
World.content:
A Bogota judge ordered Colombia’s government to remove images and videos of President Abelardo de la Espriella walking through the remains of slain suspected guerrillas from its social media accounts.

The judge also ordered the government to remove images and videos of the body bags containing the lifeless remains of four members of organized crime group ACSN who were killed in La Guajira.

According to the judge, the images could be harmful to minors.

The decision was celebrated by congressman Santiago Osorio (Green Alliance), who sued the government over the controversial social media posts.

The State and the National Government cannot engage in a contest with crime to see which of the two is the most cruel; in this regard, the Office of the President of the Republic, Mr. Abelardo de la Espriella, were ordered to promptly remove images that may have reached the cell phones of children across the country, showing a state displaying corpses as trophies. Congressman Santiago Osorio

Th publications were previously rejected by the Ombudsman’s Office, whose director, Iris Marin, urged the government not to “compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power.”

In the first video, De la Espriella and Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora walked through rows of body bags, displaying the remains of 23 alleged members of FARC dissident organizations EMC who were killed in the southern Guaviare province.

Among those killed in Operation Azarias were two minor victims of forced recruitment by the guerrillas.

The videos sought to promote the government’s hardline security policy, which vows to kill “narcoterrorists” who refuse to surrender.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”

De la Espriella said that as part of the “Barranquilla Agreements,” he asked the US for support for his hardline security policy.

We have proposed to the government—and today I reiterated this proposal to the secretary—the 21st-Century Patriot Plan to modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president promised to “start spraying, we are going to target the laboratories, the precursors, the trafficking routes, the drug trafficking kingpins, the armed narco-terrorist organizations—we are going after the money launderers, their criminal assets, and those international networks that pose a grave danger not only to the hemisphere but also to humanity.”

Rubio did not openly commit any US support other than the memorandums of understanding.

The unbinding agreements were part of Rubio’s wish list as the US seeks new sources for rare earths and miners that can be processed outside of China, which the US Government sees as its rival.

With the nuclear energy agenda, Colombia seeks to “strengthen its capacities” with US support. Both governments “reaffirm their commitment to international development and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.”

In order to create policy regarding the memorandums, De la Espriella would need congressional support, which he has yet to seek openly.

World.title: De la Espriella lifts Colombia’s 10-year gun ban
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella lifted a gun ban that had been in place since 2015.

According to De la Espriella, the decision seeks to give “good citizens” a way to defend themselves against “criminals.”

“For years, law-abiding citizens were restricted, while criminals continued to arm themselves to the teeth illegally. That has to change,” said the president on social media platform X.

99.9% of crimes committed with weapons are committed with unlicensed, illegal weapons. Anything said beyond the mathematics is just opinion. Mathematics is an exact science. So I am pleased to sign this decree. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president said that those who want to carry guns legally must comply with strict regulations and can’t have criminal records.

The ban reactivates previously approved gun licenses and allows citizens older than 25 to purchase approved hand guns from Colombia’s State military industry.

In order to be given a license, a potential gun owner must undergo fitness tests and convince the military authority that his position in society merits a firearm.

The decision has long been awaited by conservative and far-right elements in society, who have claimed that the gun ban made them sitting ducks for extortionists, particularly in the countryside.

Experts consulted by newspaper El Colombiano warned that lifting the gun ban could increase deadly violence, particularly considering Colombia’s violent history and evidence obtained in countries where guns are legal.

“There is no evidence showing that these countries have seen a decrease in theft, extortion, and threats following these measures,” said the director of the Central University’s Security Observatory, Andres Nieto. “On the contrary, the evidence does show an increase in violence among citizens,” the scholar added.

The ban was initially imposed by former President Juan Manuel Santos in 2015 and has since been upheld by his successors.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.
