Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.

My first encounter with Steve came in late 2002, after he had offered me the editor’s job—sight unseen, via e-mail—and I accepted, knowing only that I’d earn about US$500 a month and should show up in Santiago with an AP style guide and a copy of Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style. That it all seemed a bit rushed and loosey-goosey gave me pause for concern, but I was eager for an excuse to return to Chile, so hopped on a plane and flew down from Costa Rica.

Still, after our first meeting, I wondered just how wise my decision really was. It was then that I realized the Santiago Times wasn’t, as I’d imagined, a print paper. It was Internet-based, with a rudimentary website that was only half functioning. “We got hacked,” Steve told me. He also explained that he was living at that moment in Puerto Montt—1,000 kilometers to the south—and that he was recovering still from a recent and quite serious car accident. It had been a very bad year, he said.

I gave the gig a chance, though, and things gradually improved. Some energetic new interns trickled in, as they always did at the Santiago Times. A talented British/Australian writer showed up too, and I asked Steve to hire him as a kind of co-editor. The business couldn’t really afford another paid staff member, but Steve honored my request, and for the next year or so we had a great run. Then the money ran out.

“I can’t afford to pay you both, so one of you has to go,” Steve told us one morning. “I’ll leave it up to you two to decide which one.” And so we did—over a liter of beer, even though it was like nine-something in the morning. The co-editor (still a dear friend of mine) offered to go. But I’d leave too, I decided. A month or so later. The job had run its course, I thought.

We were frustrated and certainly taken aback—especially by the “decide amongst yourselves who stays and goes” part of the equation. And yet, neither of us was really surprised, because even then, we’d seen enough of Steve and his herky-jerky management style to know that this was precisely the kind of situation that could and would, as it turned out, unfold.

We couldn’t really be angry either. Or at least not stay angry. Because again, with Steve, what you saw is what you got. He was passionate about his project, but not always clear about how to make it grow. Often he’d have a new idea, and then charge ahead. And in those cases, there’d be a flurry of positive changes—new computers maybe, a new paid staff person, a larger office space. But then a particularly capable group of interns would move on, money would run scarce, the whole operation would contract, and we’d be back to square one, or so it felt.

I know this because later I joined Steve for a second, longer stint. What never varied, though, was his fighting spirit. A feisty advocate for the underdog, he was always chomping to champion a good cause—demanding accountability for human rights violations, defending the environment, shining a light on corruption and hypocrisy.

The Santiago Times was his platform, and he committed himself tooth-and-nail to making it survive, if not prosper. And in the meantime, the interns, editors, photographers and other collaborators kept coming through. They kept using Steve’s office and humble little publication as a landing point for early-career, working-abroad experiences, and as a launching pad for further adventures and professional endeavors.

If there was a method to Steve’s madcap approach, it was that with each new idea he had for the Santiago Times, with each new push to improve or revive it, he bought the business a little more time. Months turned into years and then decades. And all the while, people like myself were given an opportunity to work and learn—in large part through trial and error, because although Steve had things to teach, he also gave us space to teach ourselves.

It was his special tenacity, though, that kept the whole thing going, that gave so many people the chance, year after year, to develop their skills. We had fun too. So much fun. The office on Av. Santa María produced lasting, globe-spanning friendships, even love stories. And that was also part of Steve’s gift to us all.

He was an unabashed eccentric. Smart. Complicated. He had an entrepreneurial spirit but no real nose for business. Steve was a lawyer who wrote about politics and fruit exports. An editor with a penchant for typos. Part idealist, part cynic. A campaigner with no patience for diplomacy. He was perpetually cash-strapped, but generous. He was impulsive and impatient at times, but also deeply committed—to his various projects and causes, and to his family and colleagues. He was a teacher and a mentor. A doting father. A friend.

Goodbye Steve. Paz. And thank you.

World.title: Anti-vaccine mandate protests spread across the country, crippling Canada-U.S. trade
World.content:
Speaking to reporters at a press conference in Ottawa, Emergency Preparedness Minister Bill Blair said the blockade at Windsor’s Ambassador Bridge is particularly alarming because a quarter of all Canada-U.S. trade moves through that one crossing, which connects Canada with Detroit and points beyond.

Hundreds of millions of dollars worth of products have been held back for three days as 50 to 75 vehicles and about 100 anti-mandate protesters camp out on the main road that leads on and off the bridge.

The Canada Border Service Agency (CBSA) has closed the bridge to commercial traffic temporarily, diverting trucks to the Blue Water Bridge in Sarnia, Ont. instead. CBSA is reporting wait times in excess of four hours to make the short trip across to Port Huron, Mich.

We’ve seen the criminal acts, acts of thuggery and the obnoxiousness that they’ve inflicted on the people of Ottawa. Now they’re blocking the highways leading into our ports of entry. They’re putting their foot on the throats of all Canadians.

Labour unions representing auto workers have reported some idled Windsor plants have sent workers home while the trucker convoy holds up much-needed parts coming from the U.S.

Transport Minister Omar Alghabra said central Canada could soon see empty store shelves because so much of the region’s fresh food and produce comes into the country across that bridge.

To be honest, I find it ironic that the same people who were trying to sell Canadians fake stories about empty shelves are now causing those shelves to go empty, Alghabra said.

Windsor Mayor Drew Dilkens said the protesters appear to be determined to stay. They feel such a passion for this particular cause that they’re willing to die for it, he said.

Speaking briefly to reporters before question period, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said his government is working with Ontario and the City of Windsor to put an end to the blockade.

World.title: Excellent prospects for Mercosur beef exports, except Argentina
World.content:
The Argentine beef industry is optimistic about world meat production and global demand this year, with China again playing a leading market role. A report issued by Argentina’s Rosario Stock Exchange (BCR) and the Mercado Ganadero Department (Rosgan), world beef production will reach 58 million tons, representing a 1% increase over 2021.

This prospect would reverse the downward trend seen in 2021, mainly because of the recovery of the meat-packing industries in Brazil and Australia, the world’s first and third-largest meat exporters, respectively.

As for the global flow of imports, the expected average, according to analysts at BCR/Rosgan, is 10 million tons, which would imply an increase of 2.7% compared to last year.

China, which reduced the pace of international beef purchases in 2021 to 950,000 tons compared to more than 1.1 million tons in 2020 will once again represent 32% of global consumption. According to BCR/Rosgan, China accounted for 13% of global meat demand in 2017.

At that time, Argentina was in the top five beef exporters, having previously been in the top three. But Argentina has dropped out of the top ten beef exporters in recent years, owing to government restrictions on beef exports with the purpose of supporting the domestic market and helping with lower prices.

Nevertheless the Brazilian and Argentine beef markets had an unusual year in 2021. Traditional animal protein producers, the two countries witnessed declines in their exports, particularly in the last months of the year. Overall compared to 2020, Brazil beef sales dropped 9,92% while Argentine exports decreased 13,84%.

The reduction experienced by Brazil can be explained by the beef embargo imposed by China. In effect on September 2021, Brazil voluntarily suspended exports to China after the identification of two cases of mad cow disease in the country.

The World Organization for Animal Health (OIE) recognized that these were atypical episodes and that the risk to the national herd was negligible. Despite this, China insisted in freezing Brazilian beef exports for over three months until December 15.

The drop in Argentine beef shipments were motivated by the high price of the product in the domestic market, and thus the government suspended all exports in May 2021. ” As a consequence of sustained increases in the price of beef cuts in the domestic market, the national government decided to implement a set of emergency measures to better organize the sector, restricting speculative practices, improving the traceability of exports and avoiding tax evasion,” said the decree issued at the time.

Further measures were implemented, and given the deteriorating economic situation of Argentina and its impact on inflation, the country’s export ban on certain beef cuts was extended until the end of 2023.

As a result of this situation, Mercosur junior member Uruguay strongly benefitted and saw beef shipments increase 35%. The same can be said of the other Mercosur member, Paraguay, that also experienced a record year of beef exports in 2021.

World.title: Unemployment in Chile almost back at 2019 levels
World.content:
Chilean authorities have reported Monday that unemployment nationwide had fallen in 2021 to 7.2% while in the same period of 2020 it had hit 10.3%. In the middle of the social uprisings of 2019 it had been recorded at 7.1%.

“It is the eighth consecutive annual decrease in the unemployment rate,” said Leonardo González of the National Institute of Statistics (INE), which also reported the unemployment rate for women stood at 7.4%, and for men at 7.1%.

In the quarter of the year, 119,930 jobs were created compared to the previous quarter. With seasonal adjustment, González specified, the number of jobs recovered quarterly reached 49,625.

Around 1,436,000 jobs have been recovered, which represented 77.5% of all jobs lost during the worst part of the COVID-19 pandemic, with 81.8% accounting for jobs held by men and 73.1% for those carried out by women.

The INE also said 80.1% of formal jobs and 94.5% of informal jobs had been recovered.

“If we continue at this rate, we estimate that we will soon be able to recover all the jobs that were lost in the worst moment of the pandemic,” González stressed. He warned, however, that “we have been consistently seeing these rates rise, but we are not yet seeing pre-pandemic levels.”

Employment ended 2021 at 54.3%, while the labor force participation rate ended at 58.5%, an 8.1% yoy increase, driven by women (11.7%) and men (5.7%).

Jobs were boosted by construction (22.2%), commerce (8.5%) and the hotels and restaurants (30.9%).

Economy Minister Lucas Palacios said that during “2021 we met the goal of strongly recovering economic activity and also employment.”

“We have recovered 80% of the jobs that the pandemic and recession destroyed. It was necessary to create health, operational security and certainty conditions to reactivate the economy and especially investment, which is the main source of opportunities,” Palacios said.

Palacios also highlighted joint efforts by the public and private sectors. “Incentives from the State can be very relevant to promote investment and employment,” the minister explained.

Labor Minister Patricio Melero agreed the unemployment figures meant “great news” and praised “the measures adopted by the government, both in economic and health matters,” which were yielding “results which are very positive for the country.”

(Source: ANSA)

World.title: Argentina's foreign ministry rejects the UK guidance for companies in the Falklands
World.content:
Argentina's foreign ministry rejects the UK guidance for companies in the Falklands

16th Wednesday, September 2026 - 17:23 UTC Full article

Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno has filed three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors

Argentina's foreign ministry expressed its “strongest rejection” on Tuesday of the guidance the British government published the previous day for companies conducting economic activity in the Falklands, and said it would continue applying its legislation against firms operating hydrocarbons in the area without Argentine authorization.

What Buenos Aires says

The ministry said the archipelagos and their corresponding maritime areas “are an integral part of its national territory and are illegitimately occupied by the United Kingdom.” Its response covers, beyond the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, a wider scope than the British document, which refers only to the first archipelago. Argentina argues that the issuing of regulations, unilaterally granted licenses, calls for suppliers and British commercial promotion breach UN General Assembly Resolution 31/49, which urges both countries to refrain from unilateral modifications while a solution remains pending. It also warned that the planned hydrocarbon activity could have irreversible effects on non-renewable resources. These are Argentine government positions, contested by the United Kingdom.

What the guidance said

The document, titled “Doing business with the Falkland Islands,” was published on Monday by the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office together with the British business and trade department. It states that London has no doubt about its sovereignty, that Argentina exercises no jurisdiction and its domestic law does not apply in the islands, and that regulating economic activity is a matter for the islands' government. It offers assistance to companies receiving Argentine correspondence and says it cannot see the basis on which courts in third countries could exercise jurisdiction over those measures. These are British government positions, contested by Argentina.

The diplomatic move

Following the final investment decision by Rockhopper Exploration, British-owned, and Navitas Petroleum, Israeli, on the Sea Lion project in the basin north of the archipelago, the ministry summoned the British and Israeli ambassadors to hand them formal protest notes. There are precedents: Argentina summoned the British mission in 2010 over the start of drilling in the area, and London lodged a formal protest when the law providing for penalties against oil companies was passed.

The campaign so far

According to the ministry, it has sent around 180 warning and risk-assumption notices to individuals and companies in 30 countries, opened 60 administrative proceedings, and Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno has filed three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors. None of the allegations has been proven and no proceeding has yet resulted in a penalty.

The framework

The resolutions Argentina invokes are General Assembly texts and carry the status of recommendations, without binding force. Resolution 2065, of 1965, invites both states to negotiate; the Argentine government reiterated its willingness to resume a “constructive and substantive” dialogue. London conditions any discussion of sovereignty on the islanders' wishes; in the 2013 referendum they chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory with 99.8% of the vote.

World.title: Kirchner's defense seeks to lift her ban from office before the 2027 elections
World.content:
Kirchner's defense seeks to lift her ban from office before the 2027 elections

16th Wednesday, September 2026 - 17:12 UTC Full article

The new element is an economic audit commissioned by the defense itself, not a court-ordered expert report

Lawyers for former Argentine president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner said on Tuesday they have added a new element to the petition they are pursuing before the UN Human Rights Committee, seeking to overturn her final conviction in the Vialidad case and, more immediately, to set aside the lifetime ban from public office that prevents her from running in next year's presidential election.

The defense argues openly that the proceedings were aimed at barring her from electoral politics. The individual communication was filed in late July and documents eight alleged violations of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Among them it invokes Article 14.5, arguing that the Court of Cassation did not carry out a genuine and thorough review of the defense's grounds, and Article 14.7, contending that 49 of the 51 public works tried had already been the subject of investigations closed by dismissal or shelving.

The new element is an economic audit commissioned by the defense itself, not a court-ordered expert report. Its starting point is a spreadsheet from the National Roads Directorate that came to light on August 6, when a technical official from the agency testified in the Cuadernos case, an ongoing trial in which Kirchner is also a defendant and where the presumption of innocence applies.

According to the report, prepared by Brazilian economist Antonio Corrêa de Lacerda, companies belonging to Lázaro Báez's Grupo Austral received US$18.66 million, or 0.85% of the more than US$2 billion disbursed through one of the agency's funding sources. The study adds that the fifteen largest construction firms accounted for 75% of those resources. “The sentence was absolutely unjust and an innocent person was convicted,” lawyer Carlos Beraldi said at a press conference in Buenos Aires.

The conviction, however, did not turn on Báez's share of overall road spending. The ruling, upheld by the Supreme Court in June 2025, found Kirchner guilty of fraudulent administration over the irregular award of 51 road works in Santa Cruz province, involving overpricing, extended deadlines and advance payments, and put the loss to the state at around US$500 million. It imposed a six-year sentence, which she has been serving under house arrest for some fifteen months. The central conduct attributed to her was signing decree 54/2009, which prosecutors described as the instrument of the scheme.

Neither prosecutors nor the courts involved have commented on the filing.

The Human Rights Committee examines individual communications under the Optional Protocol to the Covenant and issues views that are not binding and do not annul domestic rulings; it may request interim measures, likewise without binding force. The defense hopes the body will agree to take up the case at its next session, expected between late October and early November, and said it would afterwards seek review of the conviction in the Argentine courts.

The team comprises, alongside Beraldi, Brazil's Rafael Valim, a lawyer for President Lula da Silva, and Spain's Javier Borrego, a former judge of the European Court of Human Rights.

World.title: EU proposes Canada as its first 'associate member', a status that does not yet exist
World.content:
EU proposes Canada as its first 'associate member', a status that does not yet exist

16th Wednesday, September 2026 - 17:07 UTC Full article

Full membership is not on the table: Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union reserves membership for European states

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed on Wednesday that Canada become the European Union's first “associate member,” a status not provided for in the bloc's treaties and whose details have not been defined.

“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada being the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen said during her annual State of the Union address in Strasbourg, addressing Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, a special guest of the European Parliament seated in the front row. The proposal drew a standing ovation. Carney is due to address the chamber on Thursday.

Full membership is not on the table: Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union reserves membership for European states. The bloc has also been reluctant in the past to entertain flexible categories of membership.

Von der Leyen further proposed moving from the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, known as CETA, to what she called an “alliance for the future,” aimed at creating a common prosperity and economic security space, with cooperation on technology, critical raw materials, energy and defense. She said the Union must urgently reimagine its partnerships and stressed the initiative “is not an alliance against anyone else.”

Carney's office welcomed the proposal, saying Canada is deepening ties with the European Union to strengthen its sovereignty. Canada's ambassador-designate to the bloc, Jonathan Wilkinson, told reporters, however, that the two sides remain far from landing an agreement.

The rapprochement responds to the trade war with the United States, destination of around 70% of Canadian exports. US President Donald Trump has imposed tariffs on Canada and has repeatedly suggested the country become the 51st state, an idea Carney rejects. Canada and the European Union had already launched a strategic partnership in 2025, whose implementation they reviewed in November.

Bilateral trade in goods and services reached €130.8 billion last year, some US$151 billion, according to the European Commission, an increase of more than 80% over the past decade. The Union is Canada's second largest trading partner. CETA eliminated 99% of tariff lines when it provisionally entered into force in 2017, though ten member states have yet to ratify it.

Finland's President Alexander Stubb had set out on June 3 a vision of a Union of up to forty states including Canada, the United Kingdom, Türkiye, Norway and Iceland, asking whether it would not be preferable for Canada to be the Union's 28th state rather than the United States' 51st. In March, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot suggested Ottawa might accede at some point.

Support in Canada is not unanimous. A survey by pollster Abacus Data put backing for deeper cooperation with the bloc at around 80% and support for eventual accession at 49%; the poll does not specify sample size or margin of error. Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre called Carney's effort misplaced and said Canada will be neither the 51st state of the United States nor the 28th of the European Union.

World.title: Argentine government says the Ushuaia naval base will monitor resources and sovereignty
World.content:
Argentine government says the Ushuaia naval base will monitor resources and sovereignty

15th Tuesday, September 2026 - 21:35 UTC Full article

Presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier said at the Casa Rosada that the facility will take on logistical functions and serve as a strategic point for Argentina's projection into the South Atlantic

Argentina's government said on Tuesday that the integrated naval base it plans in Ushuaia will allow it to monitor and control natural resources and sovereignty in the South Atlantic, and announced it will file further complaints against companies exploring for or extracting hydrocarbons without Argentine authorization in waters near the Falklands.

Presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier said at the Casa Rosada that the facility will take on logistical functions and serve as a strategic point for Argentina's projection into the South Atlantic. Days earlier, the same spokesman had stressed that the base is not military in character and will operate as a logistics hub providing operational and scientific support for projection toward Antarctica.

Ravier said the facility will strengthen naval and air protection with a P-3 Orion maritime patrol aircraft and the F-16 fighters bought from Denmark, and that commercial and civilian docks will be built to support economic activity in the region. He also said companies linked to exploration in the disputed area will not be able to contract with the Argentine state, join the large investment incentive regime, receive tax benefits or take part in Vaca Muerta, the country's main unconventional field, located in Neuquén province.

Work began in 2022, under Alberto Fernández's government, and has been all but halted since. It stands at 9.13% physical completion, consisting of a concrete slab of some 2,500 square meters within a 38-hectare site, according to government figures. Defense Minister Carlos Presti said on Friday that work will resume on January 2, once public tenders close.

The executive has reassigned some US$142 million to the project through decree 867 and is seeking the remaining funding. Ravier categorically ruled out any foreign involvement, saying there is no agreement with the United States and no support of any kind, and that the base will be entirely Argentine.

Ushuaia lies about 700 kilometers from the archipelago, a British overseas territory whose sovereignty Argentina claims. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to retain that status.

The announcement is part of the campaign launched by President Javier Milei on September 3. So far, the foreign ministry has administrative proceedings open against at least 60 individuals and companies under Law 26,659, with no penalty applied, and on September 7 filed a criminal complaint against five companies linked to the Sea Lion project, lodged with the federal court of Julián Ercolini. None of the allegations has been proven. Argentina had already barred Rockhopper for twenty years in 2013 and Navitas in April 2022.

Ravier also said at least three of the sector's largest companies had withdrawn from the Sea Lion project, and that José Antonio Kast's government in Chile had committed not to provide logistical assistance to British vessels. Neither statement has been independently confirmed.

World.title: An archipelago of 3,600 people with 86 nationalities represented
World.content:
An archipelago of 3,600 people with 86 nationalities represented

15th Tuesday, September 2026 - 21:33 UTC Full article

Foreign labor, much of it recruited through staffing agencies, sustains an economy reshaped by the growth of fishing and tourism

In a population of fewer than four thousand, the English of Stanley's streets sits alongside the Spanish of a sizeable Latin American community, the Tagalog of Filipino residents, the Afrikaans of South Africans and the Shona of Zimbabweans. The 2021 census, the most recent available, recorded 86 nationalities in the Falklands, a British overseas territory whose sovereignty Argentina claims.

That census counted 3,662 usual residents. Among those who stated a place of birth, 1,530 were born in the archipelago and 1,898 abroad: 749 in the United Kingdom, 369 in St Helena — another British territory in the Atlantic — 178 in the Philippines and 168 in Chile, plus 434 from other countries. Close to 70% of the population identifies as Falkland Islander, British, or both.

Foreign labor, much of it recruited through staffing agencies, sustains an economy reshaped by the growth of fishing and tourism. With unemployment at around 1% and a labor force participation rate of 95%, there is little room to fill vacancies locally, and many young people travel to the United Kingdom to study after secondary school.

“We're a small community, practically a town of under 4,000 people, but it functions like a small country,” says Stacy Bragger, a member of the Legislative Assembly and of the organization Multicultural Falklands, who cites the difficulty of filling teaching, medical and health-care posts.

The census records an average annual income of £30,000 for working-age people in employment and £53,100 per household. Around 30% of residents, however, are temporary: they work on short-term visas or are posted at the Mount Pleasant military base.

Alex Olmedo arrived from Santiago de Chile 36 years ago, worked in various jobs and now runs a hotel and restaurant on Stanley's main street. “It's a very good place to start a life,” he says, citing free health care and education. On immigration policy, he argues the opening has been gradual rather than total, because maintaining living standards “is only achieved by having control.”

The Chilean community is the largest Latin American group; there are also Peruvians, Colombians, Venezuelans and a small number of Argentines, most of whom came through family ties with islanders. Many keep Spanish as their everyday language and maintain their own social spaces.

The Zimbabwean community, around 1.8% of the population, formed through the recruitment of deminers to clear devices laid during the 1982 war. That work ran from 2009 to 2020, and the archipelago was declared mine-free in November of that year. Shupikaya Chipunza, now a guard at the local prison, stayed on. “My children are more local than Zimbabwean,” he says. At home they speak Shona; outside, English.

Under the 1983 nationality act, those born in the islands are full British citizens. Migrants first obtain resident status and then citizenship, after meeting residence and employment requirements.

That composition carries a political dimension. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory, a result the United Kingdom and the local government cite as an expression of the right to self-determination. Argentina does not recognize the vote and argues the population was implanted after 1833 and therefore should not decide the sovereignty question.

Pressure on the labor market could increase with the development of the Sea Lion oil project, due to begin production in 2028 and the target of the judicial and administrative campaign Argentina launched this month.

World.title: Businessman named by Washington as Maduro's frontman admits guilt in a Miami court
World.content:
Businessman named by Washington as Maduro's frontman admits guilt in a Miami court

15th Tuesday, September 2026 - 19:04 UTC Full article

The change of plea hearing was set before Judge Kathleen Williams of the Southern District of Florida. Saab, 54, faced a single count carrying a maximum of twenty years in prison

Colombian businessman Alex Saab, identified by the US Treasury Department as Nicolás Maduro's principal frontman, pleaded guilty on Tuesday in a federal court in Miami to conspiracy to launder money linked to Venezuela's CLAP subsidized food program.

The change of plea hearing was set before Judge Kathleen Williams of the Southern District of Florida. Saab, 54, faced a single count carrying a maximum of twenty years in prison. His lawyer, Neil Schuster, declined to comment and the terms of the agreement with prosecutors were not immediately public. No sentencing date was known, nor whether the agreement involves any form of cooperation.

The indictment alleges that Saab and others set up a web of companies to bribe Venezuelan officials who controlled contracts for the Local Supply and Production Committee, the program created to distribute staples such as rice, corn flour and cooking oil cheaply amid hyperinflation. According to prosecutors, the scheme involved shell companies, falsified shipping records and the skimming of public contracts to import food from Colombia and Mexico. The indictment adds that when US sanctions made payments to suppliers difficult, those involved turned to selling crude from state oil company PDVSA and channeled the proceeds through bank accounts in the United States. The conduct attributed to third parties has not been proven.

This is not his first US case. Saab was arrested in June 2020 in Cape Verde during a refueling stop on a flight bound for Iran, and extradited in October 2021. That case, opened in 2019, accused him alongside fellow Colombian Álvaro Pulido of obtaining social housing contracts between 2011 and 2015 and moving some US$350 million out of Venezuela. In November 2021, a judge dismissed seven of the eight counts because the United States had assured Cape Verde during extradition that it would prosecute him on no more than one, in order to comply with the maximum sentence allowed under Cape Verdean law. That dismissal applied only to Saab. He pleaded not guilty to the remaining count.

That trial never took place. In December 2023, Saab left US custody in a prisoner swap between the governments of Joe Biden and Maduro, with presidential clemency. Venezuela released ten Americans, a fugitive former military contractor and some twenty political prisoners. Saab was received in Caracas by Maduro.

The current case rests on a different scheme from the one behind that release. Saab was deported to the United States in May by Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, in response to pressure from Washington, which has pursued the businessman for more than a decade. Maduro has been removed from power and awaits trial in the United States, where the presumption of innocence applies.

Saab was for years among the businessmen closest to the Venezuelan government, able to work around US sanctions, place crude and import supplies during the country's economic crisis.

World.title: UK publishes guidance backing companies that do business with the Falkland Islands
World.content:
UK publishes guidance backing companies that do business with the Falkland Islands

15th Tuesday, September 2026 - 18:46 UTC Full article

London states it has no doubt about British sovereignty over the islands and surrounding waters, and that it will not discuss the question unless the islanders wish it

The British government published guidance on Tuesday for companies and individuals conducting economic activity in the Falkland Islands or supplying goods and services to the archipelago, offering assistance to those who receive correspondence or threats of legal action from the Argentine authorities.

The document was produced by the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office together with the department the publication itself identifies as the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, and comes nine days after Argentina filed a criminal complaint against five companies linked to the Sea Lion oil project.

Who it covers

The guidance applies to three categories: those operating in the islands, those supplying goods or services to them, and those involved directly or indirectly in developing the islands' economy, including the exploitation of natural resources.

What the UK government says

London states it has no doubt about British sovereignty over the islands and surrounding waters, and that it will not discuss the question unless the islanders wish it. It says the archipelago has been administered peacefully and effectively since 1833, apart from the 1982 interruption, and that Argentina exercises neither sovereignty nor jurisdiction there and its domestic law does not apply. It invokes the right of self-determination set out in Article 1 of the UN Charter and of the two 1966 international human rights covenants, and says hydrocarbon activity on the continental shelf is regulated under Falkland Islands legislation in accordance with the Law of the Sea Convention. These are UK government positions, contested by Argentina.

The practical point

The passage of greatest operational value states that the UK cannot see the basis on which courts of any country outside Argentina could legitimately exercise jurisdiction in respect of these measures. The document states expressly that it does not constitute legal advice and recommends that companies receiving Argentine correspondence obtain independent advice on their particular circumstances. It also offers to make its position clear directly to any company seeking reassurance, including subsidiaries and suppliers under pressure in third countries. The contact given is the FCDO's Overseas Territories and Polar Directorate, King Charles Street, London SW1A 2AH.

What the Argentine measures cover

Decree 868/2026, of September 4, designated Argentina's foreign ministry as the enforcement authority for Law 26,659, set ten business days for a defense and ten more for a ruling, and requires public bodies to report any potentially prohibited conduct within five business days. Restrictions may extend to direct and indirect shareholders, affiliated entities and certain suppliers, which explains why investment funds, banks and a shipping company appear among those targeted. Argentina has 60 administrative proceedings open, with no penalty applied, and filed a criminal complaint on September 7 under Article 7 of the law, which carries terms of five to ten years. None of the allegations has been proven.

Precedents

The guidance says previous Argentine measures did not prevent the islands' economy from growing, without specifying which. In 2012, Argentina barred Borders and Southern Petroleum, Desire Petroleum, Argos Resources and Falkland Oil and Gas for twenty years. In 2015, a prosecutor ordered the seizure of more than US$156 million in international equipment, including vessels, platforms and bank accounts.

The islands' Legislative Assembly welcomed the publication in a statement that largely reproduces the guidance's own wording. Argentina claims sovereignty over the islands; in the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: Milei prepares bill to toughen sanctions on companies operating in the Falklands
World.content:
Milei prepares bill to toughen sanctions on companies operating in the Falklands

15th Tuesday, September 2026 - 09:53 UTC Full article

The package will be a legislative test for Milei, whose libertarian coalition lacks majorities in Congress

Argentine President Javier Milei is preparing legislation this week to toughen sanctions against companies operating in the Falklands, a move analysts say could raise tensions with Britain beyond the oil sector.

The bill, titled the National Sovereignty Defense Law, would amend Law 26,659, which already bars unauthorized hydrocarbon activity on the disputed continental shelf and provides for disqualifications of between five and twenty years. Milei announced it on September 3 in a televised address, alongside a decree to speed up existing sanctions proceedings. The text will be introduced in the lower house.

The legislation builds on proceedings the Argentine government says it has opened against at least 60 companies and individuals linked to offshore oil exploration around the archipelago, which Argentina calls the Malvinas and claims as its own despite British control. Argentina invaded the Islands in 1982 and fought a ten-week war before surrendering to Britain. Islanders confirmed their status as a British Overseas Territory in the 2013 referendum.

Congressional aide Marcelo Seghini told Reuters the text provides for tougher penalties for unauthorized operations and would extend sanctions to affiliates and to other activities affecting Argentine natural resources. According to the same source, the government is considering including the fishing industry, which underpins much of the Islands' economy. The Argentine government has not confirmed that scope or responded to queries about the companies affected.

The move follows a criminal complaint filed last week against companies linked to the offshore Sea Lion project, operated by Israel's Navitas Petroleum alongside Britain's Rockhopper Exploration. Both maintain the project holds valid licenses from the Falklands government and do not expect Milei's actions to derail development.

A government document reviewed by Reuters lists shareholders and financial intermediaries among the firms marked for possible sanctions, including Vanguard, First Eagle, Canaccord, Interactive Investor and Hargreaves Lansdown. Oilfield services providers SLB, Baker Hughes and Halliburton have said in recent days they will not take part in activities on the Islands.

The announcement followed comments by U.S. President Donald Trump suggesting Washington could reconsider its neutral position on the dispute. For Marcelo Elizondo, Argentina's representative to the International Chamber of Commerce, this was not a bill prepared over time: Trump's remarks, he said, “created a climate that the government sought to exploit quickly.”

The package will be a legislative test for Milei, whose libertarian coalition lacks majorities in Congress. Opposition lawmaker Aldo Leiva said the president “is clearly using the Malvinas for political opportunism.”

Companies and investors are weighing whether the sanctions could ultimately reach firms with operations in Argentina, including the Vaca Muerta shale formation. Congress receives the 2027 budget proposal on Tuesday, with defense spending expected to rise.

World.title: Women farmers in Oaxaca, Guerrero report catastrophic drought
World.content:
Drought has devastated corn crops in Oaxaca and Guerrero, according to farmers in the two southern states.

Two associations of women farmers — one in Oaxaca and one in Guerrero — released a joint statement last week in which they reported the loss of up to 100% of agricultural production.

They said that drought is not only taking a toll on their crops but also on their economic well-being.

The National Water Commission’s most recent “drought monitor” report shows that large parts of Oaxaca and Guerrero are “abnormally dry” or experiencing “moderate drought.”

However, the women farmers’ associations — Red de Mujeres, Ejidatarias y Comuneras del Estado de Oaxaca and the Red Estatal de Mujeres Agraristas de Guerrero (REMA) — described the drought conditions as “severe.”

“The severe drought afflicting our states is on the scale of a catastrophe, similar to the damage caused by hurricanes, only without the wind and without [the public, media and political] spotlight,” they said.

“A hurricane destroys what is visible in a matter of hours; drought destroys our future and what sustains us over the course of months: the cornfields, water, seeds and our livelihoods,” they said.

The farmers’ associations said that communities in Oaxaca and Guerrero, in both coastal and inland regions of the two states, are “losing the capacity” to produce their own food.

Drought conditions “represent a direct threat to the food sovereignty of farming families,” they said.

The two farming associations called on state and federal authorities to declare a climate emergency in drought-affected areas of Oaxaca and Guerrero and establish programs aimed at guaranteeing food sovereignty and supporting female farmers, many of whom primarily grow corn to feed themselves and their families, but sell any surplus they have. They also asked for authorities to provide direct monetary resources to female farmers.

Women farmers in the two states are “in despair,” said Nancy Solano, a farmer and spokesperson for her fellow campesinas in Oaxaca.

She told the news outlet La Silla Rota that prices for corn and tortillas — a staple in Mexico — will go up due to drought-related maize shortages.

Adriana Paz, president of REMA, told La Silla Rota that the association she leads has requested a meeting with federal Agricultural Minister Columba López Gutiérrez to propose a comprehensive drought relief program that takes gender into account.

“A lot of the government’s public policies don’t have a gender perspective and exclude women,” she said.

“… Without women there is no corn and without corn there is no country,” Paz said.

With reports from El Universal and La Silla Rota

World.title: The Mexican Navy’s at-sea cocaine seizures are up nearly 50% this year
World.content:
Cocaine seizures by the Mexican Navy have increased significantly this year, rising 47.2% from 25.7 metric tonnes in 2025 to 37.9 tonnes this year as of Sept. 10.

“These results are the product of operations carried out by the Mexican Navy through surface, air, and Marine Corps units, focused on monitoring the coasts and national waters, as well as detecting, intercepting, and seizing vessels linked to illicit activities,” the Navy (Semar) stated in a report.

Semar’s maritime operations aim to disrupt the logistical capacity of criminal organizations operating in the maritime domain, according to Semar.

In addition to the drugs seized, the Navy’s maritime operations this year have resulted in the confiscations of 26 vessels, one low-profile vessel (LPV) and 54 outboard motorboats, as well as the arrest of 86 suspects.

The seizure of the substances “contributes to reducing their availability and circulation, as well as preventing them from reaching communities and particularly affecting younger generations,” Semar said in a statement

“With this action, the Mexican Navy contributes to the protection of youth and the creation of safer environments for children and young people.”

In a related development, on Tuesday a coordinated effort of Semar and the National Customs Agency of Mexico at the Mexico City International Airport (AICM) confiscated 1 metric tonne of cocaine that had been declared as ground roasted coffee and hidden in over 3,000 bags .

“With these actions, the Navy, Customs, the Ministry of Security and Citizen Protection (SSPC), and other security cabinet institutions are strengthening inter-institutional cooperation and reinforcing control and oversight mechanisms to protect legality in foreign trade operations,” the authorities said.

With reports from Sin Embargo and La Jornada

World.title: State of democracy improved in Mexico in 2025 as region showed signs of deterioration
World.content:
The state of democracy in Mexico improved slightly in 2025 — President Claudia Sheinbaum’s first full year in office — compared to 2024, according to the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International IDEA), an intergovernmental organization.

On Tuesday, the Stockholm-based organization released its annual report on the state of democracy in more than 170 countries around the world.

This year’s report, “The Global State of Democracy 2026,” is subtitled “Democracy in an Age of Conflict” in recognition of the wars currently being fought in various parts of the world. It focuses on the state of democracy in countries around the world in 2025.

International IDEA scores and ranks countries in four different democracy-related categories: representation, rights, rule of law and participation.

Compared to 2024, Mexico’s score improved in two of the four categories, declined in one and was unchanged in another. Mexico rose in the rankings in two categories, but fell in the other two. Its combined score across the four categories increased by 0.008 points to 1.778 out of 4 in 2025 from 1.770 in 2024.

In December 2024, less than three months after she was sworn in as president, Sheinbaum said that Mexico was “perhaps” the most democratic country in the world given that it would hold judicial elections in 2025.

However, International IDEA’s latest report indicates that Mexico is far from a global beacon of democracy. In the four categories assessed by the intergovernmental organization, Mexico is among the top 100 countries in just one of them.

However, the slight improvement in the state of democracy in Mexico in 2025, according to International IDEA, is, of course, preferable to a decline. The quality of democracy in many other countries is on the wane, according to the intergovernmental organization.

In the executive summary of its report, International IDEA wrote that in 2025, “the global challenges to democracy and the difficulty in stemming its erosion were both exemplified and compounded by political developments in the United States.”

“There, President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch and wielded it to further a narrow set of personal goals and pursue retaliation against perceived enemies,” International IDEA said.

The intergovernmental organization also said that “Latin America has become the most politically polarized region in the world after a rapid rise in polarization over the past decade.”

“Highly contentious issues such as the economy, migration, and insecurity, as well as the increasing success of anti-establishment politicians who capitalize on divisive identity-based narratives and ‘us versus them’ politics, have contributed to an erosion of democratic dialogue,” International IDEA said.

Almost two years into her six-year term, Sheinbaum remains a very popular president, according to poll results.

However, there is political polarization in Mexico, and a significant number of Mexicans believe that the state of democracy in Mexico has declined during the presidencies of Sheinbaum and her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador as a result of government-led initiatives such as the disbandment of various autonomous agencies and the election of judges affiliated with, or seen as sympathetic to, the ruling Morena party.

Mexico’s scores and rankings in the four democracy-related categories assessed by International IDEA are outlined below.

Representation: Mexico’s score and ranking declined

According to International IDEA, in the Global State of Democracy (GSoD) Indices, “Representation” is an aggregate measure of the extent of representative democracy, built from component measures of credible elections, inclusive suffrage, freedom to organize through political parties, the effectiveness of the legislature, and the practice of democracy at the local level.

Mexico scored 0.550 out of 1 on this measure to rank 83rd out of 173 countries.

Mexico’s score declined by 0.003 points compared to 2024, while it fell one spot in the rankings.

Nevertheless, Mexico achieved its best score and ranking in this category.

Mexico’s score in 2025 was on par with those of Paraguay and Hungary.

The top three countries in this category were Denmark, Germany and Costa Rica.

The United States ranked 51st while Canada ranked 25th.

Rights: Mexico’s score was unchanged, but its ranking declined

According to International IDEA, the “Rights” category is made up of liberal and social rights that support both fair representation and accountability. It is built upon four component measures — Access to Justice; Civil Liberties, including Freedom of the Press, Freedom of Expression, Freedom of Association and Assembly, Freedom of Religion, and Freedom of Movement; Basic Welfare; and Political Equality, including Gender Equality, Social Group Equality, and Economic Equality.

Mexico scored 0.407 out of 1 on this measure to rank 111th out of the 173 countries assessed.

Mexico’s score was unchanged compared to 2024, while it fell one spot in the rankings.

Mexico ranked one spot above Burkina Faso in this category and one position below Qatar.

The top three countries in this category were Denmark, Switzerland and Germany.

The United States ranked 42nd while Canada ranked 27th.

Rule of law: Mexico’s score and ranking improved

According to International IDEA, in the GSoD Indices, “Rule of Law” is an aggregate measure that includes assessments of the independence of the judiciary from government influence, the extent to which public administrators use their offices for personal gain, the predictability of law enforcement, and the degree to which people are free from political violence. Overall, the index provides a snapshot of the extent to which everyone is subject to the law and the level of safety that exists.

Mexico scored 0.370 out of 1 on this measure to rank 112th.

Mexico’s score increased 0.009 points compared to 2024, while it rose seven positions in the rankings.

Mexico ranked one spot above Thailand in this category and one position below Ukraine.

The top three countries in this category were Denmark, Germany and Switzerland.

The United States ranked 37th while Canada ranked 26th.

Participation: Mexico’s score and ranking improved

According to International IDEA, in the GSoD Indices, “Participation” is an aggregate measure of the extent to which people are actively involved at all levels of government. It is comprised of three factors that measure the space for civil society to operate freely (Civil Society), the extent to which people engage in political and non-political associations and trade unions (Civic Engagement), and voter turnout (Electoral Participation).

Mexico scored 0.451 out of 1 on this measure to rank 120th.

Mexico’s score increased 0.002 points compared to 2024, while it rose four positions in the rankings.

Mexico’s score in 2025 was on par with that of Papua New Guinea.

The top three countries in this category were Denmark, Switzerland and Norway.

The United States ranked 19th while Canada ranked 32nd.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Quintana Roo passes ‘Nicole’s Law,’ banning cosmetic surgery for minors
World.content:
The southeastern Mexican state of Quintana Roo this week passed a ban on invasive cosmetic surgery for minors, joining Durango in approving reforms known as “Nicole’s Law.”

The initiative takes its name from Paloma Nicole Arellano, a 14-year-old who died in Durango last September after cosmetic surgery. Her death exposed gaps in rules governing elective procedures for minors and intensified calls for state-level restrictions.

Two months later, Durango became the first Mexican state to enact a version of the law, with its legislators approving the measure 23-0.

The Durango law prohibits cosmetic surgery for minors except for reconstructive or medically necessary care It also strengthens penalties for people who practice medicine without proper credentials.

The federal entity of Mexico City followed suit in May, approving changes to Article 172 of its Health Law that invalidate authorizations for clinics to perform aesthetic surgery on minors.

The changes are state and city measures, not a single nationwide Mexican law.

The Quintana Roo Congress approved the reform on Monday, adding a provision to the state penal code that bars plastic, aesthetic and cosmetic surgeries on people younger than 18 when the purpose is solely to alter appearance.

The measure exempts reconstructive procedures with medical justification, including treatment for congenital malformations, cleft lip and palate, and other conditions requiring specialized care, such as accident-related injuries.

Doctors who perform prohibited procedures face six months to three years in prison, fines and suspensions from professional practice.

A congressional committee in Jalisco approved a similar package in August, though it has not yet received a final vote from the full legislature.

Coahuila could be the next state to approve a similar law. Deputy Jorge Valdés said his fellow members of Congress will debate and vote on a proposed Nicole’s Law during the current session.

Internationally, similar restrictions are uneven. The state of Queensland, Australia, has barred unnecessary cosmetic procedures for minors since 2008, and Norway also prohibits health professionals from providing higher-risk, nonmedical cosmetic procedures on minors, even with parental consent.

Comparable broad bans appear uncommon in the United States and Canada, where regulation generally centers on consent, medical judgment and procedure-specific age limits.

With reports from Excélsior, Infobae, La Jornada and N+

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico is only good for ‘tamales and tomatoes’ … and keeping the entire US economy functioning on a daily basis
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — After U.S. President Donald Trump said Mexico was only good for “tamales and tomatoes” last week, senior Mexican trade representatives held a press briefing Monday morning to clarify that while fresh tomatoes and steamed tamales are indeed foundational pillars of the national economy, Mexico also happens to provide the industrial, technological and automotive machinery that keeps the entire United States economy functioning on a daily basis.

The statement came after remarks from Trump suggested the United States could comfortably eliminate trade with its southern neighbor, omitting the fact that Mexico is the number one trade partner for the U.S.

“We want to reassure our northern neighbors that while our tamales remain world-class, our exports also include the computer servers powering their artificial intelligence, the advanced medical devices in their hospitals and the heavy auto parts keeping their assembly lines moving,” said Deputy Secretary of Trade Logistics Mateo Morales, presenting a series of charts detailing the US $60 billion in goods exported to the U.S. in July alone. “It turns out the nation feeding you lunch is also building the vehicle you drive to work.”

Morales emphasized that as the top trading partner of the U.S., Mexico’s commercial footprint extends well beyond agricultural goods, encompassing complex manufacturing networks that link factories from Monterrey to Detroit.

“If the flow of goods were to stop tomorrow, the issue would not merely be a shortage of menu items,” Morales noted. “It would be the immediate realization that half the light trucks on American highways were missing their transmissions.”

Trade officials concluded the conference by assuring consumers on both sides of the border that supply chains remain fully operational, confirming that shipments of high-tech machinery, auto components and fresh produce will continue shipping north on schedule.

World.title: In Grito, President Sheinbaum celebrates migrants, women insurgents and the dignity of Mexico’s diverse peoples
World.content:
Listen to this article

From the central balcony of the National Palace and in front of a huge crowd of celebrants gathered in Mexico City’s central square, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered the national Cry of Independence (Grito de Independencia) on Tuesday night, the eve of Mexico’s Independence Day.

“Mexicanas, Mexicanos, long live independence!” Sheinbaum declared 216 years after priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla issued the Cry of Dolores (Grito de Dolores) — a call for revolt against Spanish rule.

En el 216 Aniversario del Grito de Independencia, exaltamos a los héroes y heroínas que nos dieron patria, como Antonia Nava. También destacamos a los pueblos indígenas y afromexicanos, así como a nuestros hermanos y hermanas migrantes. ¡Que viva México libre, independiente y… pic.twitter.com/bJXNXaB43m — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) September 16, 2026

With the presidential sash draped over her torso, the Mexican flag in her left hand and her husband, Jesús María Tarriba, standing beside her, Sheinbaum issued a total of 21 arengas, or “cries of viva!“, each of which was met with a reciprocal “¡viva!” by those present in the Zócalo and Mexicans across the country.

A selection of Mexico’s independence heroines and heroes, the nation’s Indigenous and Afro-Mexican people and Mexicans living abroad were all wished long life by Sheinbaum, who made history a year ago by becoming the first female president of Mexico to deliver the Grito. In a year in which she has denounced U.S. interference in Mexican affairs, the president also issued an emphatic cry of ¡viva! in defense of Mexican independence and sovereignty.

“Long live Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla! Long live Josefa Ortiz Téllez-Girón! Long live José María Morelos y Pavón! Long live Leona Vicario! Long live Vicente Guerrero! Long live Gertrudis Bocanegra! Long live Guadalupe Victoria! Long live Antonia Nava!” Sheinbaum proclaimed.

“Long live the heroines and heroes who gave us a homeland! Long live the Indigenous and Afro-Mexican peoples! Long live our migrant sisters and brothers! Long live the dignity of the people of Mexico! Long live freedom! Long live equality! Long live justice! Long live democracy! Long live a free, independent and sovereign Mexico! ¡Viva México!”

Some of the people honored by the president, including Afro-Mexicans and the insurgent Antonia Nava, had never before been included in a national Cry of Independence.

After completing her second Grito, Sheinbaum rang the Campana de Dolores — the same bell that Hidalgo rang 216 years ago in the town of Dolores, Guanajuato — and waved the Mexican flag to the mass of people gathered in the Zócalo. The president received the flag from an escolta (color guard) made of up of six female military cadets.

After the Grito, a fireworks display lit up the sky above the Zócalo, where musical acts including the Grammy Award-winning Texan band Intocable played on Tuesday night.

Among the officials who witnessed Sheinbaum’s second Cry of Independence from National Palace vantage points were Attorney General Ernestina Godoy, Supreme Court Chief Justice Hugo Aguilar, Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez, Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard, Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla, Navy Minister Raymundo Pedro Morales and Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada.

Governors and mayors also issued Cries of Independence at ceremonies held on Tuesday night in cities and towns across the country.

No incidents reported at Mexico City’s 300,000-strong Independence celebration

The Mexico City government said in a statement that more than 300,000 people attended the Mexican Independence celebration in the Zócalo.

“The event took place peacefully and concluded without any casualties or incidents,” the government said.

“… Coordination between various agencies and the responsible participation of citizens allowed this commemoration to take place in an organized manner and in an environment of harmony,” the government said.

“The event also reflected the support of thousands of people for President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, who went to the Zócalo to participate in a day of profound significance for the history and identity of the country, as well as to hear a message to the nation in defense of our independence, dignity, and sovereignty.”

With reports from Reforma and La Jornada

World.title: Is Mexico’s soccer league a monopoly? Antitrust officials are looking to find out
World.content:
The National Antitrust Commission (CNA) has unilaterally opened an investigation into Liga MX, Mexico’s top professional soccer league and a massive cultural touchstone that captures the country’s passion for the sport.

An internal CNA document says the investigation aims to identify “the possible commission of relative monopolistic practices in the market of ‘affiliation, organization and access’ to professional federated football competitions in Mexico, as well as similar or related services.”

⚽ ¿Cómo investigamos el funcionamiento de un mercado?

José Manuel Haro Zepeda, titular de nuestra Autoridad Investigadora, explicó en @MVSNoticias las herramientas con las que contamos para analizar la organización y acceso a competiciones de fútbol profesional en México. pic.twitter.com/r2qgofrR9M — Comisión Nacional Antimonopolio (@AntimonopolioMX) September 15, 2026

In short, the CNA wants to know if a small group is violating the Federal Law of Economic Competition by unfairly controlling who can join, who can compete and how tournaments are organized, to the exclusion of other interested parties.

“After analyzing the events that occurred in recent months, the Investigating Authority determined that it has sufficient evidence to formally open an investigation on its own initiative for possible monopolistic practices in the professional soccer market in Mexico,” the CNA said in a public report.

The recent events referred to are likely related to a Liga MX decision in July to scrap promotion/relegation between the top-flight Mexican soccer league and the second-tier Liga Expansión. Liga MX also announced the end to payouts to the second-tier sides.

Promotion and relegation were scrapped in 2020 to insulate the clubs from the financial impacts of lost revenue during the enforced lockdown ordered due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Liga Expansión officials fiercely disputed the decision, even filing a suit with the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which ruled that the 2026-27 campaign was the earliest point at which promotion/relegation ought to be reinstituted.

Critics have also identified the league’s policy regarding possession of television broadcasting rights by teams as a monopolistic practice.

The commission has sought to make clear that there are no defendants identified as yet and it hasn’t been determined exactly who will be investigated. Instead, the probe will simply review whether competition law is being followed.

The investigation can last up to 120 business days, but can be extended up to three times longer if necessary. During that time, the CNA can request documents, visit offices, summon people to testify and conduct inspections.

If guilt is determined, the Liga MX and its member teams could face a penalty of up to 10% of their annual income and would be required to correct any monopolistic practices detected.

With reports from ESPN, El Economista, El Universal and SportCa

World.title: Should you be worried about the presence of brain-eating amoeba in Yucatán water bodies?
World.content:
A man died of Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM) in a Mérida hospital last week, most likely from contact with the brain-eating amoeba Naegleria fowleri, the Yucatán Health Services (SSY) reported on Monday.

The SSY confirmed the presence of N. fowleri in an artificial lake at the La Isla shopping center in Mérida, where the 34-year-old man worked as a water sports instructor.

FAMILIARES DESPIDEN A CARLOS, INSTRUCTOR QUE F4LL3C10 POR AMEBA COME CEREBROS#Video | Familiares y amigos despidieron con tristeza a Carlos, el joven instructor de wakeboard de 33 años que perdió la v1d4 tras contraer una agresiva infección por la ameba ‘Naegleria fowleri’ en… pic.twitter.com/f57zIqs8Ly — Yucatán Ahora (@yucatanahora) September 15, 2026

“It is a serious and extremely rare disease; this is the first case registered in Yucatán,” the SSY said in a statement.

The microorganism is most commonly found in stagnant, warm waters between 35°C and 46°C. It enters the body when contaminated water is forcefully inhaled through the nose, although it can also occur while swimming, diving or submerging one’s head in lakes, rivers or poorly chlorinated swimming pools.

PAM is not transmitted from person to person and is not acquired by drinking contaminated water, the SSY emphasized.

People living in the Yucatán capital have expressed concern about the water quality in nearby cenotes, where swimming is common. However, experts suggest that natural freshwater bodies are cooler, at between 24°C and 26°C, making the presence of N. fowleri far less likely.

The development of microorganisms in pools can be avoided through chlorination and pH management, and in larger water bodies through adequate water movement, which promotes aeration. Regular cleaning and maintenance can also help avoid the accumulation of sediment, organic matter, algae and biofilms in stagnant water, conditions that attract N. fowleri.

The first symptoms of PAM are usually severe headache, fever, nausea and vomiting. According to initial reports, the victim presented with severe symptoms of central nervous system infection and was taken to a hospital in the city, where he died.

Health authorities ordered the temporary closure of the water feature at La Isla while samples were tested at the Hidalgo State Public Health Laboratory, which confirmed the presence of N. fowleri. Meanwhile, cleaning efforts and technical inspections were carried out at the site.

Epidemiological investigators are conducting interviews to locate other individuals who may have come into contact with the water.

The SSY said it plans to investigate the companies responsible for water quality and lake maintenance for their compliance with Mexican rules and regulations.

“Anyone who has violated health regulations will be sanctioned,” the SSY stressed.

According to the SSY statement, once the responsible company demonstrates through laboratory tests that the lake water is suitable for recreational use in accordance with legal standards, a new verification and sampling of the water will be conducted and a decision will be made on whether to lift the temporary closure.

With reports from Reportur, La Jornada and Diario de Yucatán

World.title: Kenya vs Eritrea on September 26: Harambee Stars Host AFCON 2027 Qualifier at Nairobi’s Nyayo Stadium
World.content:
Sports: Kenya

Key Facts What. A 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying match between Kenya and Eritrea, Group D.

A 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying match between Kenya and Eritrea, Group D. When. Saturday, September 26, 2026, at 1 p.m. GMT, which is 4 p.m. East Africa Time.

Given the fixed guest capacity typical of boat parties, buying ahead is safer than hoping for availability at the dock on the night of the event.

Who the Event Is For

The party is aimed at Barbados’s existing salsa dancing community as well as newcomers curious about Latin dance styles, with music expected to draw heavily on salsa classics.

Expats and visitors without salsa experience should still find the atmosphere approachable, since boat parties of this kind typically prioritize a fun, informal vibe over formal dance instruction.

Practical Tips for a Night at Sea

As with any boat event, checking the weather forecast for September 25 and dressing appropriately for a breezy evening on the water is worth doing ahead of time.

Guests prone to seasickness should consider standard precautions in advance, since the four-hour format means there is no early exit once the boat departs.

World.title: Twelve students receive Refrigeration and Air Conditioning scholarships as Belize marks World Ozone Day
World.content:
Twelve students receive Refrigeration and Air Conditioning scholarships as Belize marks World Ozone Day

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Department of the Environment (DOE), through the National Ozone Unit, awarded 12 scholarships under the Refrigeration and Air Conditioning (RAC) Scholarship Programme.

The recipients are enrolled in RAC programmes at ITVETs in Belize City, Orange Walk, and Stann Creek, and will receive support for the 2026–2027 academic year, including tuition, a toolbox of servicing tools, and personal protective equipment.

Three of the twelve recipients are female trainees, marking a step toward greater participation of women in the RAC sector.

The ceremony coincided with World Ozone Day, observed annually on September 16. This year’s theme, “Global Action for a Cooler Planet,” marks ten years of sustainable cooling efforts under the Kigali Amendment.

The DOE said the scholarships reflect Belize’s ongoing transition toward lower-global-warming-potential refrigerants and more efficient cooling technologies, which requires a pipeline of skilled technicians.

Through the programme, the DOE said it is investing in the next generation of RAC professionals to help promote safe, efficient, and environmentally responsible cooling practices going forward.

The twelve scholarship recipients are Zadiel Dias, Patrick Zetina, Samuel Alamilla, Brandon Ysaguirre, Gerardo Magana, Milcar Ku, Rilma Urbina, Edwardo Coc, Cierra Teck, Jahleel Flowers, Erwin Colon, and Dorda Castillo.

World.title: Garbage dumped at Yo Chen Village entrance cleaned up, Department of Environment steps up surveillance
World.content:
Garbage dumped at Yo Chen Village entrance cleaned up, Department of Environment steps up surveillance

By Zoila Palma: The Department of the Environment (DOE) has cleaned up a garbage site at the entrance of Yo Chen Village following a media report regarding the issue.

The DOE said it investigated the matter promptly and worked with the Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing (MIDH) to address the concern.

The area has since been cleaned and placed under surveillance to help prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.

The DOE is reminding the public that under the Pollution Regulations, it is an offence to place or permit refuse to be placed on any land without written permission from the department.

The DOE is encouraging community members to remain vigilant and report instances of illegal dumping at this or any other location.

World.title: Belize @45 History Tour brings dialogue on Independence to Orange Walk Town
World.content:
Belize @45 History Tour brings dialogue on Independence to Orange Walk Town

By Zoila Palma: The Belize @45 Magical History Tour made its way through Orange Walk Town on September 15, continuing a series of events aimed at encouraging dialogue and reflection on the country’s history.

The tour is led by the Institute for Social & Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) in partnership with historian Dr. Assad Shoman, and focuses on Belize’s path to independence, the experiences that have shaped its national story, and ongoing conversations around decolonization.

During the day, the tour engaged students from New Hope High School, Muffles College High School, and Orange Walk Technical High School in discussions on Belize’s history, national identity, and the range of experiences that continue to shape the country. Students were given the opportunity to ask questions and share their perspectives on how the past connects to present-day Belize.

That evening, the tour held a public forum at the Banquitas House of Culture, bringing together community leaders and residents of Orange Walk Town. The forum allowed attendees to discuss the country’s shared history and consider how a deeper understanding of the past could inform Belize’s future direction.

ISCR-NICH thanked the students, educators, community leaders, and residents who took part in the day’s events, noting their questions and input as central to the tour’s goals.

The Magical History Tour is made possible through the National Celebrations Commission and the National Institute of Culture and History, along with partners including the University of Belize.

World.title: International News: Trump names Haiti security expert Austin Holmes as Ambassador nominee
World.content:
International News: Trump names Haiti security expert Austin Holmes as Ambassador nominee

By Zoila Palma: U.S. President Donald Trump has nominated Florida businessman Austin Holmes to serve as the next U.S. ambassador to Haiti, as the Caribbean nation continues to grapple with a severe political and security crisis.

Holmes’ nomination was submitted to the U.S. Senate on Monday, September 14, and he must receive Senate confirmation before taking up the diplomatic post.

Holmes has longstanding ties to Haiti through humanitarian and security work and has previously lived in the country with his family.

Earlier this year, he testified before a Senate appropriations subcommittee during a hearing examining U.S. security and foreign assistance priorities in Haiti.

During his testimony, Holmes said he has participated in security operations in Haiti, including kidnapping recoveries and emergency extractions. He cited the 2023 recovery of American humanitarian worker Jeff Frazier, who was kidnapped by gangs while participating in a food distribution mission and held captive for 43 days. Holmes said his team “successfully recovered” Frazier.

Holmes said his approach to operations in Haiti is based on local knowledge and long-term engagement. “Deep cultural fluency, long-term presence and operational leadership rooted in local context” have driven the results achieved by his teams, he said, adding that many of his personnel are Haitian and Haitian American with local experience, language skills and relationships.

World.title: Police intercept pickup carrying suspected uncustomed goods in Orange Walk
World.content:
Police intercept pickup carrying suspected uncustomed goods in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police intercepted a pickup truck near the Blue Creek Dam in Orange Walk earlier this month and reportedly discovered several boxes and sacks of food products suspected to be uncustomed goods.

According to police information, personnel from the North HIT conducted a staging operation in the area between approximately 5:30 p.m. and 8:40 p.m. on Friday, September 4.

During the operation, officers intercepted a white Dodge Ram being driven by a 25 year old man from San Felipe Village.

A search of the vehicle reportedly led to the discovery of six boxes of oxtail, five sacks of cabbage and 15 sacks of onions.

The driver and the goods were subsequently escorted to the Orange Walk Customs Department.

Police say the matter was handed over to a Customs officer for further action.

No information was provided on the estimated value of the goods or whether any charges have been filed.

World.title: Police chase ends with reckless driving charge in Orange Walk
World.content:
Police chase ends with reckless driving charge in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 24 year old Orange Walk man has been charged with reckless driving following an early morning police pursuit.

According to police information, officers were conducting mobile patrol on San Narciso Street at around 1:20 a.m. on September 15 when their attention was drawn to a black motorcycle with a defective rear light.

Police say the rider was signalled to stop but allegedly drove off and began swerving from side to side along the street.

Officers reportedly followed the motorcycle for approximately five minutes before managing to intercept the rider.

Police say the man told officers he had not been trying to escape.

A search was conducted and nothing incriminating was found. Checks on the motorcycle documents also reportedly showed that the licence and insurance were up to date.

The rider was then informed that he was being detained for reckless driving and was escorted to the Orange Walk Police Station.

Police identified him as Nathan J. Navarrete, 24, a labourer of Santa Familia Street, Orange Walk.

He was later formally arrested and charged with reckless driving.

World.title: Carmelita woman charged after police reportedly find 19.7 grams of cannabis
World.content:
Carmelita woman charged after police reportedly find 19.7 grams of cannabis

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 35 year old woman from Carmelita Village has been charged with possession of controlled drugs after police reportedly found 19.7 grams of suspected cannabis during a house search on Wednesday morning.

According to police information, officers executed a search warrant at a residence in Carmelita Village at around 9:30 a.m.
