World.title: Russian Despatch: Moscow Plays Old Cards in Balkan Elections
World.content:
Russia enters autumn in an atmosphere of foreboding. Intensified Ukrainian strikes, a gasoline deficit, and lack of progress on the battlefront are leading more and more people to surmise that the Kremlin is no longer able to wage its war against Ukraine as a distant operation that has little impact on Russian everyday life.

It will only get worse, and soon the regime will demand more sacrifices for its geopolitical adventures.

The date for change looks set for late September, following parliamentary elections.

Though the vote is tightly managed by authorities, the Kremlin still pays lip service to democratic procedures. It avoids taking unpopular steps during the campaign and strives to preserve a semblance of stability at least until after voting day.

World.title: Hungary Needs Oil from Croatia: Can the Two Sides Bury the Hatchet?
World.content:
Tug-of-war over JANAF

MOL insists it is prepared to diversify its sources of oil and gas, but needs more time. Experts say it is also likely looking to strike a better deal with Croatia’s JANAF, the state-owned pipeline operator which operates the network that links the Adriatic port Omisalj on the island of Krk to Hungary.

“We have been working on crude oil diversification for more than 10 years,” MOL told BIRN.

The company said it had invested 170 million dollars to improve the transportation and processing of alternative seaborne oil even before the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war, and since 2022 it has tested more than a dozen different types of crude at its refineries. MOL’s refineries in Szazhalombatta and Bratislava are optimised to process Russian Urals crude.

“Our overall investment program, worth 500 million dollars, is expected to be completed in 2027,” the company’s statement said.

MOL said it imported an annual average of 1.3 million tonnes of crude via the JANAF pipeline between 2022 and 2025, and 1.5 million tonnes in 2026. According to Reuters, MOL imported 9.7 million tonnes from Russia in 2025 – roughly six times more than via JANAF – an amount split almost equally between its refineries in Slovakia and Hungary.

Experts broadly agree that JANAF is Hungary’s only real alternative to Russian oil. But the pipeline’s technical capacity is contested by Hungarian and Croatian experts, let alone the transit prices, which critics say far exceed market prices.

“It is unclear if JANAF could deliver the capacities Hungary would need to fully replace its Russia supplies,” the energy expert Deak said. “Most probably, a second pipeline or at least a capacity increase would be needed to ensure full security.”

That is technically feasible, but would require significant investment from the Croatian side.

MOL told BIRN that it had conducted several short-term capacity tests, but the results were inconclusive. Before making any switch, the entire supply chain, including the capacity of the Croatian section of the Adria pipeline, should be tested at full refinery capacity, under different weather conditions and using different types of crude oil.

JANAF disputes the suggestion that it lacks the necessary capacity. The company told BIRN that it “technically and organisationally has the capacity to meet the entire annual crude oil needs of the MOL Group’s refineries in Hungary and Slovakia”.

It described itself as the only safe and reliable source of energy supplies for Croatia, the EU and neighbouring countries like Hungary. JANAF said the capacities had been demonstrated by the volumes delivered “when their [MOL’s] supply via Druzhba was suspended”.

The Druzhba pipeline, which transports Russian crude to Hungary via Ukraine, was hit by a drone strike in January on Ukrainian territory near the city of Brody, and remained out of operation for almost three months.

What MOL does not mention, however, is that by switching to non-Russian crude, the company would lose most of the profits generated by the price differential between the cheaper Russian oil and the international oil price. Transit prices via Croatia could also be added to the bill. This is where the Hungarian side believes Croatia is profiteering.

However, Jasminko Umicevic, a former deputy CEO of INA who headed up the INA office in Budapest between 1991-1997, rejects these claims as “nonsense”.

“Croatia was accused of war profiteering. It was claimed that JANAF’s prices were five times higher than world market prices and that JANAF had no capacity,” Umicevic told BIRN, saying the accusations served only one purpose: “to keep the business with Russia going”.

“When you buy oil transported by ships, at least a hundred people know the terms and conditions under which it is being bought,” he said. With pipeline delivery, it is harder to establish the prices, he added.

Umicevic also rejected the allegations of the previous Hungarian government that JANAF lacked the necessary capacity. “All of this happened because, as is now clear, they were in direct contact with Russia,” he said.

World.title: European Parliamentarians Slam Serbia for ‘Disturbing’ Funeral of Ratko Mladic
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told a debate in the European Parliament on Tuesday about the glorification of convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic that images from Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade were “profoundly disturbing”.

The debate was held a week after Mladic’s funeral with military honours in Belgrade prompted strong reactions from European institutions and several EU member states.

“It was especially disturbing to see Serbian ministers, state officials and military representatives alongside leaders and politicians from [Bosnia’s Serb-led entity] Republika Srpska, attend the funeral and publicly honour a war criminal,” Kos said.

Serbia is an EU candidate state and Kos said that Belgrade must fulfill its responsibilities. “By applying for EU membership, Serbia committed to our standards, principles, and values,” she said.

“The European Commission has been clear that the glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism is fundamentally incompatible with these values. It has no place in the EU. It has no place in the EU candidate countries,” she added.

Mladic, who died in The Hague while serving a life sentence for genocide and war crimes, was buried at Belgrade’s Topcider Cemetery in Belgrade on September 7. The funeral service was led by Serbian Orthodox Church Patriarch Porfirije, and Serbian government ministers came to pay their respects.

At Tuesday’s debate, several Croatian MEPs slammed the Serbian administration and President Aleksandar Vucic for their role in Mladic’s funeral.

Davor Ivo Stier, MEP for Croatia’s Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, which sits with the European People’s Party, EPP, group said Serbian President Vucic “did not organise a state funeral, but as commander in chief, is responsible for the military honours shown to Mladic”.

“We need to be loud and say clearly that our politics towards Serbia have been mild and ineffective and we need to show and decide that there is no place in Europe for those who glorify Ratko Mladic, and we should not give European funds to those who do not want to distance themselves from [former Yugoslav leader] Slobodan Milosevic’s politics,” Stier added.

Tonino Picula, from the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats group in the European Parliament, said that it is “justified to ask whether the European Union needs to continue negotiating with Serbia while this government is in power”.

Helmut Brandstatter, who sits with Renew Europe, said that the EPP should cut its ties with Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party.

“We cannot tolerate the celebration of a war criminal. A government that glorifies such atrocities can never be part of the European Union,” Brandstatter added.

Brandstatter also highlighted that Serbian society is European and that Serbia should be part of the European Union, but as a democracy.

Commenting on Serbia’s upcoming snap elections, Brandstatter said: “He [Vucic] wants to have a small majority again to get our money – and friendship with Russia, and that cannot happen. The Serbs are welcome here but the authoritarian regime is not part of the European Union.”

World.title: Autism Centre: 35 Million Euro Zagreb Project Gets Underway After 20+ Years
World.content:
September the 16th, 2026 – The long awaited Autism Centre is an enormous 35 million euro Zagreb project that is finally getting underway after a long 20+ year wait.

After over 20 years of announcements, the City of Zagreb has finally obtained a building permit for the construction of a new Autism Centre in Oporovec. It will provide modern and adapted conditions for learning, development and professional support for around 200 children, and will bring together programmes that are currently run at multiple locations across Zagreb.

Poslovni reports that the estimated value of the new Autism Centre in Oporovec is around 35 million euros, of which 19.3 million euros will be financed from EU funds through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NPOO), while the remaining amount will be secured from the City of Zagreb budget. Once the building permit becomes final, the preparation of project documentation and the public procurement procedure for selecting the contractor will follow. Construction is planned to start in the summer of 2027, with a planned duration of 18 months.

The new school will have 48 classroom departments and educational groups, as well as three preschool education and care groups. Specialised spaces are also planned for music and art therapy, household skills and aquatic therapy with a pool, sports halls and other facilities adapted to the needs of users.

According to the project by the architectural office SODA-ARHITEKTI, the centre will cover more than 9,600 square metres on three floors, with 60 parking spaces, nine of which are designated for people with disabilities. Attention has also been paid to the outdoor landscaping, with a main square featuring a sensory park, fountains and facilities for developing motor skills planned. “This is another of the projects that have been promised in Zagreb for more than twenty years, and now it is finally going into realisation,” said Zagreb Mayor Tomislav Tomašević.

Deputy Mayor Danijela Dolenec stressed that the new school will represent a major step forward in the quality of spatial and programmatic conditions for the education and upbringing of children and young people with autism. The Autism Centre currently cares for around 300 users through preschool programmes, primary education, full-day and half-day stay programmes, and organised housing, she said.

Dolenec added that the City of Zagreb continues to invest in the existing capacities of the Autism Centre. A public procurement for the renovation and arrangement of the sports hall in Ljevakovićeva Street, worth 250,000 euros, was recently launched, and around 750,000 euros has been invested in the renovation of the Centre’s existing facilities in recent years.

By the end of the year, the opening of a new Centre space in Juraj Dalmatinac Street is also planned, where early developmental and psychosocial support services will be provided for 40 children, as well as a stay programme for 30 adults with autism spectrum disorders. The City of Zagreb has also stated that 24 new special classroom departments and educational groups have been established in the new school year, increasing existing capacities by almost a quarter.

The number of special classroom departments has grown from 64 back in 2021 to 126 in 2026, while the network of schools implementing these programmes has been expanded to 55 schools across Zagreb, according to the City of Zagreb press release.

World.title: Zadar Mobile Boat Pharmacy is in the Final for the Best EU Project Award
World.content:
September the 16th, 2026 – The very commendable Zadar mobile pharmacy on a boat is in the final for the Best EU Project Award.

The Zadar project “Mobile Pharmacy – boat for the islands of Zadar County” has secured a place in the final of this year’s competition for the best EU project in the category Contribution to the Local and Regional Community. Morski reports that this very commendable initiative is primarily aimed at introducing a mobile pharmaceutical service in the island area in order to significantly facilitate residents’ access to medicines and professional advice, especially those in more traffic-isolated places.

The competition is organised by the Croatian Association of Counties, the Office of the European Parliament in Croatia and the portal Župan.hr, under the auspices of the Ministry of Regional Development and EU Funds. In strong competition from almost 50 projects submitted from all over Croatia, the expert jury selected a total of 36 finalists, with the Zadar mobile pharmacy competing among the 18 best in its category.

The winners in the readers’ choice category are decided by the public, and public voting officially ran from the 8th to the 15th of September, 2026.

World.title: Croatia to Get Most Modern Thermal Spa in Historic €42 Million project
World.content:
September the 16th, 2026 – Croatia is set to get its most modern and largest thermal spa as a historic 42 million euro project finally nears completion.

Works on Wellovar in Veliki Korenovo, the largest construction project in the history of Bjelovar worth €42 million, have entered the final stage. Poslovni reports that the enormous complex with a total of ten pools is already taking on its final appearance, and finishing works and system checks are currently underway before opening. Bjelovar Mayor Dario Hrebak regularly visits the construction site and emphasises that the focus is now on the details and on balancing and calibrating one of the most complex and modern heating, cooling and hot water systems in Croatia.

“Works on the largest thermal spa in Croatia, our Wellovar, are nearing completion. Only minor details remain, but this is one of the most complex and modern heating, cooling and hot water systems in Croatia. We now have to ensure that the entire system is balanced and calibrated. It is hard to say when we will open the doors. Our great wish is that it will be on the 29th of September, on the Bjelovar City Day, but it is very difficult to predict,” said Hrebak. He added that at this moment the exact opening date is not crucial; the most important thing is that the project is completed to a high standard.

“What matters is that everything we see is heading towards its final stage and that the people of Bjelovar will get a standard that 95 percent of other cities in Croatia do not have. Croatia will also get an excellent centre for the development of water sports,” he stressed. In addition to tourist and recreational facilities, Wellovar is also expected to play an important role in the development of sport. According to Hrebak, the facility has been designed to meet the standards for hosting national and international swimming and water polo competitions. “We are truly looking forward to it soon opening its doors and delighting our citizens, as well as all tourists and visitors with its facilities,” Hrebak concluded.

With the completion of this massive €42 million project, Bjelovar is set to gain a major new sports, recreational and tourist complex. Although the official opening date has not yet been confirmed, the city administration’s wish is for Wellovar to welcome its first visitors as early as the 19th of September, on Bjelovar’s City Day.

World.title: Croatia to Make Changes to ENC Usage as of March 1st, 2027
World.content:
September the 16th, 2026 – Croatia will make significant changes to ENC usage as of March the 1st, 2027, and drivers with multiple vehicles need to pay particular attention to what is coming.

The much anticipated new Croatian road toll collection system will use ENC technology, but also automatic licence plate recognition via cameras. Poslovni reports that for years now, ENC has been one of the simplest ways to pay motorway tolls across Croatia. You put the device in your car, drive through the marked lane, and the system automatically handles the payment. However, with the introduction of the new electronic toll collection system, one thing becomes much more important than before: the ENC will also be linked to the vehicle’s registration plate.

From the 1st of March 2027, when the new system starts operating, the vehicle’s registration number, data on the ENC device, and a valid means of payment will have to be registered in the system for the ENC model to be used. The law expressly stipulates that a driver using ENC must pass through the toll point in a vehicle whose registration plates are identical to those linked in the system to the ENC device in the vehicle. This means it will no longer be enough simply to take a working ENC device and put it in any car. Before driving, it will be important that the vehicle being used on the motorway is properly registered in the new system.

this is particularly important if you use one enc for multiple cars

The change is especially significant for those who currently use the same ENC in several cars. Under the current rules of Croatian Motorways, an ENC device for vehicle categories IA, I and II is not tied to a single registration number. It can be used in multiple vehicles of the same category, provided the same device is not used simultaneously in more than one vehicle. The new system introduces a different principle: the registration number becomes an integral part of the data linked to the ENC device. Therefore, drivers who currently simply move the ENC from one car to another will have to make sure that the registration of the vehicle they are using is correctly linked to the device in the Electronic Toll Collection System.

The law itself does not currently stipulate that one ENC can necessarily be linked to only one registration number. The detailed rules on use and changes to data will be regulated by the rules of the new system. However, it is clear that the previous practice of simply transferring the device without checking the registration will no longer be sufficient. The good news for existing users is that current ENC devices will not become unusable. The law obliges motorway operators to include ENC devices purchased before the establishment of the new system into the new ESNC no later than its start.

the new cameras will read license plates

The new toll collection system will use ENC technology as well as automatic licence plate recognition via cameras. For passenger cars and other light vehicles, drivers will be able to choose between the ENC model and a model based solely on the registration number and a registered means of payment. When using ENC, the system will therefore have data on both the device and the vehicle’s registration number. Cameras will record the vehicle’s passage and read the licence plates in order to identify the vehicle and verify payment. For drivers, this brings a new habit: before driving, it will no longer be enough simply to check whether the ENC is in the car and whether there are sufficient funds on the account. They will also have to make sure that the vehicle’s registration number is correctly registered in the system. This is precisely what could be particularly important for those who currently use one ENC in multiple cars.

World.title: adidas and HNS Unveil New Croatia National Team Kits
World.content:
adidas has unveiled the long-awaited new official kits for the Croatia national football team, the first set produced under a long-term partnership with the Croatian Football Federation (HNS).

Combining cutting-edge performance innovation with elements founded in Croatian culture and identity, the new kits celebrate the heritage, pride and passion that define Croatian football.

The unveiling marks the start of a new chapter for one of international football’s most recognizable national teams. Having cemented its place among the world’s leading footballing nations, Croatia will step out in an adidas kit for the first time as part of the partnership announced earlier this year.

HNS / adidas

The new home shirt offers a modern take on Croatia’s iconic red-and-white checkerboard pattern, one of the most striking visual symbols in international football. For the first time, letters from the Glagolitic alphabet — the oldest known Slavic script and an important symbol of Croatian cultural heritage — have been woven into the checkerboard design, running throughout the pattern to give one of Croatian football’s most recognizable emblems a fresh, contemporary twist. The back of the collar also features the word “HRVATSKA” written in Glagolitic script, further tying the shirt to Croatia’s cultural history.

The away shirt, meanwhile, draws inspiration from Croatia’s long tradition of lace-making, a craft passed down through generations and another significant part of the country’s cultural heritage. An intricate lace-inspired motif runs across the shirt’s navy base, offering a modern interpretation of that tradition. The design is completed by a collar detail bearing the word “HRVATSKA” in typography inspired by cross-stitch embroidery, linking the traditional craft to contemporary football design.

HNS / adidas

“These shirts are much more than innovative football kits and striking design. Working with adidas, we chose a design that perfectly combines local pride with a global perspective. Those are exactly the values Croatia has always stood for, and now a new generation of fans and players will carry them forward,” said Marijan Kustić, president of the Croatian Football Federation.

Both shirts were developed to meet the demands of football at the highest level and feature the latest adidas CLIMACOOL+ technology. Specially developed stretch fabrics and 3D body-mapping technology improve ventilation and breathability, helping players stay dry through high-intensity matches and in hot conditions. Perforated three-stripe panels and strategically placed mesh zones further boost airflow and comfort.

Croatia’s men’s national team will wear the new kits for the first time during the upcoming UEFA Nations League fixtures.

Alongside the new shirts, adidas is also launching a wider Croatia national team collection that includes shorts, socks, training wear and leisurewear, designed for fans who want to show their connection to the national team both on and off the pitch.

A video unveiling the new kits has been posted on the Instagram profiles of @adidasfootball and the Croatian Football Federation.

The new Croatia national team kits, along with the full HNS x adidas collection, are available to buy from today at the official HNS online store. Pick out your kit, step into a new era of Croatian football, and wear it with pride.

World.title: CRANE Forum 2026: Productivity as a European Priority, Judiciary as the Greatest Obstacle to Investment
World.content:
September the 15th, 2026 – The CRANE Forum 2026 was recently held, which welcomed around 200 guests from the fields of investment to politics, and from economics to financial institution representatives.

As stated, around 200 guests involved with the Croatian economy, entrepreneurs and investors, members of the Government, ambassadors and representatives of international financial institutions, as well as county prefects and mayors, gathered at the Tihočaj estate in the Žumberak – Samobor Hills Nature Park to discuss investment prospects and the frameworks in which they will be implemented.

In Jastrebarsko on the 12th of September 2026, the fourth CRANE Forum, organised by CRANE, the Croatian Association of Investors and Business Angels, was held. The location was the Tihočaj estate in the Žumberak – Samobor Hills Nature Park. Once again this year, the Forum brought together all levels of decision-making on a single investment in one place: 200 guests from the top of the Croatian economy, entrepreneurs and investors, members of the Government, ambassadors and representatives of international financial institutions, as well as county prefects and mayors.

“Since 2008, CRANE has been connecting entrepreneurs and investors and bringing together capital, knowledge and experience with those who make the decisions. For development and new investments, finding an investor is not enough. What is also needed is a state that cooperates and understands the vision, and a local environment that knows how to create the conditions for its implementation. That is why we do not build the Forum as a conference, but as a working meeting at which everyone who decides on a single investment is present,” said Davorin Štetner, President of CRANE.

The key topics of this year’s Forum were the new multiannual financial framework of the European Union after 2027, the tax system as a competitive advantage, the role of local self-government in attracting strategic investments, and investments in healthcare.

Speaking about what Croatia can expect from the EU’s multiannual financial framework after 2027, Nataša Mikuš Žigman, Minister of Regional Development and EU Funds, stressed that the priorities coming from Brussels are focused on security, defence and climate efficiency, but equally on investments in productivity and competitiveness. Croatia, she announced, has already begun preparing a future competitiveness investment programme that will combine public and private funds, with the aim of raising the productivity of the economy. Among the novelties are milder requirements for technical documentation at the application and contracting stage, the possibility for applicants with smaller tax debts not to be excluded from the procedure but to settle them before the decision on the award of support is made, and raising the threshold for the implementation of procurement procedures with simple procurement via the eKohezija platform. In the negotiations on the new multiannual financial framework, Croatia insists that administrative burden relief actually reaches end-users and does not remain only on the Brussels–Member State axis.

On the panel dedicated to the tax system, in which Tomislav Ćorić, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, Davor Baković, President of the Croatian Exporters Association and Chairman of the Management Board of Končar MT d.d., Davor Tremac, Executive Director of Fono, and Domagoj Kamenski, Executive Director of Kamgrad, participated, it was emphasised that the Croatian tax framework in itself is not an obstacle to growth, but in certain segments even represents a competitive advantage, with a corporate income tax rate lower than the average of developed countries and excellent incentives for investment and research and development.

That the tax rate is not decisive is also shown by comparison with the surrounding region: ahead of Croatia on investment attractiveness rankings are the Czech Republic and Slovenia, which have significantly higher corporate income tax rates. The key problem, as Tremac stressed, is distrust in the judiciary, because what is contracted on paper is difficult and slow to enforce before Croatian courts, and this has been pointed out for thirty years without progress. The price of this distrust is measured in capital that does not arrive: when the enforceability of contractual protections is not certain, investors do not abandon the investment, but the jurisdiction, so Croatian companies register their holding companies in Ireland, the Netherlands or Luxembourg, and the tax base moves with them. The conclusion of the panel is therefore that lowering tax rates would not solve a problem that the rates did not create; the greatest contribution to the investment climate would come from judicial reform, i.e. the speed and predictability of resolving commercial disputes.

Speaking about investments in healthcare from the Government’s perspective, Minister of Health Irena Hrstić emphasised that the Government of the Republic of Croatia has invested around €3.4 billion in the healthcare system over the past ten years or so, and that investments continue in line with the policy of balanced regional development – from the new University Hospital Centre Osijek and the project for a new University Hospital Centre for Dalmatia, which the Ministry and the Government have already given the green light, to the hospital in Blato, whose foundation stone will soon be laid and which will be the first “Carbon Zero” hospital in Europe, heated by geothermal energy and financed by European funds. The leading principle is smart investment, with the emphasis that the goal is functional healthcare equally accessible to all parts of Croatia.

A strong diplomatic dimension was given to the Forum by the presentation of new interlocutors of the Croatian business community at the international level: Ronke Amoni Ogunsulire, World Bank Director for Croatia and Slovenia, Her Excellency Anne Toft Sørensen, Ambassador of the Kingdom of Denmark to the Republic of Croatia, and His Excellency Glenn Morrison, Ambassador of Australia to the Republic of Croatia. Their presentation opens new channels of cooperation and a direct link between the domestic business and investment community and partners outside Croatia, which is crucial for attracting investment and strengthening export opportunities. In addition to them, the Forum also gathered other esteemed ambassadors and representatives of international financial institutions, thereby confirming its role as a meeting place of the Croatian economy with international partners.

what is crane?

CRANE – the Croatian Association of Investors and Business Angels is otherwise the oldest Croatian association of investors and business angels, founded in 2008. It connects ambitious entrepreneurs with investors who invest money, knowledge, skills and business contacts in their projects, with the aim that as many innovative companies in the early stage of development as possible grow into successful business stories. CRANE is the national representative of Croatia in the European Business Angels Network (EBAN) and a member of the Global Business Angels Network (GBAN), and in addition to its investment activity systematically advocates a better regulatory and tax framework for entrepreneurs and investors in Croatia and at the level of the European Union. More at www.crane.hr.

World.title: Hybrid Electro-Diesel Train Between Split and Zagreb Now Operational
World.content:
September the 15th, 2026 – The very first hybrid electro-diesel train between Split and Zagreb is now fully operational. Here are all the details.

As of today (September the 15th, 2026) the very first electro-diesel train will enter service on the Split – Zagreb Main Station route. The train departs (as it has today) from Split station at 07:54. Poslovni reports that the new train is adapted to the specific characteristics of the Zagreb–Split line, which is partly electrified and partly non-electrified. It has 150 seats, and passengers have access to free Wi-Fi, power sockets next to the seats, a modern information system, visual and audio announcements, ramps for people with disabilities, and space for bicycles. The train also features self-service machines for buying coffee and other hot drinks, water, soft drinks, sweets and snacks.

The introduction of the new electro-diesel trains for long-distance transport continues the modernisation of the HŽ Passenger Transport fleet, while at the same time reducing energy consumption, noise and greenhouse gas emissions. Experts from the KONČAR Group, in cooperation with numerous Croatian companies, were involved in the development and production of the trains.

As part of this massive project, six electro-diesel trains are being procured, financed by a loan from the European Investment Bank amounting to 57.3 million euros. All six trains will be put into service by the end of this year. As of December 2026, with the start of the new timetable, Zagreb and Split will be connected by four daily trains, further improving the connectivity of Croatia’s two largest cities and the quality of travel.

Ahead of the first regular journey of the new train, statements for the media will be given by State Secretary for Railways Žarko Tušek from the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure, President of the Management Board of HŽ Passenger Transport Željko Ukić, President of the Management Board of KONČAR Gordan Kolak, Split-Dalmatia County Prefect Blaženko Boban, and Deputy Mayor of Split Matea Dorčić. Also present on the journey will be Zadar County Prefect Josip Bilaver and Šibenik-Knin County Prefect Paško Rakić.

World.title: Brač Fire: Residents Without Electricity Told to Follow TV and Radio
World.content:
September the 15th, 2026 – Brač residents worried for their properties and indeed their lives in the recent Milna fire were very clumsily advised to follow the TV and radio – despite having no electricity.

The Early Warning and Crisis Management System (SRUUK) was activated on Saturday evening because of a large fire in the wider Milna area on Brač. Lukrecija Zderic reports for Index that residents in that area received a message on their mobile phones with a link to instructions on how to act, along with advice to follow further announcements on television and radio. At the same time, part of Brač had no electricity, which raised the question of how exactly people without power were supposed to obtain new information about the fire.

On Saturday evening, the fire, driven by strong wind, spread rapidly towards Milna as well as the bays of Duboka and Osibova, where Resort Gava with a large number of tourists is located. More than 200 firefighters were on the ground trying to stop the fire from spreading towards the populated area.

false evacuation and sruuk activation

The red sky above Brač and Milna was visible even from Split, while Index readers filmed the firestorm approaching the settlement. As the situation became increasingly serious, various pieces of information about a possible evacuation began to arrive. Shortly before 23:00, a notice about the evacuation of the population was published on the Facebook page of the Milna Volunteer Fire Department. It stated that the situation was critical and called on citizens to make their private boats available for evacuation needs. The post was deleted about half an hour later, and services on the ground reported that there was no official evacuation.

At 23:28 the SRUUK was activated. Citizens in the endangered area received a warning via SMS or Cell Broadcast about the danger, together with a link to additional information. Clicking the link opens a page of the Ministry of the Interior (MUP), i.e. the Civil Protection Directorate, containing “Instructions for Citizens.” These are general instructions on how to behave during a fire, and below them citizens are directed to follow further announcements via television, radio and links of the Civil Protection Directorate. At that moment Milna was already without electricity. The earlier post about evacuation further confused residents. Some did not know whether they should leave the place, so they prepared for evacuation and went out onto the street by the sea.

The SRUUK activated once again that evening at 00:22, when citizens once more received a link with instructions on how to act in the event of a fire. Why residents in the endangered area without electricity were recommended to follow information via TV and radio remains unknown for now. Because of the approaching fire a partial evacuation of the most endangered parts of Milna and the surrounding area was carried out, while the entire settlement was never evacuated at any point.

a fire warning for a fire on an island was received in split… on the mainland

The Civil Protection Directorate was therefore asked for an explanation as to exactly why citizens in an area affected by a power outage were directed to television and radio, who in such a situation is responsible for delivering key information, and how many times the SRUUK was activated during the fire on Brač. We will publish the answer when we receive it. However, the problem was not only in the content of the messages. Residents we spoke to said that some received the warning around 23:00 and then again after midnight, while others received only the first message. According to their accounts, some residents of Supetar received no warning at all.

At the same time, a warning about a significant fire danger was also received by some citizens who were at that moment in Split and on the island of Hvar, even though they were not on the territory of Brač. We have also requested an answer from the Civil Protection Directorate on this issue.

a heavily criticised system

The SRUUK has previously been criticised for not being activated during crisis situations. The last time this happened was during the large fire near Omiš, in which three people died and five more are still fighting for their lives. The fire left enormous consequences — people were left without homes and jobs, thousands of hectares of forest burned, and the safety of the population remains threatened due to possible landslides.

The non-activation of the system at that time was justified by Split-Dalmatia County Prefect Blaženko Boban with the assessment that sending a warning could cause panic. On Brač the opposite question has arisen: did the unclear communication from the services further contribute to confusion and panic among residents? In the fire that has been burning on Brač for several days, around 4,000 hectares of forest, low vegetation and maquis have totally burned, as have private buildings, cars and one resort. Around 700 people were evacuated and two people were injured. There is still some smouldering on the ground, the fire has not been completely extinguished, and firefighters remain on alert.

Over 200 firefighters on the ground have for days been making superhuman efforts to defend houses and protect residents. For the locals they are heroes who risk their own lives to protect people and property. Yet the question remains how much help they receive in crisis situations from a system that the state paid 8.4 million euros for. The SRUUK was conceived as a tool for timely warning of citizens. On Brač, however, it has been shown that simply sending a message is not the end of its job, the key question is whether citizens can, after that message, actually receive clear, timely and useful information when they need it most.

World.title: Homophobic slur increasingly being used to label political opponents too
World.content:
A homophobic slur that is still used in Estonian-language media as a direct insult and as a way of policing masculinity has gained an additional function: political labeling, a University of Tartu doctoral thesis has found.

People are now using the term pede ('fag') to mark political opponents, liberal values, laws and institutions, the thesis from Aet Kuusik found.

In their doctoral thesis defended at the University of Tartu, Kuusik analyzed the use of five LGBT-related terms in the Estonian media, and how LGBT communities evaluate one of these — the term kväär — alongside its English equivalent queer and its Finnish counterpart, kvääri.

Prior to their doctoral studies, Kuusik had been working as an editor, and earlier on, in their master's thesis, they already dealt with vocabulary relating to LGBT topics. "I received my master's degree in 2014, and even then many questions arose for me which I had nowhere to find answers to. The vocabulary concerning LGBT topics was partly very new, and there was no one to discuss the choices with that had to be made when writing or editing a text," they described their path to the topic of their doctoral thesis.

Combining several methods, specifically corpus linguistics, critical stylistics, slur pragmatics, and community surveys, the dissertation offers the first systematic corpus-based analysis of LGBT-related terms in the Estonian media across three decades, and links it to community evaluations as well.

Kuusik argued that understandings of sexuality, identity and rights get largely shaped through language. "I was for a long time interested in how we talk about rights, how we label people, what that labeling brings with it, and what these words do in Estonian, but at first I couldn't see an outlet for myself in an academic context," they explained. This was largely because gender and sexuality topics are so little dealt with in the field of linguistics.

In 2022, however, Kuusik embarked on their doctoral studies, in order to delve deeper into these very topics. The main driver was a wish to understand the basis on which people make choices about which terms to use to refer to LGBT people, and on the other hand to understand how these vocabulary choices position LGBT people and LGBT topics in texts, and which societal norms are made visible through them.

How are LGBT people labeled?

In their doctoral thesis, Kuusik dealt with the question of which choices have been made and how those choices position people. In one avenue of research, they looked at how LGBT people have been labeled in the Estonian media since the 1990s, and in which linguistic frames these labels appear. They analyzed more closely the Estonian terms gei ('gay'), homo (colloquial, roughly 'homo'), homoseksuaal ('homosexual'), kväär (an Estonianised 'queer') and pede ('fag'). In a second line of research, they studied how Estonian and Finnish LGBT communities evaluate the terms kväär, kvääri and queer.

The doctoral thesis revealed that words referring to LGBT people can have very different histories of use, register and ideological meaning, and that even words that seem like synonyms have a different role in a text: gei, homo and homoseksuaal may alternate within a single text simply to avoid repetition of a word, yet in media discourse as a whole they are not equivalents.

"In critical language research, that is, a line of research which examines what meanings, evaluations and oppositions are created through language use, vocabulary choice is not treated as neutral, nor are words divided in themselves into good or bad. What matters is examining the context in which a term is used, what it is associated with, and which categories or oppositions are created through it. Through the use of terms and labels one can create visibility and belonging, but also draw boundaries between different groups," Kuusik explained.

Through their doctoral thesis, Kuusik examined how the use of LGBT-related labels and the frames associated with them have altered in Estonia from the 1990s to the present day. They compared two periods: 1995–2008, and 2014–2023. The data come from the Estonian National Corpus; the terms were searched across the entire corpus, regardless of what topic a text was concerning. This brought into the analysis texts in which LGBT topics are by no means the main subject, including sports news or political commentary. This made it possible to see how the labels function in everyday media coverage.

It became clear that over three decades the vocabulary related to LGBT topics has become markedly more diverse: Alongside older labels, for example LGBT, samasooline ('same-sex') and kväär have come in. The use of the word gei has increased, the use of homo has declined sharply, and the use of the word homoseksuaal has also somewhat faded. However: "Greater visibility does not, however, mean only normalization: these words may also be increasingly politicized," they said.

According to Kuusik, greater visibility can help bring minority rights into public debate. "For me it came as somewhat of a surprise how laws can be progressive, but in language use much remains hidden. Precisely in how LGBT people are seen and portrayed on an everyday basis," Kuusik remarked.

"For me it came as somewhat of a surprise how laws can be progressive, but in language use much remains hidden."

In the earlier period, homoseksuaal appeared repeatedly in lists where different groups were named through identity labels and placed into a shared risk category: the words narkomaan ('drug addict'), prostituut ('prostitute') and AIDS appeared in the immediate proximity to the term homoseksuaal so frequently that they are statistically significant co-occurring words (collocates) in the corpus.

A typical example is a sentence stating that blood donors must not include, among others, 'narkomaanid, prostituudid ja homoseksuaalid' ('drug addicts, prostitutes and homosexuals'), or a list naming drug addicts and homosexuals as AIDS risk groups.

Kuusik outlined that the problem lies not only in the fact that the word homoseksuaal is placed alongside the labels of other marginalized groups in such lists. The plural terms narkomaanid and prostituudid also turn an activity or a social situation into a permanent category of person. In this way people are presented as groups carrying a health risk, instead of describing which specific behavior or situation is considered a risk. The evaluation thus emerges from the interaction of vocabulary choice, categorization and the structure of the list.

The list as a device persisted into the later period too, but became more politicized: Of the more closely analyzed instances of the word homo, the list was the main textual device in a quarter of cases in the earlier period and in nearly a third in the later one. A different kind of list is typical: pagulased ('refugees'), moslemid ('Muslims'), immigrandid ('immigrants'), liberaalid ('liberals'), feministid ('feminists') and homod ('homos').

Kuusik explained that these terms are not in themselves negative, but placing them side by side can concentrate very disparate groups into a shared political frame of opposition, for instance in populist politics.

The logic of such a list persists even in texts critical of populism. In one ironic opinion piece there appeared a characteristic sentence fragment: "Vanamehed pruunides ülikondades, kes kütavad õhku kahe teemaga: pagulased ja homod" ('Old men in brown suits who stoke the air with two topics: refugees and homos'). In this sentence such political rhetoric is criticized, yet the words pagulased and homod still remain side by side as categories around which conflict is allegedly generated. In the later period, the association of the word homo with migration and ethnicity topics and with other politically opposed groups indeed grows stronger.

"Rarer are constructions in which a person belonging to a sexual minority appears themselves as an acting and self-defining subject. More often the talk is of groups as collective categories, or of what institutions permit, forbid or enable for them," Kuusik noted.

Another observation was that in the mainstream media the term gei dominated more clearly than in conservative-populist publications. In the latter, the share of the word homoseksuaal was considerably larger: in the analysis of the later period it made up 32 percent in conservative-populist sources, and 9 percent of the examined instances in the mainstream media. Nevertheless, gei remained, even in conservative-populist publications, the most frequent of the three labels compared (gei, homo and homoseksuaal).

Political labeling

The frequency of use of the slur pede has remained relatively stable over three decades, but its function has changed. Direct insult and the policing of masculinity persist, but in the later period political labeling becomes much more visible.

In the earlier time-frame, individual insult and the policing of masculinity were more central, while in media texts the slur also often appeared in quoted or ironic use. Approximately 80 percent of the earlier period's usage came in mediated form, as a quotation or a joke. In the later period the usage is more direct and aggressive, especially in online comments.

According to Kuusik, the term pede can have several functions in a text, while context is always highly significant. People may use the word to insult someone even when it is not known how that target person defines their sexuality, nor may it be relevant in the context. "The word can be a means of policing masculinity: Even long hair on a man can count as a deviation from masculinity, which is why he may be insulted with this term," they said

"The word can be a means of policing masculinity: Even long hair on a man can count as a deviation from masculinity, which is why he may be insulted with this term."

In the later material, alongside the labeling of appearance and behavior, the labeling of political stances and worldviews is also more clearly added. The label can also be applied to men whose views are considered too liberal — for example, supporters of feminism.

During the earlier period studied, such usages were rare and somewhat figurative; in the later one however this becomes systematic. A characteristic phrase is, for example, "feminiseeritud ja pedestatud" ('feminised and fag-ified'), with which liberal political space is depicted in one fell swoop as both unmanly and ideologically abhorrent. "Alongside individual insult, the term pede has also become a means of political stigmatization, with which boundaries are drawn between us and them," said Kuusik.

In the later period, the slur pede is associated, among other things, with opposition to liberal and European values. Such usage is characterized by expressions like pedepropaganda ('fag propaganda') and pedealdelikud väärakused ('fag-ish perversions'), where pede is appended to the name of ALDE, the European liberal party family, or by the sentence "Pedesid, mustlasi ja Brüsselit tuleb karta" ('Fags, gypsies and Brussels are to be feared'). In such usages, according to Kuusik, the word does not necessarily refer directly to sexuality, but is used to disparagingly label political values, institutions and opponents.

As the latter component of a compound word, the word can also appear as a "humorous" intensifier for enthusiasts of particular pursuits, such as train spotters or foodies, as in the terms rööpapede ('train fag'), autopede ('car fag') or toidupede ('food fag'). This does not necessarily render it a non-offensive term, however.

"My contention is that in seemingly non-sexual or humorous use, the word's earlier disparaging meaning potential does not disappear. With the word, an evaluative frame of deviation, excess or ridicule remains available," the academic noted.

"In seemingly non-sexual or humorous use, the word's earlier disparaging meaning potential does not disappear."

Kuusik stressed different modes of conversation too. Kitchen table talk, media discourse and conversing with a stranger are all very different communicative situations, they noted, and the same term can function differently in each of them. "During my research I did not deal with the question of whether one word is suitable or another is forbidden, but with how these words appear in a text," they said.

Evaluating the terms

The second half of the doctoral thesis looks at how people in LGBT communities evaluate the labels. A survey conducted in October 2022 was answered by 353 people within seven days. Of them, 93 percent were aware of the word kväär, but only 35 percent used it, and the evaluations were spread across the whole scale, leaning somewhat towards the negative.

In the Estonian-language context, the evaluation was most clearly associated with gender identity: Non-binary respondents on average related to the word more positively, as did those under 30.

The comparison with the Finnish community, which Kuusik made together with Meri Lindeman, a researcher at Finland's University of Turku, demonstrated that the same international term has taken root differently in two closely related languages: In Estonia the localized form kväär is better known and more widely used than kvääri is in Finland, where respondents more often use the English queer.

In the open responses, broadly three attitudes appeared. Some respondents said they consider the word kväär a neutral or positive umbrella term encompassing very different gender and sexual identities. Others saw in it an empowering word of resistance: kväär sounds like väär (meaning 'wrong'), and it is precisely this that may represent the word's strength, as a label with which people who differ from the norm have been disparaged is reclaimed with pride as one's own – just as was done deliberately with the English word queer.

Back in the 1980s this term was still predominantly an insult. However, some respondents did not want to associate themselves with such a provocative shade of meaning. "For the community, the label is at once a means of meaning-making, strategy and risk management: a person may support the word but not use it, if it seems dangerous, or consider the word unsuitable but acknowledge its political potential," Kuusik said.

"Disparaging words do harm, and the impact of one's own language use is certainly worth analyzing. But respectful language use does not mean finding one magical term."

One conclusion to Kuusik's doctoral thesis is that language change does not consist in one so-called bad word being replaced by a good one. "Disparaging words do harm, and the impact of one's own language use is certainly worth analyzing. But respectful language use does not mean finding one magical term. Evaluations can also be expressed through which lists labels are placed in, which oppositions are created with them, what a text presupposes, or who is granted the right to permit or forbid something. So alongside the choice of label, it also matters whether the person denoted by that name is portrayed in the text as a person just like those who do not belong to a minority," Kuusik said.

According to Kuusik, in the very act of communicating, people are constantly having to make linguistic choices, mostly without consciously thinking them through. "We may not be aware of these choices every time, as we use language all the time, after all," they noted.

Aet Kuusik defended their doctoral thesis in linguistics "Naming, normativity and negotiation: LGBT-related labels in Estonian media discourse and community evaluation, 1995–2023" at the University of Tartu on August 31.

World.title: Eesti 200: Government to curb infrastructure investments to rein in deficit
World.content:
Some planned infrastructure and real estate investments will have to be postponed or canceled to cut next year's budget deficit and, if possible, fund modest pay raises for teachers and rescue workers, Education Minister Kristina Kallas told ERR.

According to Kallas, the government has reviewed all revenue and spending in the budget negotiations and looked for savings across all areas.

"We have also reviewed the investment portfolio and the state's real estate costs, so all the reviews in the budget negotiations are complete and the budgets for the coming years are now broadly in place. We know where we are spending, but we still need to tie up the final loose ends on what we can invest additional money in next year," she said.

Kallas said there is no more room to cut investments in people, such as benefits and wages, so the government has turned to infrastructure investments and real estate costs.

"We cannot start cutting benefits, such as higher education funding or hobby education funding — in other words, the investments we make in people. I don't see any room for cuts there; we have already cut them significantly," Kallas said.

"Then there are real estate and infrastructure investments where the state spends quite heavily — Estonia ranks first in Europe in terms of the share of its budget spent on infrastructure and real estate investments. There are certainly some things that can be dropped, meaning we don't carry out those construction projects or that can be postponed until later. That's also possible, in order to improve the budget position," she added.

Erkki Keldo (Reform), who was economy minister at the time, has also previously said that some investments will have to be cut.

Improving the budget position has been the Reform Party's position both before and during the budget talks. More specifically, the party wants to reduce next year's deficit by half a percentage point to 4 percent of GDP.

Kallas said that while there is agreement on cutting investments, Eesti 200 and Reform have not yet agreed on the 4 percent target.

"No, we have not agreed on that target because we said from the outset that we first wanted to see where it was actually possible to make savings and where those cuts could come from. We have now gone through all spending and can see that savings can be made on infrastructure and real estate investments," Kallas said.

Infrastructure investments mainly involve road construction and Rail Baltica. "There are also port and building construction projects, but relatively few. The state invests most heavily in infrastructure. A couple hundred million euros' worth can either be dropped or spread out over a longer period," she said.

Kallas added that the government believes Estonia's infrastructure construction sector is close to overheating because of the construction of Rail Baltica, another reason for the state to scale back its investments for now.

"Estonia's infrastructure construction market is worth about €1 billion and is currently almost at capacity. If the state were to add significantly more investment, the market would overheat and prices would rise, so that may not make sense at all," she said.

Rescuers and teachers still have hope for pay rises

Kallas has previously said that while raising teachers' salaries is a goal in the budget talks, she saw no way to do so because no new spending could be added to the state budget.

She now said work is still underway to find the money.

"Our position is that we have to find the money to provide at least some pay increase because salaries for rescue workers and teachers have lagged behind average wage growth. From Eesti 200's perspective, it is important that the state is still able to invest in areas other than defense because all other areas have had to make cuts over the past four years. The state cannot function on just one area. We have to be able to provide healthcare and school education for children," she said.

"We are currently fighting, if I can put it that way, to find further infrastructure cuts so that we can also direct money toward salaries. So, to put it plainly: I can't promise anything, I don't dare promise anything, but we are working on it," Kallas added.

However, the government cannot meet the Education Personnel Union's demand to raise the minimum teacher salary to Estonia's average wage of €2,312 next year.

"That would require finding €112 million in the state budget next year. That's 0.2 percent of GDP," Kallas said.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal will submit the state budget to the Riigikogu in the final week of September.

Public transport to receive millions in additional funding

Minister of Regional Affairs and Agriculture Hendrik Terras (Eesti 200) told ERR that his areas of responsibility will face a one-time cut of €900,000. It has not yet been decided where exactly the cut will be made.

"We haven't decided on the details yet; we simply agreed that we would make the cut. But broadly speaking, it won't affect public transport. Public transport is our main focus anyway and accounts for most of our ministry's budget, and costs in that area keep rising. Once again, operating public transport has become €10 million more expensive compared with last year," Terras said.

As a result, public transport funding will actually increase next year. With fuel prices currently difficult to predict due to global developments, some of the funding will remain in the government's reserve.

"We agreed on an additional €7.5 million for transport. We also agreed that around €8 million to €10 million would be allocated from the reserve. That's because the situation with fuel prices is so uncertain that we can't currently estimate how much additional money may be needed if fuel prices rise," Terras said.

"In the second and third quarters of next year, we can look at actual fuel prices and how much was spent and the government can then allocate money for fuel from the reserve accordingly," he added.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal will submit the state budget to the Riigikogu in the final week of September.

World.title: Drivers urged to be cautious of wildlife on the roads as nights draw in
World.content:
At a time of year when the shortening daylight hours can make driving more hazardous, road users should exercise due care the Transport Board (Transpordiamet) announced.

Drivers should keep in mind wildlife always has the right of way, the authority added, noting fall is also a time of increased wildlife activity and is mating season for some species,

"During periods of increased activity, situations in which wild animals venture onto roads get more frequent, increasing the risk of collisions between vehicles and wildlife. It is consequently important that we as road users remain especially vigilant and take note of wild animals approaching the road. It is also worth keeping in mind that if one wild animal crosses the road, others may follow," said Villu Lükk, head of the board's environmental management unit.

"Wild animals often have established routes they follow, and many of these traverse roadways, hence it being important to pay heed to heed warning signs and cut speeds when necessary," Lükk went on.

"The autumn mating season of moose and red deer increases the movement of wild animals and so also the risk of them getting on the road and getting involved in collisions. If you spot an animal from a distance, you should slow down, brake smoothly and switch your hazard lights on. You should not sound the car horn or try to maneuver around the animal. When startled, a wild animal may behave unpredictably, including turning back across the road to return the way it came," noted Urmas Salmu, project manager of the national hunting society's "Wildlife on Roads" project.

Last year, the Emergency Response Center registered 3,212 reports related to wildlife accidents, a fall on the 3,779 cases reported in 2024.

Road users in Estonia are also warned about stretches of road with a particularly high risk of wildlife by moose warning signs, which drivers should heed and take into account when traveling through the areas they cover. These signs are installed in places where traffic accidents involving wild animals have been known to happen in the past, or where animals have been observed entering the road more frequently.

Since local hunting associations re responsible for removing injured and dead large game animals from roads and therefore know the problem areas well, warning signs are often installed in locations at their proposal-

Starting this week, the Transport Administration has also begun displaying LED-tupe warnings (pictured) after dark on variable-message information boards in areas where wild animals frequently cross roads.

A detailed heat map showing wildlife accident locations is available here.

Another map layer showing large game animals killed on roads last year, as recorded by hunters, is available here. The map provides an overview of the stretches of road with the biggest incidences of accidents involving wildlife.

World.title: Koos party still struggling to open a bank account in Estonia
World.content:
The Koos party is still struggling to open a bank account after banks refused to provide one, leaving it unable to pay the election deposit for the upcoming Riigikogu elections.

ERR's news portal reported in April that the Koos party had been unable to open a bank account with credit institutions operating in Estonia, raising the question of how the party would be able to pay election deposits for its candidates.

The party has now sent a new letter to the National Electoral Committee confirming that it intends to participate in the Riigikogu elections on March 7 next year.

In the letter, sent on September 15, the party said the situation had not changed: It still does not have a valid bank account through which it can make payments.

"The party has repeatedly approached banks with the aim of opening a bank account but has received refusals," Koos board member Igor Hopp said, attaching confirmations of the banks' refusals.

This has left the party in a catch-22: It must pay an election deposit to participate in the elections, but doing so requires a bank account. Without an account, it cannot make the payment. And without confirmation of the payment, the party cannot submit a complete set of documents to register its candidates.

The party is asking the National Electoral Committee to establish a specific, lawful and practically feasible mechanism that would allow it to meet the legal requirement in a situation where it objectively has no bank account despite its efforts to open one.

"For us, it is fundamentally important to receive practical guidance: What exactly must the Koos party do to pay the election deposit, obtain proper confirmation that it has been paid and be allowed to register candidates for the 2027 Riigikogu elections?" Hopp wrote.

Arne Koitmäe, head of the State Electoral Office, has previously said that under the Riigikogu Election Act, before submitting candidates for registration, a party must transfer the required election deposit for each person submitted for registration to the Ministry of Finance's bank account. The documents submitted must include a copy of the payment order proving that the deposit has been paid.

"In practice, this requires the existence and use of a bank account controlled by the party. The law does not provide for alternative payment methods or special procedures," Koitmäe explained. He added that a third party is not permitted to pay the election deposit on behalf of a party.

The Koos party was registered on May 8, 2023. It initially sought to register under the name Estonian Patriots Party Koos, but the registration department did not approve the application. The party has 723 members, the best known of whom is Aivo Peterson, who has been convicted of treason by two court instances. According to the latest Norstat poll, the party's support stood at 1.0 percent.

World.title: Experts: Energy truce between Ukraine and Russia will not lower price of oil
World.content:
Estonian experts say restoring oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz would have a far greater impact on global markets than an energy infrastructure truce between Ukraine and Russia.

On Monday evening, U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on social media that Ukraine had agreed not to strike targets related to Russia's energy infrastructure and that Russia had agreed to do the same. The president said the rise in global diesel prices was mainly due to the war between Russia and Ukraine, rather than Iran.

Alan Vaht, a member of the management board of Estonian fuel retailer Terminal, disagrees with that claim.

"Russian diesel exports have fallen by 500,000 barrels per day, while the decline in the Persian Gulf region has been more than 1.1 million barrels per day. So we're actually talking about figures that aren't comparable at all," Vaht said.

Economic expert Raivo Vare believes Trump himself is the one who primarily needs an energy truce between Moscow and Kyiv.

"Now gallon prices have risen from $3.80 (€3.29) to $6.30 (€5.43) and continue to rise. The midterm elections are coming up and that's why Trump is worried. Why? Because he needs those prices to come down," Vare said.

Ukraine immediately agreed to the proposed energy truce. But why does Russia need it?

"Russia is having difficulty supplying itself with gasoline and diesel and that has been a strong argument for Ukraine. If that leverage is now taken away, Ukraine's position objectively becomes weaker and that has to be taken into account," Vare said.

However, Russia wants more than simply an end to Ukrainian attacks on its oil refineries.

"Second, of course, the sanctions, those illegal restrictions on supplying energy resources to the global market, must be lifted. Only then can the world, the global market, be supplied with petroleum products and prices begin to fall," Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.

For now, however, fuel prices at filling stations are rising not only in the United States but also here in Estonia.

"The only thing that would genuinely help the world and the global fuel market, including Estonia's fuel market, is an agreement between Iran and the United States and the resumption of flows of crude oil and refined petroleum products through the Strait of Hormuz. That is the only effective solution for bringing fuel prices down," Vaht said.
