World.title: Azerbaijan to reduce SOFAZ's transfers to budget by $2.05 over 4 years
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 16. Transfers from Azerbaijan’s State Oil Fund (SOFAZ) to the state budget are expected to be gradually reduced in the coming years.

This is reflected in the Statement on the Initial Indicators of the State and Consolidated Budgets for 2027 released by Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Finance.

According to the State Budget Parameters for 2027 and the Following Three Years included in the statement, SOFAZ is projected to transfer 11.9 billion manat ($7 billion) to the state budget in 2027. This is 935 million manat ($550 million) less than the 12.835 billion manat ($7.55 billion) transfer approved for 2026.

The volume of transfers from SOFAZ to the state budget is also expected to decline in subsequent years. The transfer is projected at 11.05 billion manat ($6.5 billion) in 2028, 10.2 billion manat ($6 billion) in 2029 and 9.35 billion manat ($5.5 billion) in 2030.

Thus, compared with the amount approved for 2026, transfers from SOFAZ to the state budget are expected to decline by 3.485 billion manat ($2.05 billion), or about 27.2 percent, by 2030.

At the same time, total state budget revenues are projected to increase in the coming years. State budget revenues are expected to reach 39.234 billion manat ($23.079 billion) in 2027, 39.478 billion manat ($23.222 billion) in 2028, 39.9369 billion manat ($23.492 billion) in 2029 and 40.577 billion manat ($23.869 billion) in 2030.

According to the forecasts, non-oil and gas revenues are expected to increase as oil and gas revenues and transfers from SOFAZ decline. Non-oil and gas revenues are projected at 23.754 billion manat ($13.973 billion) in 2027, 25.288 billion manat ($14.875 billion) in 2028, 26.7269 billion manat ($15.722 billion) in 2029 and 28.337 billion manat ($16.669 billion) in 2030.

Meanwhile, state budget spending is expected to amount to 42.4 billion manat ($24.941 billion) in 2027, 42.82 billion manat ($25.188 billion) in 2028, 43.491 billion manat ($25.583 billion) in 2029 and 44.2365 billion manat ($26.021 billion) in 2030.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s non-oil and gas sector to reach 82% of GDP by 2030
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 16. The share of Azerbaijan’s non-oil and gas sector in GDP is projected to increase significantly from 2027 through 2030.

This is reflected in the Statement on the Initial Indicators of the State and Consolidated Budgets for 2027 released by Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Finance.

According to the statement, the baseline scenario assumes an average annual export price of $65 per barrel of oil in 2027–2030. Azerbaijan’s GDP is projected to reach 141 billion manat ($82.9 billion) by the end of 2027, of which 109.1 billion manat ($64.2 billion) will account for non-oil and gas GDP. Based on these figures, the share of the non-oil and gas sector in GDP will stand at about 77.4% that year.

By the end of the forecast period, in 2030, the country’s GDP is expected to reach 169.1 billion manat ($99.5 billion), while non-oil and gas GDP is projected at 138.6 billion manat ($81.5 billion). Thus, the share of the non-oil and gas sector in GDP is projected to rise to 82% in 2030, an increase of about 4.6 percentage points compared with 2027.

The statement notes that real GDP growth in Azerbaijan is projected to average 3.3% annually over the medium term, while real growth in non-oil and gas GDP is expected to average 4.4%. Thus, growth in the non-oil and gas sector is expected to outpace overall economic growth, accompanied by a greater role for the non-oil sector in the structure of economic growth in the coming years.

According to a chart included in the statement, real GDP growth is projected at 1.4% in 2025, 1.7% in 2026, 2.7% in 2027, 2.6% in 2028, 4.2% in 2029 and 3.6% in 2030.

Growth in the non-oil and gas sector is expected to stand at 2.7% in 2025, 3.1% in 2026, 4.4% in both 2027 and 2028, 4.3% in 2029 and 4.5% in 2030.

At the same time, the oil and gas sector is projected to contract by 1.6% in 2025, 1.8% in 2026, 1.8% in 2027, 3.5% in 2028 and 4% in 2029. In 2030, real growth in the oil and gas sector is expected to be zero.

Thus, the non-oil and gas sector is projected to strengthen its position in 2027–2030, both in terms of real growth and its share of GDP. During this period, its share of GDP is expected to increase from 77.4% to 82%.

World.title: Landcare group prepares for new battle against billion-dollar mine
World.content:
A tiny landcare group in Central West NSW is bracing itself for another showdown in its ongoing fight against a mining giant.

Plans for a billion-dollar silver mine near Mudgee are once again before the Independent Planning Commission (IPC).

It comes after the previous approval of the Bowdens Silver mine near Lue was overturned by the NSW Supreme Court of Appeal.

Lue resident and member of the Bingman Catchment Landcare Group, Susannah White, said no changes had been made to the project which was previously approved by the IPC.

"We've seen this show before," she said.

" We're not holding our breath about the independence of any outcome. "

The company behind the project, Silver Mines Limited, wants to extract up to 30 million tonnes of silver, lead and zinc over 23 years.

But those plans were thrown into disarray when a panel of judges found the impacts of a transmission line had not been properly assessed.

Protests were previously held by locals in opposition to the proposed mine. (ABC Central West: Mollie Gorman)

Redetermination underway

A new three-person panel of commissioners has been appointed to assess the proposal, which has not been amended since the Court of Appeal's judgement.

"The previous determination has no influence on this new assessment," the IPC said in a statement.

"The new panel is independent of the previous panel and will start afresh in considering the entire application on its merits."

The Bowdens Silver mine is seeking approval to extract 30 million tonnes of ore near Mudgee. (ABC Central West: Mollie Gorman)

If the project is approved, Silver Mines Limited will offer community members voluntary blood testing to track their lead levels.

Ms White said the mine would be located 2 kilometres from the Lue Public School, leaving parents with a decision to make.

"Do they subject their children to routine blood tests to make sure they can monitor their levels of lead that will potentially increase as a result of lead being mined in the community?" she said.

A 'major step forward'

In a statement, Silver Mines managing director Jo Battershill said the hearings, which will mark the start of the IPC's assessment process, were "a major step forward in the approvals process".

"The Bowdens team has delivered a robust, environmentally responsible project … and offers substantial long-term economic and social benefits," he said.

The project's previous approval by the IPC was overturned in 2024 following a decision by the NSW Supreme Court of Appeal. (ABC Central West: Mollie Gorman)

Mr Battershill said community health concerns were taken "seriously" and the project had undergone extensive technical assessment, government and independent peer review.

"[The assessment and reviews] found the project is not expected to result in adverse human health impacts, including from lead exposure," he said.

The 13-kilometre transmission line at the centre of the Court of Appeal's challenge is now being assessed separately from the rest of the project following a determination by the NSW Planning Secretary in May 2025.

Community frustration

Written submissions will be open until October 23, and public hearings will be held across two days in Mudgee on October 14 and 15.

Susannah White says parents are concerned about children being impacted by the development. (Supplied: Susannah White)

Ms White said giving the community less than a month to prepare for the IPC hearings was unreasonable.

"The company has had as long as it's needed to get its ducks in a row," she said.

" The onus falls on the community in a very short space of time to become planning experts. "

A spokesperson for the IPC said in a statement that the panel would also consider submissions that were made to the commission in 2022 and 2023.

"The time provided to stakeholders to consider and make submissions is on par with any new state significant development applications involving a public hearing," the spokesperson said.

The project was referred to the IPC by the NSW Department of Planning, which has recommended the project be approved.

Economic concerns

Ms White said the mine could put the Mudgee region's tourism and agriculture industries at risk.

"Why an open-cut lead mine is a good idea in a region like this is beyond me," she said.

"Decision makers need to take a cold, hard look … at what is the right decision for a sustainable, thriving economy in the Mudgee region.

"I can guarantee it is not an open-cut lead mine."

The proposed Bowdens Silver mine would be located in the Lawson Valley at Lue, if approved. (ABC Central West: Mollie Gorman)

Mr Battershill said the project would provide more than 300 direct full-time jobs over its life span.

"Mining is a significant contributor to the economy of the region, and we expect Bowdens to enhance that position," he said in a statement.

Ms White said it was too early to say whether the Bingman Catchment Landcare Group would launch another appeal if the mine is once again approved.

"Whether there will be any grounds for a legal objection or appeal, we will just have to wait and see," she said.

World.title: Family members pay tribute to Qld woman who died in Indonesia fall
World.content:
The family of a woman who fell to her death at an Indonesian beach have paid tribute to her while seeking public assistance to help bring her home.

Brianna Cronin, 29, died after falling from a cliff at a popular tourist site at Kelingking Beach on Nusa Penida island, east of Bali, on Saturday.

Kelingking Beach in Nusa Penida is one of the most popular destinations for Bali tourists. (ABC News: Max Walden)

Ms Cronin's family has released a video speaking about "Brianna, our daughter and sister", and calling for help bringing her back to Australia.

"She was bubbly, a little quirky, a friend to everyone, and happiest out in nature," the family said.

"Brianna passed away in Bali, and right now she is so far from home."

They said a fundraiser had been launched to repatriate Ms Cronin's remains so the family could "hold her close and say goodbye".

" No family should have to grieve from the other side of the world. We just want our girl home. "

Ms Cronin's family says she was "always growing, always dreaming, and always making room for other people." (Supplied)

The fundraiser said Ms Cronin graduated from the University of Queensland in 2022 with a Bachelor of Science and Bachelor of Arts, and described how she "lit up every room she walked into".

"She practised yoga with grace and joy, climbed mountains, explored rainforests, and travelled the world with wide-open eyes, from the lakes and peaks of Europe to the canals of Venice," the family wrote.

"She was always growing, always dreaming, and always making room for other people."

The family has launched a fundraiser to repatriate Ms Cronin's remains so the they can "hold her close and say goodbye". (Supplied)

The family also thanked everyone who had provided support and assistance.

"We are deeply grateful to our families and friends, to Brianna's friends and colleagues, for your love, support and condolences," the family wrote.

"To the consular staff and officials in Bali and Australia, thank you for taking care of her."

They said any money left over from the appeal would go toward fulfilling Ms Cronin's dream of building an environmentally-friendly greenhouse complex, and an organisation she supported.

Kelingking Beach is one of the most popular destinations for Bali tourists, with a lookout at the top of the cliff offering panoramic views of the coast nicknamed "T-Rex Beach".

Bali Governor Wayan Koster ordered the partially built lift to be demolished within six months. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Construction of a 182-metre elevator down to the beach had been taking place until the works were suspended late last year, amid widespread opposition from tourists and local politicians.

More than 6.9 million international visitors went to Bali last year, according to the Bali Hotels Association, with Australians making up the largest cohort of those visitors at 23 per cent.

World.title: Housing Trust apologises to tenant after delays to remove black mould
World.content:
The SA Housing Trust has apologised to one of its tenants, after it took four years to remove black mould from her home.

The apology was prompted by an investigation by the SA Ombudsman, who found the public housing authority failed to ensure the property met "reasonable standards of health and safety".

In a report published in July but not made public until Wednesday, Ombudsman Emily Strickland also found the SA Housing Trust (SAHT) "erred in its handling" of multiple reports made by the tenant about the mould dating back to February 2021.

"The four-year delay in addressing the safety concerns is unreasonable and has meant the SAHT is failing to meet its obligations to the [tenant]," Ms Strickland wrote.

"I am concerned that the [tenant] has been living in a property with high (mould) contamination levels for over four years, despite raising with the SAHT that she had a lung condition."

The SA Housing Trust took several years to address the black mould complaints. File image. (ABC News: Alice Pavlovic)

According to Ms Strickland, in the years since the tenant first reported the mould, the contamination had "worsened significantly".

She wrote the tenant made further reports to the authority, but despite "works orders" being raised by the trust, no "substantive work" to address the mould contamination had been carried out by the time she launched her investigation in February this year.

The ombudsman noted that ongoing exposure to mould could cause serious health issues, but the trust did not get the property tested until April this year.

According to Ms Strickland's report, the testing found active mould contamination on the bathroom ceiling and in the hallway carpet.

"The [tenant] raised with the SAHT, on several occasions, that the contamination at her property was impacting her health," she wrote.

" It is my view that the mould contamination at the property would not have met the minimum standards of housing. "

Ms Strickland noted the authority tried to undertake work at the home when the mould was first reported in 2021, but it had trouble accessing the property.

She wrote the tenant was told to contact maintenance to arrange for contractors to come back to the property, but the tenant did not re-approach the authority about the issue until 2022.

"From 2022 onwards, there is a pattern of works orders being raised following reports from the [tenant] about mould contamination," she noted.

"The works orders do not get carried out or are cancelled, without the reported issue being addressed."

Ms Strickland made four recommendations to the Housing Trust, including that it address the mould contamination and change its complaints handling procedure.

An SA Housing Trust spokesperson said they acknowledged the ombudsman's findings and had apologised to the tenant.

"We accept the ombudsman's recommendations and have been engaging with the tenant to access the property to undertake remedial works," they said.

"The Trust is relocating the tenant to another property to undertake the required remedial works at the property."

World.title: Cold case trial told tenant was murdered over $2k in rent arrears
World.content:
A man accused of murdering his tenant over $2,000 in rent arrears more than 20 years ago is facing trial in the Supreme Court.



Steven Johnson has pleaded not guilty to one charge of murder, in relation to the disappearance of 38-year-old Christopher Jarvis near Warrnambool.

Mr Jarvis went missing from his Wangoom home on June 13, 2006.

His burnt-out car was found at the regional city's popular coastal lookout, Thunder Point, later that day.

His body has never been found.

During the trial opening on Wednesday in Victoria's Supreme Court sitting at Warrnambool, Crown prosecutor Mark Gibson KC told the jury Mr Jarvis left for work on the morning of his disappearance, and has not been heard from since.

"He never made it to work, he never made it home from work, he was never sighted again by those closest to him," he told the jury.

The jury was told Mr Johnson was Mr Jarvis's landlord and that the pair were in dispute over $2,000 in rent arrears.

Mr Gibson told the jury Mr Jarvis claimed he had completed plumbing work at the property and wanted that cost deducted from the rent he owed.

Prosecution lays out case

The court heard that the prosecution's case was that Mr Johnson wanted to scare Mr Jarvis into paying the rent owed and vacating the house, and recruited another man, who cannot be named for legal reasons, to assist.

Mr Gibson said the pair ambushed Mr Jarvis in the driveway, as he left for work in the early morning dark.

Christopher Jarvis was living at this Wangoom property when he disappeared. (ABC News: Matt Neal)

Mr Gibson said the Crown would argue that Mr Johnson came up behind Mr Jarvis and threw him to the ground, before firing a starting pistol near his head, which caused him to bleed from the ear.

The court heard the Crown would argue Mr Johnson, with the help of the other man, then put Mr Jarvis in the back of his car and drove out to Framlingham Forest, near Warrnambool.

Mr Gibson said the Crown would argue that at the forest, the men dug a shallow grave and Mr Johnson fatally hit Mr Jarvis on the head with a baseball bat before they placed the deceased man in the hole.

The prosecution will argue Mr Johnson then drove Mr Jarvis's silver 1991 Ford Falcon station wagon to Thunder Point, poured petrol inside, and set it alight.

Christopher Jarvis's burnt out car was found at Thunder Point the same day he disappeared. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

Mr Jarvis's disappearance was filed as a missing person's case until police began a new investigation into his disappearance in 2021.

The court heard in November that year, police interviewed and arrested Mr Johnson and seized an imitation gun from his property.

The jury was told Mr Johnson was charged with murder in 2022, but the charge was discontinued only to be reinstated in 2025.

Defence responds

The court heard it would be the defence's case that Mr Johnson had no involvement in Mr Jarvis's disappearance, and that the defence could not say what happened to him.

Mr Johnson's defence lawyer, Pat Doyle, told the jurors they must presume his client innocent and carefully consider the evidence presented during the trial.

"It is critical you keep an open-mind until you hear all of the evidence," Mr Doyle told the jury.

He said there was no dispute of certain facts, including whether Mr Johnson was Mr Jarvis's landlord, or that Mr Jarvis's body had never been found.

"Those are sad facts," he said.

World.title: Broncos NRLW stars credit 'Princey blow-up' for season turnaround
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos NRLW stars Romy Teitzel and Tamika Upton insist an emotive half-time address from coach Scott Prince was the catalyst for the team's return to form.

The defending premiers host Newcastle in an elimination final on Saturday at Brisbane's Langlands Park.

They enter the match on a three-match winning streak, which followed a mid-season slump.

The Broncos' last loss was a 28-20 defeat to the Gold Coast Titans on August 23.

Broncos, Titans record wins The Broncos thrash the Warriors to hit peak form before the finals, while the high-flying Titans beat the Knights in the concluding round of the minor premiership.

It was their third consecutive defeat.

Trailing 14-4 at half-time in that match, TV footage showed Prince laying down the law in no uncertain terms.

"We are a great team with great standards and we weren't living up to them," Teitzel said.

"We deserved every single word that he threw at us.

"The response comes from having a lot of respect for Princey and believing in his game plan.

"Everything is driven from that respect factor and believing in what he is trying to drive here at the Broncos."

Following the loss to the Titans, the Broncos beat Parramatta 44-10 and St George Illawarra 24-16, before thrashing the Warriors 52-18 at home last Sunday.

Tamika Upton says the players have deep respect for their coach, Scott Prince. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Broncos captain Upton said Prince, who coached the team to the premiership last year, told the players home truths they needed to hear.

"We had a few little things we had to fix, and we weren't doing it, hence the Princey blow-up," Upton said.

"To be honest, we are used to it. He is a very passionate coach. That's the thing, we are all competitors."

Upton said she and her teammates had enormous respect for Prince, who captained the Wests Tigers to the 2005 NRL premiership during his decorated playing career.

"I would rather him be yelling at us than not speaking to us," she said.

"Honestly, you feel that because he was a player.

"When he is talking like that, you feel the energy, and you respect that a lot because he has been there and done it before.

"He wouldn't do it if he didn't care. I respond to that."

AAP

World.title: Families stunned by order to remove 'non-compliant' tributes from grave sites
World.content:
Families have been left heartbroken by a bureaucratic order to remove headstones, tributes and other keepsakes from loved ones' graves in a West Australian cemetery.

The Bunbury Cemetery Board sent out letters last month, alerting custodians to a grave site audit.

The letter cited a need to keep memorial gardens and the cemetery "safe, tidy and fair for everyone", giving those contacted a 28-day notice to remove tributes "not compliant" with regulations.

The move has sparked backlash from locals, with a family's online petition to get the by-laws changed garnering almost 800 signatures.

Linda McDonald's family have been paying tribute at her gravesite for more than a decade. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Mother 'broken' by move

When Denise Thornborough's daughter, Linda McDonald, died 13 years ago, she and her family could not afford a headstone.

On top of funeral fees, a headstone can cost families up to $5,000, with even simpler plaques and grave markers advertised at hundreds of dollars.

Instead, the family began leaving handmade items, crosses and an angel statue, to mark Linda's final resting place and to pay tribute to her and her legacy.

When Linda McDonald died 13 years ago, her family began placing handmade tributes at her grave. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Heartbroken family members spent Tuesday night clearing the gravesite, ahead of the cemetery board deadline.

"I didn't even get close to it; I only glanced over, and it feels like it's just broken," Ms Thornborough said.

" I just walked past and you can see there's nothing there — it's just empty. "

Linda McDonald's gravesite after her family removed their tributes. (Supplied)

Linda's sister, Jaimie Jones, said the cost should not dictate how a family remembers their loved ones.

"That's not what this is about. It's not what grief is about," she said.

Board bound by by-laws

Bunbury Cemetery Board chief executive Kristy Constantine said it was a state government authority, bound by laws and safety requirements.

"We are responsible for every member of staff and every member of the public that comes to site," she said.

" If the headstones are unauthorised and they have items that can be broken or may cause detriment to the cemetery, to the cemetery workers and any members of the public … they have to be removed. "

By-laws have been in place for more than 30 years.

The Bunbury Cemetery Board by-laws have been in place for more than 30 years. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Ms Constantine said the lawn cemetery, where Linda's grave was located, posed particular challenges when it came to upkeep.

She said there was no ability to grant individual exemptions.

"We have to use machinery, and we need to make sure that everybody is safe," she said.

"We're not able to show any preferential treatment to anyone on site."

The Bunbury Cemetery Board manages thousands of graves. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Families confused by timing

Ms Jones said she did not understand why her sister's resting place had to be disturbed after 13 years.

"That's probably one of the biggest things that has confused and frustrated us because it's been so long," she said.

"There was nothing, no breakables or anything, that could hurt anyone."

Linda's family is not alone.

Shane Trenerry's grave has included flowers and an angel statue for almost seven years. (Supplied)

Peter Trenerry's son Shane died seven years ago.

Mr Trenerry said the angel statue placed at his son's grave was an important part of how he and his wife grieved.

"We didn't have much money at the time … so we wanted to do as good as we can," he said.

"So we got the angel. It was just perfect.

" It breaks your heart to see that after a few years, someone's come along and said: 'You've got to get rid of your son's grave.' "

Ms Constantine said the board understood the stress placed on loved ones.

"It's not something that we do lightheartedly," she said.

"But we need to make sure that everyone is compliant."

World.title: One Nation volunteer previously promoted neo-Nazi ideologies
World.content:
A man who volunteered for One Nation during the party's successful West Australian by-election was previously named by a federal tribunal for promoting neo-Nazi ideologies.

David Donis handed out how-to-vote cards for One Nation in the state seat of Secret Harbour last month, sparking fresh questions about vetting months after Pauline Hanson revealed the party had shut branches she said were "infiltrated by extremists".

Mr Donis was a founding member and president of the Society of Western Australian Nationalists (SWAN), a now-deregistered organisation the Administrative Appeals Tribunal (AAT) found was a racist extremist group.

The tribunal's comments about Mr Donis were made in a 2023 case concerning an army reservist's security clearance.

Mr Donis was identified by other political volunteers at the Singleton Primary School polling booth on August 27 and later pictured standing near the stage at One Nation's victory party that night.

Two people told the ABC there was an incident during the day where Mr Donis yelled at a voter leaving the polling station, prompting other volunteers to intervene and calm the situation.

A One Nation spokesperson said the individual the ABC identified as David Donis was "not a member of One Nation".

"Our party does not condone extremist views, and where such issues are identified they're acted upon swiftly by the party," the spokesperson said.

It is understood Mr Donis was a volunteer rather than a formal member and would not be permitted to continue associating with One Nation.

A Liberal source told the ABC that Mr Donis had previously been a member of the party as a teen but ultimately left when it became known his views were "not welcome".

One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen claimed victory in the Secret Harbour by-election. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Mr Donis has previously denied promoting neo-Nazi ideologies, but in 2023 the AAT said it was satisfied he and other SWAN members had done so.

One Nation's vetting has previously come under scrutiny, with Senator Hanson revealing in June that the party had shut down four branches.

"I'm being infiltrated by these extremists, so it's all the time happening with One Nation; they set us up all the time," she told Nine papers.

One senior West Australian Liberal told the ABC that One Nation has had "years of warnings" about problems with candidates and people associated with the party.

They said background checks should be "second nature".

"That includes basic vetting to ensure people publicly representing the party do not have verifiable links to neo-Nazis, white supremacists or organisations advocating political violence," the Liberal said.

David Donis was identified by other political volunteers standing near the stage at One Nation's victory party. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Man adhered to "neo-Nazi ideologies"

In mid-2023, the AAT accepted evidence Mr Donis was a member of SWAN, which it determined was a "nationalist and racist extremist group".

Mr Donis denied the allegation, but the tribunal said it was satisfied he and other SWAN members "adhere to, and promote, racist and neo-Nazi ideologies" and supported politically motivated and communal violence.

The findings about Mr Donis emerged in a case in which the AAT upheld ASIO's decision that an army reservist posed a security risk and should lose his NV1 clearance.

Why Labor lost safe seat to One Nation WA Labor will be conducting a post-mortem of its crushing defeat in the Secret Harbour by-election to see where it went wrong.

The AAT said the reservist had close ties to Mr Donis and SWAN, which the tribunal accepted was a nationalist and racist extremist group after hearing "closed evidence" — classified material that could not be disclosed publicly.

The case noted SWAN came into existence around 2018 or early 2019, with Mr Donis as a "founding member and president".

Incorporation documents show SWAN members voted to voluntarily deregister the organisation due to "inactivity" in October of 2023, three months after the AAT findings.

One Nation WA pre-empts volunteer revelation

West Australian One Nation leader Rod Caddies appeared to pre-empt potential controversy over a party volunteer last week in a video shared on social media.

Mr Caddies criticised state Liberal MP Anthony Spagnolo for submitting a series of questions on notice to the Labor government "probing some tie" between One Nation's "Secret Harbour campaign and neo-Nazis".

David Donis was to the right of WA One Nation leader Rod Caddies as he gave his victory speech. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

He accused Mr Spagnolo of taking a page out of the "radical left playbook" by "trying to take One Nation down and tie us to Nazis".

"I don't know what sad little 'gotcha' the member thinks he has. I suspect it's something about some low-level volunteer or some link like that," the WA One Nation leader said.

Mr Caddies said if that were the case it meant the Liberal Party would have to own "everything their volunteers have said or done".

"The next time someone loosely affiliated with the Liberal Party has a shady background or says something crazy, I'll make sure every one of their members are set to the same standard you set," he said.

Mr Caddies then said even if the Liberals did "uncover something" it would not prove anything.

"If it turns out some idiot has managed to weasel his way into One Nation, we'll expel him; that's simple. If an extremist has infiltrated One Nation, it's by hiding their extremism," he said.

Volunteer witnessed shouting at voter

Mr Donis initially attracted the attention of volunteers from other political parties at a Secret Harbour by-election polling booth last month after he yelled at a voter.

One witness said it was before midday when they saw Mr Donis interact with a mother and daughter leaving the venue after voting.

They overheard Mr Donis wish the pair a "good day" before adding he hoped they had put One Nation "first" and Labor "last" on the ballot paper.

The witness said the woman replied she was more likely to put One Nation last, which prompted Mr Donis to accuse her of supporting abortion and setting a "bad example" for her daughter.

They said the woman gave a dismissive response, but Mr Donis kept yelling as she walked away across the car park.

The witness said the One Nation "booth captain" at the school intervened to try and quiet Mr Donis, as did a nearby Liberal member who urged him to "settle down".

They said there were no further incidents at the booth involving Mr Donis that day.

Later in the evening, Mr Donis was spotted at an event for supporters of One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen.

The ABC has been unable to contact David Donis.

World.title: ASX set to slump, Wall Street falls as Fed chief spooks investors; Microsoft AI chief sends Anthropic warning
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slump, Wall Street falls as Fed chief spooks investors; Microsoft AI chief sends Anthropic warning Stan Choe Updated September 17, 2026 — 8:09am ,first published 4:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks slipped after the Federal Reserve hiked its main interest rate for the first time in three years and suggested more may be ahead as it tries to get the nation’s high inflation under control. The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent after giving up a modest gain from earlier in the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 631 points, or 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was nearly unchanged after edging down by less than 0.1 per cent. Fed chair Kevin Warsh’s warnings on inflation spooked Wall Street. AP Photo/Seth Wenig The Australian sharemarket is set to decline sharply, with futures at 6.21am AEST pointing to a fall of 68 points, or 0.8 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.3 per cent on Wednesday. Investors generally prefer lower interest rates because higher rates slow the economy’s growth and undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



The US stock market initially held onto its modest, early gains after the Fed announced its decision. The short-term pain of a slower economy may be worth it if it starves inflation of its fuel and gets further increases for the cost of living back to the Fed’s 2 per cent target. View post on X But stock prices weakened later in the day as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said repeatedly in a press conference that inflation remains too high and the US economy appears to be strengthening. That could imply the economy is solid enough to withstand more hikes to rates, and other officials at the Fed provided their own forecasts suggesting rates may need to go still higher. The median Fed official expects the federal funds rate to end this year at 4.1 per cent, according to forecasts published after the central bank’s meeting. That’s up from its current range of 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent following Wednesday’s increase, and it’s up from the median forecast of 3.8 per cent that Fed officials gave three months ago. Traders, meanwhile, suspect the Fed may go even further. They’re betting on a 38 per cent probability the Fed could hike the federal funds rate to a range of 4.25 per cent to 4.50 per cent by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group.



“Our decision comes at a time when the American economy appears to be strengthening,” Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in his press conference. He pointed to solid US hiring trends, corporate profits and investments by businesses. A report on Wednesday morning, meanwhile, showed shoppers spent much more at US retailers last month than economists expected. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks at a news conference following the decision. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said. He later added, “Today’s action starts to show we’re serious about this.” It’s the first hike by the Fed to interest rates in three years. The central bank had been on pause for months following cuts to rates in 2024 and 2025, even though inflation has consistently remained above the Fed’s 2 per cent target.



President Donald Trump has been lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher. On Wall Street, bank stocks fell to some of the market’s sharper losses. A slower US economy could mean less demand for loans from them. Banks also get hurt when the gap narrows between short-term interest rates and longer-term ones because the industry makes profit off the difference. Following the Fed’s announcements, the two-year Treasury yield jumped to 4.74 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Tuesday. It tends to closely follow expectations for what the Fed will do with the federal funds rate. The yield on the longer-term 10-year Treasury, meanwhile, takes into account expectations for economic growth and inflation years down the line. It had a more modest increase, ticking up to 5.01 per cent from 5.00 per cent late Tuesday. Huntington Bancshares fell 5.6 per cent, Citizens Financial Group sank 4.8 per cent and JPMorgan Chase slipped 1 per cent.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Trump set to explode if his man does his job Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The largest loss in the S&P 500 came from J.B. Hunt Transport Services, which lost 13.3 per cent. Its chief financial officer told a conference of analysts late Tuesday that it’s facing higher costs and expects its earnings to drop 5 per cent to 10 per cent from the second quarter to the third. Stocks of oil companies also weighed on the market after the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 2.7 per cent to $105.83. It was the first drop of the week for Brent, which has gotten near $110 in recent days. Helping to limit the market’s losses were gains for some influential stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry. Nvidia rose 0.8 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices climbed 1.6 per cent to recover more of their losses from earlier in the week. AI stocks slid worldwide Monday after leaders of the AI industry called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity.



Microsoft slipped 1.4 per cent. Overnight, its artificial intelligence chief Mustafa Suleyman warned infusing tools like Anthropic’s Claude with humanlike characteristics increases the risks of such systems going rogue. In an essay, the longtime artificial intelligence developer took aim at some of the language in the guiding documents behind Claude, Anthropic PBC’s popular family of large language models. Claude’s constitution expresses ambiguity about whether the assistant is a moral entity, positing that the software may have “some functional version of emotions or feelings.” All told, the S&P 500 fell 33.92 points to 7,551.81. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 631.21 to 51,461.90, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 3.15 to 25,978.42. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.4 per cent for one of the world’s biggest gains. Inflation is a worldwide problem, and the European Central Bank hiked rates last week to help diminish it.

World.title: New Today show hosts announced after Sarah Abo confirms departure
World.content:
Sylvia Jeffreys and Tom Steinfort have been announced as the new hosts of the Today show after Sarah Abo confirmed this week she was leaving the show. “We can announce that Sylvia Jeffreys and Tom Steinfort have been named the new hosts of Today in 2027. With a collective four decades of experience, their appointments mark a new era for the program,” newsreader Jayne Azzopardi said during a news update. Tom Steinfort and Sylvia Jeffreys. Jeffreys said it was “very exciting as a cat’s out of the bag”. “There are a lot of mixed feelings for everyone today. I know that here on the floor, and for you at home as well,” she added. “But I know that Tom and I are going to work really, really hard to carry on the amazing work of Sarah, of Karl [Stefanovic], of the whole team, everything they’ve been doing for years for you, our viewers. And yes, 2027 is going to be a huge year.”



Steinfort said he was “pumped as well”. “I’m stoked to be doing it alongside you, and yeah, I’m just thrilled to be part of such an iconic show.” Loading In a statement on Wednesday, Abo said: “Words can’t express how grateful I am to our viewers for letting me into your homes to be part of your morning routine. Without you, there is no Today show. “Together with 60 Minutes, I’ve spent my time at Nine chasing stories, travelling and reporting from all over the world, interviewing some incredible and inspiring people from all walks of life.”



Before the new hosting team was announced, Abo was farewelled on the show. “Sarah will always be such a much loved part of this Today family, no matter what,” Jeffreys said. “And talking to her last night, I know that she’s been feeling so much love from you, our wonderful viewers. After she shared that news and thanked Australia for welcoming her into your homes and letting her be part of your every morning routine. Sarah Abo has been on maternity leave since July. Nine Jeffreys thanked for Abo “giving so much of yourself to this show and for being such a joy to share our mornings with. But of course, now that belongs to beautiful [son] Sonny and [partner] Cyrus.” The program also played a greatest hits package of Abo’s time on show with former host Karl Stefanovic, with clips of her interviewing the prime minister and former Australian of the Year Richard Scolyer, as well as celebrities.



Abo also posted a video message on her Instagram account yesterday announcing her departure from Today and Nine. In the video, she said she “loved every minute” and the Today crew felt like family. She also thanked the viewers at home for “being incredibly supportive”. Abo also said “there was more to come”, and that would be announced in “due course”. The journalist’s next steps have been the subject of rumour, with New Idea reporting she is due to join the rival Seven network to read the news in Melbourne. It has been a year of immense change for Abo, who gave birth in July, after years of struggles with infertility. She acknowledged this in her farewell statement on Wednesday, writing: “Becoming a mum has heralded a new chapter and sharing that with our audience has been truly special. As many of you know, this has been a significant journey for my family and will continue to be my greatest achievement.



“I’d like to thank the wider Today team – the amazing crew, incredible producers and my wonderful fellow hosts – you all know how much you mean to me. It takes a special kind of crazy to wake up at the hours we do, but it’s so much easier when the team feels like family. I’ll miss you all dearly.” The breakfast program was thrown into turmoil earlier this year with the sacking of long-time host Stefanovic, who had his contract terminated after he interviewed convicted fraudster and right-wing agitator Tommy Robinson on his podcast, The Karl Stefanovic Show. Loading Today’s weatherman, Tim Davies, also announced his resignation last month. His last broadcast is due on Friday. A rotating line-up of Nine personalities has been filling in for Stefanovic and Abo, including former Sunrise host Armytage, who joined Nine in 2024 after 21 years at Seven.



Related Video Video icon 0:33 Karl Stefanovic drops podcast teaser amid legal battle Nine executive director of news and current affairs Fiona Dear paid tribute to Abo, saying: “Sarah has been an integral part of the Today team, bringing warmth, energy and first-class journalism to the program each morning. “It takes enormous skill to front 3½ hours of live television every day, and Sarah did it with sharp journalistic instincts. We thank her for everything she brought to Today, and wish Sarah and her family all the very best.” In other news, Hugh Riminton is reported to have announced his departure from Ten. The veteran journalist, who has been with the network for the past 17 years, said in a note to staff that “48 years in daily news is probably enough. This reporter’s life has given me the world. I leave with nothing but gratitude for every hour of it.” Nine is owner of this masthead.

World.title: Fed defies Trump, raises US interest rates for first time in three years
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaFederal Reserve Fed defies Trump, raises US interest rates for first time in three years Michael Koziol Updated September 17, 2026 — 6:50am ,first published 4:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The US Federal Reserve has lifted interest rates for the first time in three years in a bid to rein in persistently high inflation fuelled by the ongoing war with Iran and its impact on the cost of energy. While widely expected, the move risks enraging President Donald Trump, who has furiously campaigned for the central bank to cut rates – piling pressure on his new handpicked Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh. Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh speaks at a press conference following the announcement. AP But the Fed’s rate-setting committee voted unanimously on Wednesday (US time) to raise the target rate by 0.25 percentage point, to a band of 3.75 to 4 per cent. In a set of quarterly projections, the Fed also signalled that its committee expects to hike rates again this year to 4.1 per cent. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said at a news conference. “This [American] summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.”



The call to raise rates was the first unanimous, 12-0 decision by the Fed since May 2025. Warsh described it as a sober and responsible decision, and would not countenance future rate hikes, though reporters pointed out that increases were rarely one-off. “I’m not going to prejudge any future decisions we make,” he said. Nor would he comment on any discussions with Trump. View post on X Economists widely tipped a rate rise after last week’s official data showed US inflation stuck at 3.4 per cent – above the Fed’s target of 2 per cent, driven largely by increasing energy costs. The consumer price index ticked up 0.4 per cent in August in seasonally adjusted terms, with petrol up 3.9 per cent. After falling back to nearly pre-war levels, the price of Brent crude – the international oil benchmark - is back above $US100 a barrel.



That was compounded by new attacks by Iran-backed militants in Yemen and Iraq, targeting oil supplies that avoid the Strait of Hormuz by using the Bab al-Mandab Strait between Yemen and the African coast. Saudi Arabia closed the East-West Pipeline across the Arabian Peninsula last week following drone attacks. Bloomberg reported the kingdom was aiming to restore about half the pipeline’s capacity within days. The highly anticipated interest rates decision being watched live in the New York Stock Exchange. Bloomberg Warsh indicated deteriorating geopolitical circumstances in the seven weeks since the Fed’s last meeting were a factor in its decision to lift rates. “There’s no hiding from hotspots around the world,” he said. “Our judgment about what is the most likely or least likely in the geopolitical situation has changed.”



Trump has consistently pressured the central bank to cut rates, and led a vicious campaign against former chairman Jerome Powell for his failure to do so. Two weeks ago, he said Warsh and the Fed “must get smart” and “BE PATRIOTS for a change”. He threatened: “LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT.” President Donald Trump swore in Fed chairman Kevin Warsh with an extensive White House ceremony in May. Bloomberg On Wednesday afternoon, following the decision, Trump doubled down on his trade threats but stopped short of criticising Warsh or the governors directly. “Interest Rates in the United States should be 1% or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World - BY FAR,” he wrote on Truth Social. “If we stopped Trading with every country that we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year.



“We are ‘carrying’ almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” White House economics spokesman Kush Desai told Fox News the Fed’s decision to increase rates was “rather unfortunate” and “not backed by a particularly compelling economic case”. Rising petrol prices in the US due to the war against Iran have contributed to persistently high inflation. AP Lingering inflation was “entirely driven by an energy supply shock, by what’s going on with oil prices in the Middle East”, Desai said. “These are things that have nothing to do with interest rates and are not affected by interest rates.” Analysts had warned that Wednesday’s decision was a test of the Fed’s independence and credibility, with persistently high inflation leaving Warsh and his fellow governors with little choice but to hike rates or be accused of cowing to Trump’s wishes.



Warsh told Congress in July that the Fed had “no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation”. And at the bank’s August 28 summit at Jackson Hole, he said inflation was “concerning”, and that governors had opted to wait for more information before deciding to raise rates. Related Article Opinion

US politics Alarms flashing red as Trump takes US debt to level almost beyond comprehension Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent “This is where the chairman has effectively painted himself into a corner,” said JPMorgan chief global strategist David Kelly on Monday, adding that both Warsh and the governing committee would “lose serious credibility” if they did not raise rates. Warsh denied that market expectations played a role in the outcome. “Today was our decision,” he said, adding that he preferred to look at trends over time rather than “noisy” individual data points. The Fed’s governing committee said economic activity was expanding at a solid pace, with the unemployment rate steady, productivity growth strong and capital investment robust. Though it noted uncertainty remained elevated, “owing, in part, to geopolitical developments”.

World.title: Love Island meets Shakespeare in this show with a looksmaxxing twist of fate
World.content:
CultureTheatrePerforming arts Love Island meets Shakespeare in this show with a looksmaxxing twist of fate Linda Morris September 17, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When director Marion Potts looks at William Shakespeare’s As You Like It, she sees more than a 16th-century pastoral comedy – she sees the thematic DNA of modern reality television franchises like Love Island. “People are falling in love at first sight. There are betrayals, jealousies, recriminations and confessionals,” says Potts. “There’s even an exile that feels like an eviction. I began thinking, my gosh, there are really close parallels with reality television and what it says about popular culture. That’s where the play became truly fascinating for me, exploring that heightened, performative reality the characters inhabit.” Bell Shakespeare artistic director Peter Evans and director Marion Potts. Janie Barrett Potts returns to direct As You Like It for Bell Shakespeare’s 2027 season, marking the company’s first staging of the 1599 work in 12 years. Next year’s line-up also features a “dark and dangerous” 90-minute adaptation of Measure for Measure, directed by Saro Lusty-Cavallari. As You Like It follows exiled nobles escaping court corruption into the Forest of Arden. Free from rigid social constraints, they undergo unpredictable romantic entanglements. “It’s liberating and incredibly freeing, but they’re also in freefall,” Potts says.



Both the Elizabethan court and modern reality television construct hyper-gendered environments where men are expected to be buff, women hyper-feminine, and everyone preens for courtship. Potts’ production avoids a literal time and place. “If anything, it’s set in a world where concrete reality and mediated reality are confused,” he says. “A world not unlike our own, where characters are in constant performance as though they’re being watched, even without cameras. “It taps into the troubling phenomenon of identity construction, vanity, status anxiety and ‘youthaholicism’ – exploring the blurry line between truth, fake truth and self-deception. That distortion gives rich scope for satire, mirroring the culture of Instaworthy photos, cosmetic surgery and influencers.” This pop-culture exploration arrives at a pivotal moment for Bell. Facing post-COVID instability, shifting audience habits and severe financial pressures, theatre companies confront a landscape where audiences are risk-averse, booking late and demanding familiar entry points. Mackenzie star Kimberley Hodgson (left) and playwright Yve Blake. Steven Siewert



Bell Shakespeare artistic director Peter Evans acknowledges these realities, stressing the company is charting a path to absorb rising production costs without scaling back. “We are unwilling to employ fewer artists or do less work,” he says. Related Article Performing arts Celeste Barber, Tim Minchin and Whitlam’s dismissal: Inside Sydney Theatre Company’s 2027 season To secure long-term stability without compromising artistic scale, the company is launching a permanent financial endowment. By preserving the principal investment, annual interest will be reinvested directly into programming. To keep houses full, Evans is leaning into traditional stagings with commercially savvy crossover productions. Building on the success of 2022’s pop musical The Lovers, the company is bringing back Mackenzie. Reimagining Macbeth as a 13-year-old child star and Lady Macbeth as her ruthlessly ambitious stage mother, Mackenzie drew an unprecedented 25 per cent first-time ticket buyers. It now returns for an extensive three-month national tour alongside main stage runs in major capital cities and the Sydney Opera House.



“To see the play packed in with people aged from 16 to 30, repeat customers, is a huge win, and I would say quintessentially part of Bell’s mission statement,” Evans says. For Potts, bringing a 21st-century lens to classic texts honours Shakespeare’s inherent flexibility. “Shakespeare’s work exists to be performed, defined by its poetic breadth,” she says. “The plays are not museum pieces – they remain dynamic vehicles that reveal profound truths about contemporary life.” The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. World.title: ‘It was crippling’: New endometriosis plan aims to save women from years of agony
World.content:
Exclusive NationalHealthcare ‘It was crippling’: New endometriosis plan aims to save women from years of agony Melissa Cunningham September 17, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lilia Tennant still remembers being curled up on the floor of a store on Chapel Street with agonising abdominal pain. Tennant was 13, shopping with their mother, and days away from getting their first period. It took six years for Lilia Tennant to be diagnosed with endometriosis despite her being in debilitating pain every month. Justin McManus “It was pretty crazy, I literally fell to the floor the pain was so bad,” the now 22-year-old said. “It was a sign of what was to come.” It would take more than six years for doctors to finally diagnose Tennant with endometriosis, a chronic, inflammatory condition in which tissue similar to the inner lining of the uterus grows in other parts of the body, causing episodes of severe, often crippling pain.



Doctors initially brushed off Tennant’s debilitating abdominal symptoms as muscle pain due to running. Related Article Women's health ‘It’s exhausting’: How an inquiry into women’s pain exposed a systemic culture of medical bias “It was crippling. I literally had terrible pain my entire menstrual cycle and the days leading up to it and my doctors almost didn’t even bring up menstruation or period-related issues as even an option of being the cause of this,” the pharmaceutical science student said. “I found I had to do all the research and the work myself to understand what was going on in my body.” Despite endometriosis affecting an estimated one in seven Australian women, it takes an average six to eight years for the condition to be diagnosed.



But under Australia’s first national endometriosis management plan, being launched on Thursday, people like Tennant will no longer have to wait years for a formal or surgical diagnosis via a laparoscopy to begin managing their pain properly with their general practitioner. Related Article Exclusive

Women's health ‘Green whistle’ for IUDs and new pain standard after inquiry reveals women’s suffering Project lead Professor Danielle Mazza said the online plan, which was co-designed with people living with endometriosis and pelvic pain, aims to raise the standard of care and treat the condition like any other serious, chronic and debilitating illness. “Women and doctors still haven’t really conceptualised endometriosis as a chronic disease, but that’s exactly what it is,” Mazza, who is head of Monash University’s Department of General Practice, said. “We don’t have a cure so what we’re seeking to do is detect it really early and manage the symptoms far better to try and avoid the long-term complications of the condition, which is really what we do with any chronic disease like diabetes or arthritis.”



Severe long-term complications include infertility, chronic pelvic pain and potential impairment of neighbouring organs . Many women report being ignored, dismissed or belittled when they seek care for their symptoms. “Symptoms can be complex, non-specific and vary from person to person,” Mazza said. “We want patients to understand their condition, know what their options are, and have a clear management plan they can return to and review with their GP, rather than feeling hopeless and like there they have nowhere to turn.” The chronic and progressive nature of the condition also frequently inflicts significant psychological and financial strain on women.



Related Article Updated

Women's health ‘It makes no sense’: Minister blasts secrecy over investigation of gynaecologist Mazza said every woman will be able to get the health management plan through their GP, which will be available online after their appointment and personalised depending on symptoms. It includes the most effective, non-pharmacological treatments alongside evidence-based medications. It will also give women access to Medicare subsidised allied health services, such as physiotherapy, mirroring what Australians with other chronic illnesses have access to. Tennant’s endometriosis was finally confirmed with an ultrasound at age 19.



The disease was so far advanced they were in an operating theatre within weeks, and it took almost a year for them to feel back to normal. Tennant welcomed the national endometriosis management plan and hoped it would put the condition at the forefront for healthcare professionals diagnosing and treating it. “It takes the burden from the patient of having to do all the work themselves and advocate to have their symptoms taken seriously,” Tennant said. “As a teenager, I would have loved something like this.” Mazza said the document will also give women self-management guidance and online tools to be able to track their symptoms, measure the severity of their physical pain, menstrual bleeding and mental health as well as supporting them to reach their fertility goals. “I’ve got patients who have suffered terribly and had awful chronic pain that stopped them from living their lives and doing what they want to do,” she said.



Mazza said more research was urgently needed to determine whether starting teenagers on early treatment can offset long-term harm and complications. Related Series

Medical misogyny Medical misogyny Royal Australian College of General Practitioners president Dr Michael Wright said the new model of treatment had the potential to change lives. “Too many Australians living with endometriosis spend years seeking answers, often while managing significant pain and disruption to their daily lives,” Wright said. “By supporting earlier management, shared decision-making and co-ordinated multidisciplinary care, this initiative has the potential to improve health outcomes and quality of life for people.”



Monash University research showed the proportion of women presenting to GPs with endometriosis has almost doubled in recent years. Doctors across Australia will receive training on the new model of care which was developed by Monash University’s SPHERE Centre of Research Excellence and GP college and funded by the federal government. The nation’s first Inquiry Into Women’s Pain this year found that many women had been gaslit by medical professionals or made to feel at fault when asking for medication for their pain. Of 13,000 women who shared their experiences with the eight-month process, 90 per cent of respondents experienced pain that lasted over a year, with 54 per cent experiencing it daily. World.title: ASX set to slump, Wall Street falls as Fed chief spooks investors; Microsoft AI chief sends Anthropic warning
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slump, Wall Street falls as Fed chief spooks investors; Microsoft AI chief sends Anthropic warning Stan Choe Updated September 17, 2026 — 8:09am ,first published 4:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks slipped after the Federal Reserve hiked its main interest rate for the first time in three years and suggested more may be ahead as it tries to get the nation’s high inflation under control. The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent after giving up a modest gain from earlier in the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 631 points, or 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was nearly unchanged after edging down by less than 0.1 per cent. Fed chair Kevin Warsh’s warnings on inflation spooked Wall Street. AP Photo/Seth Wenig The Australian sharemarket is set to decline sharply, with futures at 6.21am AEST pointing to a fall of 68 points, or 0.8 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.3 per cent on Wednesday. Investors generally prefer lower interest rates because higher rates slow the economy’s growth and undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



The US stock market initially held onto its modest, early gains after the Fed announced its decision. The short-term pain of a slower economy may be worth it if it starves inflation of its fuel and gets further increases for the cost of living back to the Fed’s 2 per cent target. View post on X But stock prices weakened later in the day as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said repeatedly in a press conference that inflation remains too high and the US economy appears to be strengthening. That could imply the economy is solid enough to withstand more hikes to rates, and other officials at the Fed provided their own forecasts suggesting rates may need to go still higher. The median Fed official expects the federal funds rate to end this year at 4.1 per cent, according to forecasts published after the central bank’s meeting. That’s up from its current range of 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent following Wednesday’s increase, and it’s up from the median forecast of 3.8 per cent that Fed officials gave three months ago. Traders, meanwhile, suspect the Fed may go even further. They’re betting on a 38 per cent probability the Fed could hike the federal funds rate to a range of 4.25 per cent to 4.50 per cent by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group.



“Our decision comes at a time when the American economy appears to be strengthening,” Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in his press conference. He pointed to solid US hiring trends, corporate profits and investments by businesses. A report on Wednesday morning, meanwhile, showed shoppers spent much more at US retailers last month than economists expected. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks at a news conference following the decision. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said. He later added, “Today’s action starts to show we’re serious about this.” It’s the first hike by the Fed to interest rates in three years. The central bank had been on pause for months following cuts to rates in 2024 and 2025, even though inflation has consistently remained above the Fed’s 2 per cent target.



President Donald Trump has been lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher. On Wall Street, bank stocks fell to some of the market’s sharper losses. A slower US economy could mean less demand for loans from them. Banks also get hurt when the gap narrows between short-term interest rates and longer-term ones because the industry makes profit off the difference. Following the Fed’s announcements, the two-year Treasury yield jumped to 4.74 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Tuesday. It tends to closely follow expectations for what the Fed will do with the federal funds rate. The yield on the longer-term 10-year Treasury, meanwhile, takes into account expectations for economic growth and inflation years down the line. It had a more modest increase, ticking up to 5.01 per cent from 5.00 per cent late Tuesday. Huntington Bancshares fell 5.6 per cent, Citizens Financial Group sank 4.8 per cent and JPMorgan Chase slipped 1 per cent.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Trump set to explode if his man does his job Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The largest loss in the S&P 500 came from J.B. Hunt Transport Services, which lost 13.3 per cent. Its chief financial officer told a conference of analysts late Tuesday that it’s facing higher costs and expects its earnings to drop 5 per cent to 10 per cent from the second quarter to the third. Stocks of oil companies also weighed on the market after the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 2.7 per cent to $105.83. It was the first drop of the week for Brent, which has gotten near $110 in recent days. Helping to limit the market’s losses were gains for some influential stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry. Nvidia rose 0.8 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices climbed 1.6 per cent to recover more of their losses from earlier in the week. AI stocks slid worldwide Monday after leaders of the AI industry called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity.



Microsoft slipped 1.4 per cent. Overnight, its artificial intelligence chief Mustafa Suleyman warned infusing tools like Anthropic’s Claude with humanlike characteristics increases the risks of such systems going rogue. In an essay, the longtime artificial intelligence developer took aim at some of the language in the guiding documents behind Claude, Anthropic PBC’s popular family of large language models. Claude’s constitution expresses ambiguity about whether the assistant is a moral entity, positing that the software may have “some functional version of emotions or feelings.” All told, the S&P 500 fell 33.92 points to 7,551.81. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 631.21 to 51,461.90, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 3.15 to 25,978.42. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.4 per cent for one of the world’s biggest gains. Inflation is a worldwide problem, and the European Central Bank hiked rates last week to help diminish it.



AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: New Today show hosts announced after Sarah Abo confirms departure
World.content:
Sylvia Jeffreys and Tom Steinfort have been announced as the new hosts of the Today show after Sarah Abo confirmed this week she was leaving the show. “We can announce that Sylvia Jeffreys and Tom Steinfort have been named the new hosts of Today in 2027. With a collective four decades of experience, their appointments mark a new era for the program,” newsreader Jayne Azzopardi said during a news update. Tom Steinfort and Sylvia Jeffreys. Jeffreys said it was “very exciting as a cat’s out of the bag”. “There are a lot of mixed feelings for everyone today. I know that here on the floor, and for you at home as well,” she added. “But I know that Tom and I are going to work really, really hard to carry on the amazing work of Sarah, of Karl [Stefanovic], of the whole team, everything they’ve been doing for years for you, our viewers. And yes, 2027 is going to be a huge year.”



Steinfort said he was “pumped as well”. “I’m stoked to be doing it alongside you, and yeah, I’m just thrilled to be part of such an iconic show.” Loading In a statement on Wednesday, Abo said: “Words can’t express how grateful I am to our viewers for letting me into your homes to be part of your morning routine. Without you, there is no Today show. “Together with 60 Minutes, I’ve spent my time at Nine chasing stories, travelling and reporting from all over the world, interviewing some incredible and inspiring people from all walks of life.”



Before the new hosting team was announced, Abo was farewelled on the show. “Sarah will always be such a much loved part of this Today family, no matter what,” Jeffreys said. “And talking to her last night, I know that she’s been feeling so much love from you, our wonderful viewers. After she shared that news and thanked Australia for welcoming her into your homes and letting her be part of your every morning routine. Sarah Abo has been on maternity leave since July. Nine Jeffreys thanked for Abo “giving so much of yourself to this show and for being such a joy to share our mornings with. But of course, now that belongs to beautiful [son] Sonny and [partner] Cyrus.” The program also played a greatest hits package of Abo’s time on show with former host Karl Stefanovic, with clips of her interviewing the prime minister and former Australian of the Year Richard Scolyer, as well as celebrities.



Abo also posted a video message on her Instagram account yesterday announcing her departure from Today and Nine. In the video, she said she “loved every minute” and the Today crew felt like family. She also thanked the viewers at home for “being incredibly supportive”. Abo also said “there was more to come”, and that would be announced in “due course”. The journalist’s next steps have been the subject of rumour, with New Idea reporting she is due to join the rival Seven network to read the news in Melbourne. It has been a year of immense change for Abo, who gave birth in July, after years of struggles with infertility. She acknowledged this in her farewell statement on Wednesday, writing: “Becoming a mum has heralded a new chapter and sharing that with our audience has been truly special. As many of you know, this has been a significant journey for my family and will continue to be my greatest achievement.



“I’d like to thank the wider Today team – the amazing crew, incredible producers and my wonderful fellow hosts – you all know how much you mean to me. It takes a special kind of crazy to wake up at the hours we do, but it’s so much easier when the team feels like family. I’ll miss you all dearly.” The breakfast program was thrown into turmoil earlier this year with the sacking of long-time host Stefanovic, who had his contract terminated after he interviewed convicted fraudster and right-wing agitator Tommy Robinson on his podcast, The Karl Stefanovic Show. Loading Today’s weatherman, Tim Davies, also announced his resignation last month. His last broadcast is due on Friday. A rotating line-up of Nine personalities has been filling in for Stefanovic and Abo, including former Sunrise host Armytage, who joined Nine in 2024 after 21 years at Seven.



Related Video Video icon 0:33 Karl Stefanovic drops podcast teaser amid legal battle Nine executive director of news and current affairs Fiona Dear paid tribute to Abo, saying: “Sarah has been an integral part of the Today team, bringing warmth, energy and first-class journalism to the program each morning. “It takes enormous skill to front 3½ hours of live television every day, and Sarah did it with sharp journalistic instincts. We thank her for everything she brought to Today, and wish Sarah and her family all the very best.” In other news, Hugh Riminton is reported to have announced his departure from Ten. The veteran journalist, who has been with the network for the past 17 years, said in a note to staff that “48 years in daily news is probably enough. This reporter’s life has given me the world. I leave with nothing but gratitude for every hour of it.” Nine is owner of this masthead.

World.title: Fed defies Trump, raises US interest rates for first time in three years
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaFederal Reserve Fed defies Trump, raises US interest rates for first time in three years Michael Koziol Updated September 17, 2026 — 9:00am ,first published 4:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The US Federal Reserve has lifted interest rates for the first time in three years in a bid to rein in persistently high inflation fuelled by the ongoing war with Iran and its impact on the cost of energy. While widely expected, the move risks enraging President Donald Trump, who has furiously campaigned for the central bank to cut rates – piling pressure on his new handpicked Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh. Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh speaks at a press conference following the announcement. AP But the Fed’s rate-setting committee voted unanimously on Wednesday (US time) to raise the target rate by 0.25 percentage point, to a band of 3.75 to 4 per cent. In a set of quarterly projections, the Fed also signalled that its committee expects to hike rates again this year to 4.1 per cent. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said at a news conference. “This [American] summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.”



The call to raise rates was the first unanimous, 12-0 decision by the Fed since May 2025. Warsh described it as a sober and responsible decision, and would not countenance future rate hikes, though reporters pointed out that increases were rarely one-off. “I’m not going to prejudge any future decisions we make,” he said. Nor would he comment on any discussions with Trump. View post on X Economists widely tipped a rate rise after last week’s official data showed US inflation stuck at 3.4 per cent – above the Fed’s target of 2 per cent, driven largely by increasing energy costs. The consumer price index ticked up 0.4 per cent in August in seasonally adjusted terms, with petrol up 3.9 per cent. After falling back to nearly pre-war levels, the price of Brent crude – the international oil benchmark - is back above $US100 a barrel.



That was compounded by new attacks by Iran-backed militants in Yemen and Iraq, targeting oil supplies that avoid the Strait of Hormuz by using the Bab al-Mandab Strait between Yemen and the African coast. Saudi Arabia closed the East-West Pipeline across the Arabian Peninsula last week following drone attacks. Bloomberg reported the kingdom was aiming to restore about half the pipeline’s capacity within days. The highly anticipated interest rates decision being watched live in the New York Stock Exchange. Bloomberg Warsh indicated deteriorating geopolitical circumstances in the seven weeks since the Fed’s last meeting were a factor in its decision to lift rates. “There’s no hiding from hotspots around the world,” he said. “Our judgment about what is the most likely or least likely in the geopolitical situation has changed.”



Trump has consistently pressured the central bank to cut rates, and led a vicious campaign against former chairman Jerome Powell for his failure to do so. Two weeks ago, he said Warsh and the Fed “must get smart” and “BE PATRIOTS for a change”. He threatened: “LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT.” President Donald Trump swore in Fed chairman Kevin Warsh with an extensive White House ceremony in May. Bloomberg On Wednesday afternoon, following the decision, Trump doubled down on his trade threats but stopped short of criticising Warsh or the governors directly. “Interest Rates in the United States should be 1% or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World - BY FAR,” he wrote on Truth Social. “If we stopped Trading with every country that we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year.



“We are ‘carrying’ almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” Trump later told reporters he still had confidence in Warsh. “I ... talked to Kevin,” Trump said, appearing to confirm an interaction that the Fed chief himself has so far declined to corroborate. “And I said you might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They’re very political. They’re doing the wrong thing.” Rising petrol prices in the US due to the war against Iran have contributed to persistently high inflation. AP White House economics spokesman Kush Desai told Fox News the Fed’s decision to increase rates was “rather unfortunate” and “not backed by a particularly compelling economic case”.



Lingering inflation was “entirely driven by an energy supply shock, by what’s going on with oil prices in the Middle East”, Desai said. “These are things that have nothing to do with interest rates and are not affected by interest rates.” Analysts had warned that Wednesday’s decision was a test of the Fed’s independence and credibility, with persistently high inflation leaving Warsh and his fellow governors with little choice but to hike rates or be accused of cowing to Trump’s wishes. Warsh told Congress in July that the Fed had “no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation”. And at the bank’s August 28 summit at Jackson Hole, he said inflation was “concerning”, and that governors had opted to wait for more information before deciding to raise rates. Related Article Opinion

US politics Alarms flashing red as Trump takes US debt to level almost beyond comprehension Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent “This is where the chairman has effectively painted himself into a corner,” said JPMorgan chief global strategist David Kelly on Monday, adding that both Warsh and the governing committee would “lose serious credibility” if they did not raise rates.



Warsh denied that market expectations played a role in the outcome. “Today was our decision,” he said, adding that he preferred to look at trends over time rather than “noisy” individual data points. The Fed’s governing committee said economic activity was expanding at a solid pace, with the unemployment rate steady, productivity growth strong and capital investment robust. Though it noted uncertainty remained elevated, “owing, in part, to geopolitical developments”.
