World.title: Love Island meets Shakespeare in this show with a looksmaxxing twist of fate
World.content:
CultureTheatrePerforming arts Love Island meets Shakespeare in this show with a looksmaxxing twist of fate Linda Morris September 17, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When director Marion Potts looks at William Shakespeare’s As You Like It, she sees more than a 16th-century pastoral comedy – she sees the thematic DNA of modern reality television franchises like Love Island. “People are falling in love at first sight. There are betrayals, jealousies, recriminations and confessionals,” says Potts. “There’s even an exile that feels like an eviction. I began thinking, my gosh, there are really close parallels with reality television and what it says about popular culture. That’s where the play became truly fascinating for me, exploring that heightened, performative reality the characters inhabit.” Bell Shakespeare artistic director Peter Evans and director Marion Potts. Janie Barrett Potts returns to direct As You Like It for Bell Shakespeare’s 2027 season, marking the company’s first staging of the 1599 work in 12 years. Next year’s line-up also features a “dark and dangerous” 90-minute adaptation of Measure for Measure, directed by Saro Lusty-Cavallari. As You Like It follows exiled nobles escaping court corruption into the Forest of Arden. Free from rigid social constraints, they undergo unpredictable romantic entanglements. “It’s liberating and incredibly freeing, but they’re also in freefall,” Potts says.



Both the Elizabethan court and modern reality television construct hyper-gendered environments where men are expected to be buff, women hyper-feminine, and everyone preens for courtship. Potts’ production avoids a literal time and place. “If anything, it’s set in a world where concrete reality and mediated reality are confused,” he says. “A world not unlike our own, where characters are in constant performance as though they’re being watched, even without cameras. “It taps into the troubling phenomenon of identity construction, vanity, status anxiety and ‘youthaholicism’ – exploring the blurry line between truth, fake truth and self-deception. That distortion gives rich scope for satire, mirroring the culture of Instaworthy photos, cosmetic surgery and influencers.” This pop-culture exploration arrives at a pivotal moment for Bell. Facing post-COVID instability, shifting audience habits and severe financial pressures, theatre companies confront a landscape where audiences are risk-averse, booking late and demanding familiar entry points. Mackenzie star Kimberley Hodgson (left) and playwright Yve Blake. Steven Siewert



Bell Shakespeare artistic director Peter Evans acknowledges these realities, stressing the company is charting a path to absorb rising production costs without scaling back. “We are unwilling to employ fewer artists or do less work,” he says. Related Article Performing arts Celeste Barber, Tim Minchin and Whitlam’s dismissal: Inside Sydney Theatre Company’s 2027 season To secure long-term stability without compromising artistic scale, the company is launching a permanent financial endowment. By preserving the principal investment, annual interest will be reinvested directly into programming. To keep houses full, Evans is leaning into traditional stagings with commercially savvy crossover productions. Building on the success of 2022’s pop musical The Lovers, the company is bringing back Mackenzie. Reimagining Macbeth as a 13-year-old child star and Lady Macbeth as her ruthlessly ambitious stage mother, Mackenzie drew an unprecedented 25 per cent first-time ticket buyers. It now returns for an extensive three-month national tour alongside main stage runs in major capital cities and the Sydney Opera House.



“To see the play packed in with people aged from 16 to 30, repeat customers, is a huge win, and I would say quintessentially part of Bell’s mission statement,” Evans says. For Potts, bringing a 21st-century lens to classic texts honours Shakespeare’s inherent flexibility. “Shakespeare’s work exists to be performed, defined by its poetic breadth,” she says. “The plays are not museum pieces – they remain dynamic vehicles that reveal profound truths about contemporary life.” The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. World.title: ‘It was crippling’: New endometriosis plan aims to save women from years of agony
World.content:
Exclusive NationalHealthcare ‘It was crippling’: New endometriosis plan aims to save women from years of agony Melissa Cunningham September 17, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lilia Tennant still remembers being curled up on the floor of a store on Chapel Street with agonising abdominal pain. Tennant was 13, shopping with their mother, and days away from getting their first period. It took six years for Lilia Tennant to be diagnosed with endometriosis despite her being in debilitating pain every month. Justin McManus “It was pretty crazy, I literally fell to the floor the pain was so bad,” the now 22-year-old said. “It was a sign of what was to come.” It would take more than six years for doctors to finally diagnose Tennant with endometriosis, a chronic, inflammatory condition in which tissue similar to the inner lining of the uterus grows in other parts of the body, causing episodes of severe, often crippling pain.



Doctors initially brushed off Tennant’s debilitating abdominal symptoms as muscle pain due to running. Related Article Women's health ‘It’s exhausting’: How an inquiry into women’s pain exposed a systemic culture of medical bias “It was crippling. I literally had terrible pain my entire menstrual cycle and the days leading up to it and my doctors almost didn’t even bring up menstruation or period-related issues as even an option of being the cause of this,” the pharmaceutical science student said. “I found I had to do all the research and the work myself to understand what was going on in my body.” Despite endometriosis affecting an estimated one in seven Australian women, it takes an average six to eight years for the condition to be diagnosed.



But under Australia’s first national endometriosis management plan, being launched on Thursday, people like Tennant will no longer have to wait years for a formal or surgical diagnosis via a laparoscopy to begin managing their pain properly with their general practitioner. Related Article Exclusive

Women's health ‘Green whistle’ for IUDs and new pain standard after inquiry reveals women’s suffering Project lead Professor Danielle Mazza said the online plan, which was co-designed with people living with endometriosis and pelvic pain, aims to raise the standard of care and treat the condition like any other serious, chronic and debilitating illness. “Women and doctors still haven’t really conceptualised endometriosis as a chronic disease, but that’s exactly what it is,” Mazza, who is head of Monash University’s Department of General Practice, said. “We don’t have a cure so what we’re seeking to do is detect it really early and manage the symptoms far better to try and avoid the long-term complications of the condition, which is really what we do with any chronic disease like diabetes or arthritis.”



Severe long-term complications include infertility, chronic pelvic pain and potential impairment of neighbouring organs . Many women report being ignored, dismissed or belittled when they seek care for their symptoms. “Symptoms can be complex, non-specific and vary from person to person,” Mazza said. “We want patients to understand their condition, know what their options are, and have a clear management plan they can return to and review with their GP, rather than feeling hopeless and like there they have nowhere to turn.” The chronic and progressive nature of the condition also frequently inflicts significant psychological and financial strain on women.



Related Article Updated

Women's health ‘It makes no sense’: Minister blasts secrecy over investigation of gynaecologist Mazza said every woman will be able to get the health management plan through their GP, which will be available online after their appointment and personalised depending on symptoms. It includes the most effective, non-pharmacological treatments alongside evidence-based medications. It will also give women access to Medicare subsidised allied health services, such as physiotherapy, mirroring what Australians with other chronic illnesses have access to. Tennant’s endometriosis was finally confirmed with an ultrasound at age 19.



The disease was so far advanced they were in an operating theatre within weeks, and it took almost a year for them to feel back to normal. Tennant welcomed the national endometriosis management plan and hoped it would put the condition at the forefront for healthcare professionals diagnosing and treating it. “It takes the burden from the patient of having to do all the work themselves and advocate to have their symptoms taken seriously,” Tennant said. “As a teenager, I would have loved something like this.” Mazza said the document will also give women self-management guidance and online tools to be able to track their symptoms, measure the severity of their physical pain, menstrual bleeding and mental health as well as supporting them to reach their fertility goals. “I’ve got patients who have suffered terribly and had awful chronic pain that stopped them from living their lives and doing what they want to do,” she said.



Mazza said more research was urgently needed to determine whether starting teenagers on early treatment can offset long-term harm and complications. Related Series

Medical misogyny Medical misogyny Royal Australian College of General Practitioners president Dr Michael Wright said the new model of treatment had the potential to change lives. “Too many Australians living with endometriosis spend years seeking answers, often while managing significant pain and disruption to their daily lives,” Wright said. “By supporting earlier management, shared decision-making and co-ordinated multidisciplinary care, this initiative has the potential to improve health outcomes and quality of life for people.”



Monash University research showed the proportion of women presenting to GPs with endometriosis has almost doubled in recent years. Doctors across Australia will receive training on the new model of care which was developed by Monash University’s SPHERE Centre of Research Excellence and GP college and funded by the federal government. The nation’s first Inquiry Into Women’s Pain this year found that many women had been gaslit by medical professionals or made to feel at fault when asking for medication for their pain. Of 13,000 women who shared their experiences with the eight-month process, 90 per cent of respondents experienced pain that lasted over a year, with 54 per cent experiencing it daily. World.title: Grey Power welcomes scrapping of mandatory cognitive testing for older drivers
World.content:
New guidance on ways older drivers are assessed by doctors Nine To Noon Download MP3 4m

Older drivers will no longer be required to take a cognitive test in order to keep their driver's licence.

New clinical guidance for health practitioners allows them to assess a person's fitness to drive individually.

When people reach 75 years old they must get a medical certificate to renew their licence and then again at 80 and every two years after that.

While cognitive screening is still an option, doctors will consider a person's overall health and driving history.

The changes follow an independent University of Auckland review of cognitive testing and driving safety which found that available evidence did not support screening otherwise healthy older adults as part of fitness-to-drive assessments.

It found that commonly used cognitive screening tools were not reliable predictors of driving ability.

Grey Power president David Marshall told Nine to Noon his group had been campaigning for the test to be dropped on the basis that they could find no evidence that it predicted someone's driving ability.

"Many of our members have reported that they've had their licence cancelled purely on the basis of the cognitive test."

Grey Power worked with New Zealand Transport Agency and the Office for Seniors to commission a study by Auckland University to look at the literature, he said.

"And that's come up saying 'look it's not predictive and should not be used as the sole reason for failing someone's licence.'"

It would be up to GPs to make the decision about whether an older person was competent to continue driving, he said.

"What we have been concerned about is that everyone was given a cognitive test and not everyone remembers an address or can suddenly recite 20 items in a supermarket which seem to be quite apart from driving ability."

He said hopefully the focus would now be more on issues like the driver's feeling of confidence with driving, any accidents they may have had, along with medical issues such as their sight.

GPs would still have the option of using a cognitive test, he said.

"If someone's clearly got more advanced dementia and they shouldn't be on the road, we don't want them on the road."

But GPs could use the test if they thought someone was showing early signs of dementia and then go on to do further evaluations, he said.

World.title: Taboo factor has a role in Fiji HIV crisis - lecturer
World.content:
A health lecturer says gaps in sexual health knowledge have contributed to Fiji's HIV crisis.

Fiji's government has declared a national HIV emergency, expanding free rapid testing and giving clean needles to drug users.

Dr Jalal Mohommed from the University of Canterbury said Fiji was facing a once-in-a-generation health crisis.

He told Morning Report there were a number of factors contributing to it, including underfunding in the health sector and Fiji's position on the "drug highway".

"There's been multiple natural disasters, health worker migration, Covid-19 and its impacts. But there's also been, importantly, gaps in sexual health knowledge," he said.

"It is quite a taboo subject in Fiji, so not enough has been done. So if you've taken those public health workers out of the public health system and put them into the curative health system, there isn't that public health education going on."

Mohammed said traditionally Fiji had spent quite a low portion of its GDP on health - below the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommendation.

Fiji govt declares national HIV emergency Morning Report Download MP3 5m

"WHO recommends that a country spends about 5 percent. Fiji's traditionally been spending about 3 percent of its GDP, and so there's been significant underinvestment in the health sector.

"What's really now needed is about 6 to 7 percent, so we've got an ailing health infrastructure, a very fragile health system. There has been a focus on clinical services over public health services in Fiji, just because it's so short-funded."

Mohammed said 1.6 percent of Fiji's population between the ages of 15 and 49 have been diagnosed with HIV, but there's also a segment of the population that hasn't been diagnosed.

World.title: Westpac approved to issue digital IDs
World.content:
Westpac has become the first New Zealand bank that can issue digital identification credentials.

It said its business customers would soon be able to set up digital IDs they could share with customers and other third parties, to make banking more secure.

The accreditation was issued under the government's Digital Identity Services Trust Framework.

"This means businesses don't need to download a bank statement, redact information by hand or send documents using less secure methods such as email - saving them time and reducing the risk of fraud and scams," said Westpac NZ chief data, digital and AI officer Russell Jones.

"We know trust and control are very important to New Zealanders when sharing personal information online. Digital ID provides a modern, trusted and simple way to share it while keeping you in control.

"Digital ID and its benefits have been talked about for a long time but it needs positive action to make it a reality. We've invested heavily to become the first bank and only the third organisation to reach this milestone because we're keen to help lead the rollout."

He said digital ID would be increasingly important as more aspects of life went online.

Could I run out of money in retirement and other questions experts wish you'd ask No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

"The ability to know in a verifiable way who is who online is absolutely, super important. That is the fundamental basis for why we are doing this.

"We, along with the rest of the industry, for years have been talking about digital identity and there has been some really good work done and continues to be done building on things like RealMe."

Digital ID will give people buying from a Westpac business customer more confidence that they were paying into the correct bank account.

Jones said someone buying a car from a dealer who banked with Westpac might ask for proof of the dealer's bank account details. After downloading the Govt.nz app wallet, the dealer could log in to Westpac One Business, choose an account and generate a QR code.

The dealer would scan the Westpac QR code in the wallet, then enter a code sent by text message. They now have a Westpac Business Bank Account credential, valid for 72 hours, to show the buyer as proof of the account.

"Digital ID's potential goes well beyond banking. Imagine the convenience of having a digital version of your driver's licence or passport in your phone," Jones said.

The plan was to make the digital ID accreditation available to retail customers in future, Jones said.

Customers buying groceries could eventually find checkouts that were able to check they were over 18 with digital ID, he said.

"Wouldn't it be great if every government department would work with agreed credentials? Then you wouldn't need to have 20 logons to log on to various different things. You could just have one - you wouldn't have multiple user IDs for councils, for utilities, for all sorts of things - you could use your one credential to do that.

"Everything from proving your age to setting up utilities to travelling overseas could be simplified without compromising on security. There's an exciting future ahead, with more choice, convenience and customer control.

"At the same time, digital ID will only succeed if there's large scale adoption of credential verification. That means a wide range of sectors including banking, hospitality and telecommunications working with local and central government to make digital ID part of the everyday customer experience.

"As we continue to invest in our rollout, we're keen to share our experiences with organisations who are at the start of their digital ID journey."

World.title: India free trade agreement edges closer after Parliament passes legislation
World.content:
The free trade agreement with India has passed through its third reading in Parliament, moving one step closer to being officially rubber-stamped.

The legislation passed by a vote of 93–29, with support from the opposition Labour Party.

New Zealand First, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and the two independent MPs voted against the legislation.

The free trade agreement eliminates or reduces tariffs on 95 percent of exports, including kiwifruit, apples, meat, coal, wool, and forestry.

Trade Minister Todd McClay said the promise to have it in force by the end of the parliamentary term had almost been delivered.

“The India FTA opens the door for Kiwi exporters to one of the world’s largest and fastest-growing economies,” McClay said.

“Parliament today overwhelmingly backed the long-term benefits the agreement will deliver for all New Zealanders.”

McClay hoped exporters would be able to use the agreement to build new relationships with Indian businesses and help double two-way trade by 2030.

“We are already seeing strong momentum as exporters, customers and investors respond to the increased engagement between our countries,” he said.

“This agreement turns India from a market of future promise into a practical opportunity for more New Zealand businesses.”

World.title: Government announces 'commonsense changes' to hospitality drop-off services
World.content:
The government will change regulations so hospitality businesses that offer drop-off services to their customers will not be stung by fees.

Pubs and clubs often offer courtesy vans to get their patrons home. But if they accept financial contributions towards the costs of running the transport service, or if they charge patrons to use the service, then it triggers passenger service requirements.

Minister for Regulation David Seymour said this meant that some hospitality businesses offering rides to get their patrons home safe were treated the same as a taxi service.

"I heard from one business who were paying about $12,000 per month to offer their customers rides home. That was coming straight out of their pocket," he said.

"Not being able to cover those costs in a meaningful way prevents more venues from offering this service."

The Ministry for Regulation's recent hospitality review, which has also made recommendations around licensing fees and food safety requirements, found that financial contributions towards a ride service did not make a difference to how safe it was.

The Ministry has recommended the rules be scrapped.

Transport minister Chris Bishop said the change would make it easier for hospitality businesses to ensure their customers got home safe, and reduce the risk of drink driving.

"Some hospitality businesses, mainly clubs, offer transport services to their customers and members. This is often done to prevent customers or members drinking and driving to make our roads safer," he said.

"We want more hospitality businesses to have the means to offer them, so more Kiwis can benefit from them. That's why we are making this change."

Bishop said the changes would be added to existing regulatory reform work, and would be in-place by mind 2027.

World.title: Person assaulted by group while sleeping in vehicle on Auckland's waterfront
World.content:
Police say a person parked in their vehicle on Auckland's waterfront was assaulted while sleeping in the early hours of Thursday morning.

Officers were called to the attempted robbery on Jellicoe Street at Wynyard Quarter around 2.20am, Acting Detective Senior Sergeant Craig Burrow said.

Three men allegedly tried to remove the victim from the vehicle and later fled after the victim alerted nearby members of the public.

World.title: West Coast tourism operators say lack of information about SH6 costing them
World.content:
West Coast tourism operators say lack of communication from the Transport Agency (NZTA) about travel on State Highway 6 is costing businesses visitors and bookings.

State Highway 6 was closed on 28 August during a significant winter storm, but a few days later it partially opened for three daily escorted convoys as work continued to repair the damage from slips, rockfalls and inundation.

Google Maps has been directing all travelers on a nine-hour detour from Franz Joseph to Wanaka after the highway was legally closed.

Motorists are still escorted through the affected area in three daily convoys.

Franz Josef Wilderness Tours owner Dale Burrows said bookings were down about 40 percent compared with the same time last year.

Visitors were cancelling because they believed the highway was impassable, he said.

One of the slips on SH6 in August. NZTA / SUPPLIED

Burrows said the road was open without convoys at weekends, but this was not being clearly communicated by NZTA.

"There's just a real lack of communication from NZTA, but also Google and Apple Maps and all of those outfits are pulling data from who knows where and putting it online with no update as to where it's coming from or how you can actually update it with the correct information," he said.

He said there was also a longer-term impact on the West Coast's reputation, with some travel agents, tour groups and buses choosing not to include the region in their itineraries because of concerns about the roads.

NZTA Lower South Island area manager Chris Harris said because the highway was legally closed, it needed to show as closed on its journey planner.

World.title: 'Broken hearts': Ponsonby eatery Mekong Baby closes
World.content: “We have worked through long days, late nights, incredibly challenging times and all of the ups and downs that come with running a hospitality business. We have always believed that if we worked hard enough, cared enough and kept giving our best, we could keep going.

World.title: WTA Finals hoped to become 'Super Bowl of women's sports'
World.content:
The season-ending WTA Finals will be held in North Carolina for at least three years from 2027, as the tour seeks to take greater control of its flagship event amid financial concerns.

The finals, featuring the season's top-eight singles players and doubles ​teams, will be played in Charlotte at the venue which hosts the Hornets NBA team.

WTA chair Valerie Camillo said the tour wanted to build ‌the finals into the "Super Bowl of women's sports".

Camillo said the WTA would operate the event itself rather than rely on the type of outside-promoter arrangement previously used.

"The WTA will be taking greater ownership and control of the event and investing ⁠alongside our partners," Camillo said.

Financial details ​of Charlotte's package were not disclosed ‌ahead of a planned announcement by local partners.

Rybakina downs Sabalenka for US Open title Elena Rybakina already took Aryna Sabalenka's world number one ranking, now she takes her US Open title as well.

Camillo said it represented a "meaningful investment" that gave the WTA confidence to commit to the city.

The move follows the WTA's decision to relocate the November 2026 finals to Indian Wells, California, after ending an agreement under which Riyadh had hosted the event with the backing of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment ​Fund.

British newspaper The ‌Telegraph reported last week internal WTA projections showed the tour could run out of cash next year and move into debt by autumn 2027 if its spending pattern continued.

The report said the WTA expected operating ⁠losses of $US23 million ($32 million) in 2026 and cited the loss of ‌revenue associated with the Saudi finals deal ‌as a major contributor.

Camillo said 2026 was a transitional year and the tour was tightening spending while absorbing ‌the unexpected cost of moving the finals to Indian Wells.

The WTA has not yet set prize money for the 2027 finals.

Camillo said equal prize money remained an important goal, but added the tour was considering alternatives, including ⁠a profit-sharing model with players.

"We want this event to be built together with the players," she said.

"Why stop at equal prize money?"

The WTA also plans to establish a greater operational presence in Charlotte as it builds the event.

Reuters

World.title: Aussie F1 Grand Prix loses season-opening honour but gains sprint race
World.content:
Melbourne's Australian Grand Prix will not have the privilege of opening the 2027 Formula 1 season, but it will boast two races in its biggest weekend yet.

After landing the chance to open the F1 year in 2026 as it once traditionally did for two decades, the Albert Park event will be the third stop on next season's record-equalling 24-race program.

The main race will take place later than usual on April 4, with Bahrain replacing Melbourne as the season-opening venue on March 14.

Jeddah will host the Saudi Arabia Grand Prix a week after the Bahrain race.

Antonelli edges closer to historic title as teammate concedes the fight Kimi Antonelli is on the brink of becoming the youngest F1 champion in history, while his nearest rival says he is out of the fight.

But the key development will be the introduction of a sprint race in Melbourne on Saturday, on the eve of the grand prix itself.

Instead of two sessions of practice on the Friday before the grand prix, there will be just one with sprint race qualifying taking place in the afternoon.

On the Saturday, there will be the double attraction of a sprint race, followed later by qualifying for the main event.

Melbourne will be one of 10 circuits to stage a sprint race in 2027, four more than this year.

F1 bosses clearly believe the 30-minute shorter races on the Saturday are the way forward.

They claim data showed broadcast viewership of sprint weekends was 12 per cent higher than non-sprint weekends, with qualifying three times more popular with fans than free practice.

Portugal (June 20) and Türkiye (October 3) are additions to the program, with the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort and Barcelona having dropped off.

AAP

World.title: Daly Cherry-Evans has arrived at the end of forever
World.content:
Years ago, when Daly Cherry-Evans was merely in his early 30s, he'd say that he was going to play forever and he was only ever half-joking.

Every time he'd be asked about his future, be it at the beginning of a season or at the end, he'd grin widely and assure whoever wanted to know that he, in fact, would never, ever stop.

Most of the time it felt like a gag, a way for one of the slickest operators in the NRL to disarm the inquiry and Cherry-Evans follow with all the usual patter we hear from the greybeards — that he'd play as long as his body held up or as long as he was still enjoying it.

Plenty say that but Cherry-Evans has lived it. He lived it long enough that he reached the end of the "lifetime" deal he once signed with Manly, long enough that younger men than him succumbed to the ravages of age and long enough that maybe the joke was on us the whole time for not believing him in the first place.

Cherry-Evans has enjoyed another consistent season after joining the Sydney Roosters this year. (Getty Images: Matt King )

It is only now, a few months before he turns 38 years old, that Cherry-Evans has finally arrived at the end of forever.

Win or lose, the Sydney Roosters sudden-death semifinal against Cronulla on Saturday is the beginning of the last days, the ones that seemed like they would never arrive.

A defeat will mark Cherry-Evans's final NRL match before he links with Hull FC in Super League next year where's he's odds on to, at least once, play with or against someone a full two decades younger than him.

A win will push the Roosters into a preliminary final against the Dolphins and keep the dream of a farewell premiership alive.

If the Tricolours do manage to go all the way, Cherry-Evans will break Lote Tuqiri's record for the longest gap between grand final wins by one season.

That premiership back in 2011 is still definitional to Cherry-Evans and what he's been for all this time.

In becoming the first rookie halfback to win a grand final since 1978 and because he was one of Manly's best through the finals and on the big day in their win over the Warriors, Cherry-Evans was able to transcend many of the slings and arrows launched during the rise of franchise playmakers.

Cherry-Evans made history in his very first NRL season. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan )

Instead of the typical hero journey most halfbacks endure, with its peaks and valleys and rises and falls, Cherry-Evans's success as a rookie gave him a kind of instant validation.

There was never any talk of what he might be one day once he matures, or what he would eventually become once he developed this part of his game or not.

There was no debate whether he would one day be enough to lead a team to glory because he had already done it. It was instant proof of concept.

So many of young halfbacks are defined by their future, the possibility of what they might be, but ever since that first season, Cherry-Evans has instead existed in a blissful and seemingly eternal present.

His game has changed in subtle ways since that first year with Manly but through a bird's-eye view the similarities of his 16-year career is remarkable.

Why Daly Cherry-Evans is rugby league's ultimate survivor At 33, Daly Cherry-Evans might only be one more series loss away from his last game for Queensland – but if the decider was anything to go by, the Maroons' skipper isn't going anywhere.

This season was the 15th of those years where he managed at least 20 games and he has as many try assists this year at age 37 as he did the year he turned 25.

Old halves are supposed to run less but his return in that part of his game this year (51 run metres per game and five line breaks from 24 matches) is not miles away from his return as a rookie (57 per game and 11 line breaks from 27 matches).

They're meant to be worse at defending as well, but this year Cherry-Evans has had the third-best tackle efficiency of his career.

That's not to say there hasn't been some ups and downs for Cherry-Evans through his long career, but because of where he started and how long he's been there it was always easy to ride out the downs because, even as he reached his mid-30s, he had more time.

A bad option or a poor game or a sprayed kick, as rare as they were, or even a season where his team didn't make the finals were easier to accept because there was always more to come. He could always come back to what he had always been.

The end of that reality was put into stark relief in Sunday's qualifying final loss to Penrith even as, at the end of all things, Cherry-Evans can absolutely still cut it in a game of such quality and intensity.

It was only a month ago that he scored both tries in a 12-6 Tricolours win over the Panthers that remains their best performance of the season.

This time, with Sam Walker sidelined, Cherry-Evans slotted back into halfback and taken the lion's share of the kicking game and his field position chess match with Brian To'o as he hunted a 40/20 in the second half was a highlight.

Cherry-Evans missed the mark with what would have been an equaliser against Penrith last week. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

In the end, two kicks Cherry-Evans got wrong cost the Roosters badly.

First it was a screwball torpedo of a thing with ten minutes left that he launched from his own 40 metre line that found the grass and seemed perfect until it took one bounce too many and trickled dead.

It was unfortunate and nothing more. Not even someone as experienced as Cherry-Evans, who will likely bring up his 450th first class game next year, can predict how a ball bounces.

Penrith rolled up the field on the seven-tackle set and took the lead through a Nathan Cleary one-pointer but it was not necessarily a death blow given Cherry-Evans is the modern day field goal king.

He's kicked 31 of them in his career, the most of anyone in the NRL era.

He's kicked them to cap off big wins and to break stalemates at the last second — seven of them came in golden point extra time and his most recent match-winner was just a few weeks back against Newcastle.

Cherry-Evans is the player to look to when the scores are close. (Getty Images: Matt King )

He's kicked them off both feet, in howling gales and monsoonal rain.

He's never met a way he couldn't do it and he's met all the ways it can be done.

But this time his only attempt, from inside 20 metres and right in front, was a shank the likes of which we've rarely seen during his career.

Even the best can get it wrong, but both moments brought into stark relief just how things have changed for Cherry-Evans.

Roosters coach Trent Robinson was circumspect about it after the match, pointing out that Cherry-Evans had iced games before for the Roosters and would do so again.

Manly face uncertain future as Cherry-Evans comes home With Manly's season teetering on the edge, the Sea Eagles faithful welcomed former skipper Daly Cherry-Evans to Brookvale Oval in enemy colours for the first time. But it was the prodigal son who won the day.

The former is a fact but the latter is closer to a prediction than a guarantee.

There might still be a next week for Cherry-Evans, but it only might be. There will not be a next year.

On Saturday night against Cronulla, with Walker still out, Cherry-Evans must become the system once again.

He will play sharp and smart, like he always does, like he always has, and maybe it will be enough to earn another day.

But after seeming ageless for so long, he is running out of tomorrows. He has reached the end of forever and after seeming immune to time for so long it is coming for him at last.

The story might not have its final chapter against the Sharks or the Dolphins, but the last page is nigh and the final days of Daly Cherry-Evans in the NRL are a reminder of how the present, after seeming fixed for so long, becomes history wholesale — not at all and then all at once.

World.title: Australia's 43-year MotoGP streak continues with Senna Agius signing
World.content:
There will be a full-time Australian rider in motorcycle racing's premier class for the 43rd consecutive year with 21-year-old Senna Agius signing on to race for KTM Tech3 next year.

The Sydneysider currently sits fourth in the Moto2 standings after placing 10th in 2025.

He has four grand prix wins in Moto2, including at the Circuit of the Americas in the United States and Jerez in Spain earlier this season.

He won his home Moto2 grand prix at Phillip Island last year, and will be in MotoGP for next year's maiden Australian Grand Prix at the new Adelaide street circuit.

Agius has signed on for KTM Tech3, which has former F1 team principal Guenther Steiner has the team's chief executive.

"Today a lifelong dream of mine has come true, reaching MotoGP," Agius said.

"So many years of hard work have gone into this moment and I'm incredibly grateful to Guenther and everyone at Tech3 for believing in me and giving me this opportunity.

"I can't wait to repay their faith. I know the challenge ahead, but I'm ready to learn, work hard, and become the best version of myself with this team."

Australia has had a full-time rider in the premier class since 1985.

In the modern era of grand prix motorcycle racing, which began in 2002 when 500cc two-stroke bikes were replaced with 990cc four-stroke engines, Agius will become the 11th full-time Australian rider.

He will also be the only Australian on the grid next season, with Jack Miller ending his 12-year MotoGP stint and moving to World Superbikes in 2027.

World.title: Alex de Minaur readies for Davis Cup tie between Australia and Poland
World.content:
A Davis Cup tie has come at the perfect time for Alex de Minaur as he searches to recapture a spark after nearly a decade on tour.

The Australian, ranked as high as number five in the world earlier this year, fell to ninth after his shock second-round US Open loss earlier this month.

A quarterfinalist at the Australian Open this year, the 27-year-old has missed golden opportunities to go further in majors since, with Alexander Zverev instead netting two titles as Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz both endured injury-hit seasons.

De Minaur headed straight to Brisbane after his Flushing Meadows disappointment, training with Australian Cup captain Lleyton Hewitt for more than a week before their qualifying tie against Poland begins on Saturday.

De Minaur crashes out of US Open Alex de Minaur has crashed out of the US Open at the second-round stage, beaten in straight sets by Botic van de Zandschulp.

"Back here, around the boys, some good practice, a great team environment; it's been a great little change-up for me," de Minaur said.

"This is exactly what I need to get that spark back that maybe I was missing.

"I've had that spark for 10 years, every single day, right?

"There are stages through your career where things happen, and maybe you don't feel your best. But the timing of this week, it feels like everything's clicking together."

De Minaur has previously taken his losses hard; he copped his most recent defeat to Botic van de Zandschulp with uncharacteristic nonchalance.

But he is adamant the competitive edge remains as he prepares to head a team that includes doubles ace Max Purcell fresh off an 18-month ban for an anti-doping breach.

"Physically I'm great, and mentally I'm in great shape," de Minaur said.

"A rough patch … I've been very fortunate in my career to not have many of those.

"The tennis is still there, mentally there's been matches I haven't played the way I would like.

"But I've got a lot to give, a lot left in the tank, and hopefully I can show it.

"I haven't plateaued in my career. I'm hungry for more and feel I've got the opportunities to achieve it."

De Minaur burst onto the scene when, after being handed a late wildcard, he surged to the Brisbane International semifinals in 2017.

A year later he made his Davis Cup debut at the same venue, losing in a fifth-set tie-break to Zverev.

"I love team competitions … it brings that extra oomph in my game," said de Minaur, who is 17-10 in Davis Cup singles matches.

Poland are without former world number six Hubert Hurkacz, who has skipped the tie as he manages his return from injury, and will be led by world number 73 Kamil Majchrzak.

Rinky Hijikata and Purcell trained together, against Hewitt and de Minaur, at Wednesday's training in a sign they will contest Sunday's doubles tie.

The full draw will be announced on Friday.

AAP

World.title: Tszyu changes tune on controversial draw, eyes off fights in US
World.content:
Believing his domestic duties are done, Nikita Tszyu is ready to take on America after changing his tune and claiming victory in his controversial draw with countryman Ben Mahoney.

Tszyu surprisingly but sportingly conceded he thought he had lost the pair's Brisbane bout last month after the judges, with three vastly different scorecards, declared a stalemate.

Mahoney danced around the ring like he had won a world title, prompting derision from Tszyu's brother Tim, before his team cried highway robbery.

But after watching replays of the super-welterweight stoush, Tszyu is now adamant he should have been awarded the contest.

Tszyu's stunning admission, says Mahoney 'edged' thrilling draw Nikita Tszyu and Ben Mahoney have fought themselves to a standstill in thrilling contest that was scored a split decision draw on the Gold Coast on Wednesday night.

"I'm not a very good judge," he said of his initial verdict.

"I scored it 7-3. In a good way, 8-4. I thought I won the majority of the middle rounds. I gave him the first two rounds and the last two rounds, but [I won] everything else in between.

"I don't regret it, because it was what I felt at the time."

The still-undefeated Sydney slayer hopes his best nights lie ahead of him — and ideally in the US.

The 29-year-old and his team have always been happy to take things slowly and not rush into taking big fights in the boxing mecca.

But Tszyu (12-1-0, 10KOs) finally feels ready, despite Tim relinquishing his IBO super-welterweight belt in the US to Sebastian Fundora, as well as losing a rematch and copping a brutal beat down in another world-title loss in America to Bakhram Murtazaliev.

"I think I can figure it out," Tszyu told AAP.

"This fight was a great learning curve for me and it puts things a lot into perspective. I've got to be a lot more professional with the way I do things.

"I can't be landscaping close to the fight. I can't be doing woodworking close to the fight. Just some bad habits I do.

"Yeah, I've got to be a professional athlete."

No Limit Boxing is known to be pushing for Tszyu to feature on the undercard to the David Benavidez-Michal Cieslak unified blockbuster in Phoenix, Arizona, on December 12.

But if a US date does not eventuate, No Limit has confirmed Tszyu will fight at least once more in 2026 in Australia.

AAP

World.title: Bazzana whacks two home runs in vital MLB win for Guardians
World.content:
Australian Travis Bazzana has continued his impressive rookie season with two home runs, helping Cleveland secure a crucial 7-6 win over the Chicago White Sox in its battle for a Major League Baseball play-off berth.

The Guardians have beaten the White Sox at home in their last two games, meaning they trail Chicago by just half a game in the American League Central standings.

Whoever finishes their division on top will go through to the post-season. Cleveland has topped the AL Central standings for the last two years.

Even if they finish second behind the White Sox, the Guardians are also well placed to progress with a wildcard berth.

It was the second time in his debut MLB season that Bazzana has hit two homers in a game. The first Australian number one baseball draft pick has racked up hits in his last five games.

On Wednesday (AEST), the all-star second baseman hit a solo homer in the first inning to give Cleveland a 3-0 lead.

The Guardians were 6-4 down in the bottom of the sixth when Bazzana hit another solo shot.

Brayan Rocchio ripped a two-run double with two outs in the ninth inning, scoring two runs to win the game.

The shortstop, nicknamed "Rocctember" and "Playoff Rocchio" for his late-season heroics, starred with two for three, including a walk and two runners batted in (RBIs).

Bazzana hit two for four with two RBIs.

The Guardians improved to a 77-75 record and have 10 games left in the regular season, while the White Sox are at 77-74.

AAP

World.title: NRLW greats Elliott, Baxter announce retirement at end of finals
World.content:
The NRLW will farewell two of its most influential figures with Sydney Roosters pair Millie Elliott and Corban Baxter announcing their retirements.

Elliott and Baxter confirmed on Wednesday that this NRLW season would be their last, leaving the duo on track to go out with another premiership at the Roosters.

Elliott's decision to call it a day is a shock.

She is 28 and hopes to play for Australia at the end-of-year World Cup, but after having a child last year the front-rower wants to prioritise a growing family.

An emotional Baxter said on Thursday she had made the call after returning from last year's ACL rupture.

Corban Baxter was among the Roosters' foundation players. (Getty Images: Matt King)

The 32-year-old has still starred for the Roosters at fullback, but felt her body was finding it hard to keep up with the demands.

Both have been stars of the NRLW since its second season in 2019, with Baxter missing the opening four-week competition through a shoulder injury.

Elliott was the first player to win premierships at three clubs and has also had one of the loudest voices in the growth and direction of the competition.

"In a little while we'll look back and realise how significant this time was and the inception of the NRLW," Elliott said.

Can anyone stop the Roosters in the NRLW? After completing the most dominant regular season in NRLW history, the big question around the Sydney Roosters is simple: can anyone hope to stop them?

"When the competition came in, let's be honest no-one really cared. I'm not sugarcoating it.

"But the fact we're sitting here in a press conference room, we've got State of Origin where we have millions of people tune in.

"We go to a footy game and people know who we are; that's just crazy."

Elliott, who grew up in Cobargo on the NSW south coast, won two premierships at Brisbane in 2019 and 2020, before taking a title at Newcastle in 2022 and another at the Roosters in 2024.

The Tri-colours are unbeaten this year, headed into the finals with their only defeat in the past two seasons coming in the 2025 decider against Brisbane.

She was the Roosters' captain for their premiership in 2021 and has set the culture for the club, now a powerhouse of the competition.

In a career halted at times by pregnancy and injury, the mother of three played her first of seven Tests for Australia in 2016 and also played in seven Origins for NSW.

"The Roosters are going to be strong for a very long time because of that foundation that we've built and I'm proud of that," she said.

"What I love is seeing the ones in our systems really thriving from playing football from a young age and coming through and playing with us now."

AAP

Tech.title: The 2.5-hour AI-generated Odyssey movie is 2.5 hours too long
Tech.content:
Christopher Nolan’s engrossing take on The Odyssey dominated at the box office and spurred a newfound interest in classic literature among filmgoers. But a new retelling of the story made entirely with AI is so bad that it might just make viewers hate the original tale altogether.

The new film, called Odysseus: The Fall, comes via AI firm Fountain 0 and is written and directed by company cofounder Ash Koosha, who also lent his likeness to the title character and created all of the music. (The film’s credits are very short.) The studio’s only previous work is an AI film called Dreams of Violets that made it into Tribeca earlier this year. The Fall is, on its face, a much more ambitious project, billed as “the first completely AI generated film produced at the level of a Hollywood blockbuster.” In reality, it’s nothing close to “the level of a Hollywood blockbuster.” That may not necessarily be surprising, but after watching the entire 2.5-hour production I nonetheless found myself constantly surprised by just how much worse things could get. The Fall is the opposite of a glimpse at the future of AI filmmaking — it’ll make you wonder if there’s really any future in it at all.

The movie is available to rent now for $9.99 and, as far as I can tell, you can only watch it via a web browser. In order to view it on my living room TV I had to mirror the screen from my phone, which is not exactly IMAX in 70mm. Things didn’t get much better once I pressed play.

The Fall is plagued by two main issues. The first is consistency. The world of the film is constantly morphing, to the point that it’s incredibly distracting. The height of the cyclops that traps Odysseus and his men changes from shot to shot, waves move in the opposite direction of the wind, mouths don’t match the words spoken (and sometimes they move without producing a sound at all), and oars bend and twist as sailors row. In one scene a huge fleet of boats is racing through the ocean and one of them is inexplicably moving sideways. The AI-produced voice-overs can be incomprehensible, and at various points the names of both Odysseus and Zeus are pronounced wrong.

If it were just the odd hiccup it might be understandable, but there are so many faults in The Fall that it can be hard to focus on anything else. I watched the movie with my 13-year-old kid and it basically became a game of finding the weirdest mistakes. I noticed that a sword magically turned into a dagger, and then she one-upped me by spotting an alien carcass roasting over a spit. The Fall seems like a film designed to prove why script supervisors exist.

The thing is, while all of the AI-induced errors are distracting, they’re also the most entertaining part of the movie. There isn’t really much to distract from in The Fall because it is so dull. Because current AI models are really only capable of generating scenes that last a few seconds, the movie feels like a disjointed collection of moments from the odyssey that have been stitched together with little rhyme or reason. If you didn’t already know the story going into this, I don’t think you’d have any idea of what was going on, because the film explains very little. You don’t even learn about Penelope’s suitors until the movie is almost over.

I also can’t think of a single aspect of The Fall that feels improved because of AI. The “acting” is bafflingly bad, with characters pausing for seconds at a time for no apparent reason and bursts of laughter that jolt you out of nowhere. There’s no weight to the action, as if this takes place in a world where things like physics and gravity are suggestions rather than constants. Similarly, there aren’t any cool or impressive effects that wouldn’t be possible without the technology. The monsters look like shabby stop-motion creatures from the 1930s, which is all the weirder when they’re put beside the smooth, hyperreal human characters that AI spews out. It’s not just jarring, it’s boring and ugly.

Koosha claims that he adapted this story because he “always felt passionately about Homer’s epic tale since [he] originally read it years ago.” It seems much more likely that he’s trying to skate by on the hype and energy created by Nolan’s film, turning AI slop into a modern-day iteration of direct-to-video cash grabs. But this also puts the film at an incredible disadvantage from the very beginning, inviting comparisons to one of the most critically and commercially successful movies of the last few years, one that was especially beloved because of the director’s insistence on human craftsmanship. Nolan is someone who cares deeply about film, and his passion and enthusiasm is why stars want to work with him and viewers flock the theaters to see his movies.

The existence of The Fall, meanwhile, shows utter contempt for the medium, attempting to boil the work of hundreds of skilled workers into slop produced by a tiny team. It’s so terrible it’ll make you appreciate human-made art all the more.

Tech.title: The AI data center e-waste problem is huge — and getting bigger
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

E-waste from the AI boom has been vastly underestimated, a new report warns. By 2050, it could become enough trash to fill 23 million shipping containers — roughly enough 40-foot containers to circle the world six times if lined up in a row.

It’s a significantly higher estimate of AI’s e-waste than previous studies have found because the authors of the new report factor in all the infrastructure needed to support servers in data centers. The broader scope provides a clearer picture of junk AI leaves behind, according to the nonprofit Basel Action Network (BAN), which published the paper today.

”AI may feel weightless, but every model depends on an enormous amount of highly specialized, cutting edge hardware,” Jim Puckett, founder and chief of strategic direction at BAN, says in a press release. “If companies and governments do not begin planning for this new waste tsunami, today’s AI buildout could become an even more cataclysmic toxic waste crisis than we are already experiencing.”

“Today’s AI buildout could become an even more cataclysmic toxic waste crisis than we are already experiencing.”

Less than a quarter of the 68.3 million tons of e-waste created each year worldwide is formally collected and recycled. Most e-waste is ultimately dumped into shadowy “informal” waste collection where burning or burying equipment can expose workers and the local environment to toxic materials like lead and chromium.

BAN predicts e-waste generated globally will triple in amount to up to 211 million metric tons a year by 2050. It attributes about 15 to 20 percent of that garbage to AI. Unlike previous AI e-waste estimates that focused on servers and GPUs, BAN expands its count to include other categories of equipment: power supply and distribution, cooling systems, backup power, and networking equipment. Notably, BAN also counts what it calls “AI Waste Contagion” — a wide-ranging category that incorporates everything from telecommunications infrastructure to personal devices likely to become obsolete and replaced earlier as a result of advances in AI.

Counting it all up, BAN expects 70,000 metric tons of e-waste per gigawatt of data center capacity. It cites a McKinsey projection of total data center capacity reaching up to 219GW by 2030.

Considering AI-related electronic equipment retired between 2025 and 2050, BAN concludes that’ll add up to between 395 to 617 million metric tons of e-waste by the middle of the century. It breaks down to about 8.6 million to 13.1 million metric tons of equipment retired each year as a result of AI.

Previous estimates of AI’s e-waste have been more conservative. But by focusing on servers and accelerators, past studies miss about 87 percent of a data center’s electro-mechanical infrastructure, according to BAN.

A separate study published in 2024 predicted that e-waste from AI could reach between 1.2 million and 5 million tons by 2030. Another study published in February found that AI servers could create between 131,000 and 225,000 tons of e-waste annually by the end of the decade — an amount that’s still comparable to all the e-waste produced by a country the size of Denmark.

Tech.title: Resident Evil is a comedy first and a thrilling nightmare second
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

When Paul W.S. Anderson’s Resident Evil hit theaters in 2002, video game movies were largely seen as a niche. Films like Mortal Kombat and Tomb Raider had proven that big-screen game adaptations could be successful, but the commercial and critical failure of projects like the 1993 Super Mario Bros. still cast a long shadow. And while Anderson’s vision of Raccoon City might have captivated audiences on the whole, many hardcore fans of Capcom’s games were left disappointed by the way the original movies wildly deviated from the source material.

Weapons director Zach Cregger’s new take on Resident Evil is a return to the franchise’s fundamentals and a choice example of how video game movies have evolved. Its story is stripped down and its zombified monsters are terrifying. It’s also chiefly a movie that’s trying to make you laugh. Cregger uses humor to amplify his Resident Evil’s horror — his spin on the games’ infected ghouls are meant to be as funny as they are disturbing. The film feels like it could be the beginning of a fantastic new era for the franchise, but what’s most impressive is how well it can work as one and done.

Though this Resident Evil is peppered with nods to Capcom’s games, it focuses on Bryan (Austin Abrams), a medical courier character created for the movie. Like most people living in his mountain town, Bryan knows that a drive over to Raccoon City in the middle of winter can be hell, but a last-minute, high-paying delivery gig is enough to convince him to make the trip. Even with the treacherous weather and spotty cellphone reception, Bryan’s journey with his mysterious cargo is mostly uneventful as he first sets out. But he begins to understand what kind of danger he’s wandering into when he accidentally runs over a shambling woman (Andrea Miltnerová) who doesn’t seem to realize that she’s just been hit by an out-of-control car.

Resident Evil’s first big scare almost immediately establishes the sense of humor Cregger leans into throughout the film. You can feel the fear oozing out of Bryan as he trudges into the woods looking for the woman, but that tension momentarily evaporates as the film smash-cuts to him coaxing her into his car so that he can get her the medical help she clearly needs. The same dread rushes to the fore when Bryan witnesses how Resident Evil’s infected humans can mutate into creatures that feel like nods to Katamari Damacy and The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild. But it’s hard not to laugh when Bryan muses about how interesting the zombies’ transformations are to see up close.

Cregger knows that while viewers might not be familiar with Resident Evil’s lore, we can all appreciate how horror movies need their characters to make poor decisions. Abrams plays Bryan with a wide-eyed guilelessness that’s charming, but what really makes the character work is the way each monster encounter forces him to evolve into someone with better survival instincts.

By building the film around a civilian instead of highly trained special agents, Cregger and co-writer Shay Hatten give themselves the ability to tell a story that leans into the survival aspect of survival horror. Because Bryan is a bit of a dolt who’s constantly screaming in terror and fumbling his bullets when he’s scared, it often feels like the movie is replicating the experience of playing (or watching someone else play) a Resident Evil game for the first time. Bryan finds a couple of guns and a very limited number of bullets, but they’re nowhere near enough to make him feel safe as he trudges toward Raccoon City making the occasional stop to search seemingly empty buildings in hopes of finding a way to call for help.

The movie’s indoor scenes where Bryan’s rifling through drawers and tiptoeing down dark hallways are its most suspenseful because Cregger establishes early on that danger is always lurking just around the corner. Those moments are when it really seems like Cregger is channeling the essence of Capcom’s games, but you can also feel the director winking at his audience whenever Bryan talks about video games teaching him how to navigate his situation.

Image: Columbia Pictures

There’s a general straightforwardness to Cregger’s Resident Evil that sets it apart from many other recent video game adaptations. The film isn’t as concerned with overall character development as The Last of Us and its set pieces aren’t as large as The Super Mario Galaxy Movie’s. But those qualities work in the movie’s favor because they help draw your attention to all of the imaginative ways Cregger interpolates classic elements of Resident Evil storytelling and gameplay.

Especially coming after Weapons, Resident Evil feels like Cregger putting his mark on a beloved gaming property while breathing new life into a film franchise that was always fun, but lost its way as it grew in scale. Cregger has found a way to make the world of Resident Evil seem primed for more cinematic exploration, and to show us how far video game movies have come.

Resident Evil also stars Zach Cherry, Will Merrick, Zoé Bellas, Chris Lew Kum Hoi, Griffin Newman, and Magdalena Sittovaas. The movie hits theaters on September 18th.

Tech.title: Walmart takes a bite off the cost of Metroid Ravenous physical preorders
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Metroid series is going back to its 2D roots again with Metroid Ravenous for the Nintendo Switch 2, the first side-scrolling game in the series since 2021’s Metroid Dread for the Nintendo Switch. If you’re already excited enough to consider preordering, you can save $10 on the physical version of the game when you buy it from Walmart. It’s $59.88 instead of $69.99, about the same as buying it digitally. The game launches on January 28th, 2027, but it’s not clear how long the preorder discount will last. If it’s anything like other Walmart preorders, it may occasionally disappear.

Nintendo first showed off the side-scrolling adventure game at its September 2026 Direct, with a frantic trailer cutting between cinematic sequences, Samus dashing and rolling across a variety of environments, and engaging a number of enemies and bosses in battle. Samus absorbs some powerful abilities at the conclusion of Dread, and Ravenous seem to be all about plowing through anyone stopping her from escaping the planet. Other details of the story, including unique new mechanics, are being kept under wraps for the time being.

If you haven’t played Metroid Dread, I recommend it, especially at its $41.99 discounted price at Amazon. It’s part of Nintendo’s “Customer Appreciation” sale happening through September 26th, and several other games and accessories are cheaper, too.

Tech.title: Apple might make servers again to cash in on the AI rush
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

According to The Information, Apple is planning to get back into the server game and might just pair up with Nvidia to make it happen. Apple retired its Xserve line in 2011 and has largely left enterprise machines to other manufacturers since. But the growing demand for compute power as the AI industry continues to expand has apparently led the company to believe there is an opening for its powerful but efficient ARM-based M processors. Its Mac Mini and Mac Studio have proven popular with AI developers, which has led to shortages.

The server product, whether it’s called Xserve or something else, likely won’t debut until 2029. Word is that it will run on two or four (depending on the model) M8 Ultra chips. Apple only just announced the M6 in August, so the M8 line is a ways out.

It’s also rumored that Apple’s servers could incorporate Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion tech, which connects multiple chips together so they can operate as one. While the two companies have historically had a frosty relationship behind the scenes, recently Apple turned to Nvidia chips to power its revamped Siri servers. Incorporating NVLink could lead to further collaboration between the two, but plans could still change.

Tech.title: Your ‘health age’ is fake
Tech.content:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.

During last week’s Apple Watch announcement, I let out a distinct “Noooo!” in the Steve Jobs Theater. Along with a new readiness metric and a redesigned Health app, Apple had just announced that later this year, it’d be introducing a new longevity feature called Health Age.

This is a familiar concept in the wearable and health tech world. The idea is that if you put effort into your health and fitness, your physiological age could be “younger” than your chronological age. (Or older if you’re not putting in the effort.) Whoop has “Whoop age.” Oura has a “cardiovascular age” metric. My Withings scale just introduced various “longevity intelligence” features that include separate “heart age” and “vascular age” metrics. Garmin also has a “fitness age score.” At CES, I sat in front of a so-called longevity mirror that measured the blood flow in my face from a 30-second selfie to estimate my “physiological age” and my “facial skin age.” Earlier this week, I woke up and found out that my $5,000 smart mattress topper is also estimating my “biological age.”

If you ask Whoop, I’m supposedly 42. Over the past two years, Oura says my heart has been anywhere from seven years younger to 1.5 years younger than my chronological age. (It’s currently sitting at two years younger.) Withings says my vascular age is a year older than I am, while my heart is four years younger. Garmin says my fitness age is 36.5 years old. That longevity mirror? My facial skin age was apparently 26 (sunscreen, baby!), while my physiological age was 35. My very rude bed said I’m “trending older” this week at 38.7 years old.

My actual age is 38 years old — and that’s what I’m sticking with.

I’m not trying to rain on Apple’s (or other wearable makers’) parade. Frankly, I won’t rule on Apple’s version of the feature until I can test it for myself. I bring this all up to illustrate a point about when this type of feature can be genuinely helpful — and when you should treat it with a healthy dose of skepticism. As with most metrics, it’s all in the framing.

It’s true that through a healthy diet, good sleeping habits, and regular exercise, your physiological condition might be better than that of other people who are the same age and fit within a similar demographic. Depending on how a company defines its various longevity-related age scores, your results can identify areas where you can improve. For example, my Whoop age is somewhat cursed because it heavily weights strength training workouts in the algorithm. The last time I tested Whoop, I wasn’t going super hard on lifting heavy and perhaps was a bit too into cardio. If I wanted my Whoop age to improve, lifting weights would’ve been an easy way to tilt that number in my favor.

What do you mean I will be 80.6 years old when I’m 80?! Screenshot: Eight Sleep

Objectively, recalibrating my training habits to be more balanced would be a good thing for my long-term health. If you leave it exactly at that, there’s nothing wrong with this type of feature. But culturally speaking, that’s not how these “health age” scores work.

The way I’ve seen people talk about this metric largely hews toward fluffing up your ego. If your health age is older, you probably don’t talk about it. It’s “shameful” even though, really, it’s not. That’s because culturally — at least in the West — getting old isn’t considered a good thing. If your health age is younger, it becomes something to bandy about. Apple’s vice president of health, Sumbul Desai, even says in this Instagram Reel that Health Age could be something you brag about to your friends. That explains why tech entrepreneur Bryan Johnson, famous for his quest to never die, would post this absurd take on X about how aliens would struggle to distinguish him from his teenage son, alongside a chart titled “Is Bryan Johnson More 18 or 49?” Johnson is 49; he looks a little younger, maybe, and his metrics might be comparable to someone much younger on average, but his current state is ultimately just what 49 looks like for him.

Furthermore, your wearable-determined age is oftentimes not capturing the whole picture. You could game the Whoop Age metric to the letter, get your annual physical, and find out that your cholesterol level is through the roof. A reader once related this exact story to me. You could optimize all the controllable lifestyle health factors — diet, exercise, and sleep — like Bryan Johnson and still end up with autoimmune gastritis, as he has. Some of your health is encoded in your genetics, and while you can better the odds, your ultimate fate is not always something you can decide. We all know of someone who was healthy as a horse and died tragically young because of a freak accident.

Personally, my various health ages have always indicated I’m moderately younger than my chronological age. But even then, that’s not an accurate picture of how I’m aging either. I’m definitely fitter now at 38 than I was at 18. As a teen, I couldn’t even run a mile nonstop, and in my 30s, I have multiple half-marathons under my belt. But my bones also snap, crackle, and pop more. I can’t pull all-nighters without caffeine like I used to, even though I eat much healthier. It doesn’t matter what potions I slather on my hair or what supplements I take; the grays keep coming. I was fitter last year, and my wearables all praised my consistent training to the point that I kept getting injured. I’m less fit this year. I’ve lost roughly 5 pounds of muscle, if smart scales are to be believed, but my metabolic biomarkers are all much, much, much healthier. To the point where earlier this week, my doctor patted me on the back and said she saw all the effort I’d put in over the past year. Yet until recently, my wearables were all convinced my health was in a death spiral.

Health ages, I genuinely believe, were meant to be a helpful way of visualizing how small lifestyle changes can improve overall health as you age. But because they’re all defined differently and use a range of parameters, they’ve become these odd “scores” that can pass faulty judgments on how well you’re doing. I look at my hodgepodge of “ages,” and I can’t tell you what any of it truly means.

I am proudly 38 years old in this photo and whatever my hair’s doin’, I feel pretty alright.

Not to get too philosophical, but time, as far as we know it, can only move forward. My rude bed is kind of right. Every week, I will be trending older because that’s simply how time works. No matter the wearable metric or magic new drug, none of us is Benjamin Buttoning our way out of that fact.

Which brings me to my current philosophy: I am irreversibly 38, and am doing pretty alright if you ask me.

Tech.title: Google will now let any AI agent run your smart home
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Google is opening up its smart home to AI agents, letting tools like Claude and Open Claw access and control your connected devices and analyze your home’s data using the standardized Model Context Protocol.

Google Home MCP is a new integration that lets third-party AI agents control and monitor your smart home and act on your behalf. It “allows any AI agents that support MCP, including Google Antigravity, Claude, Hermes or Open Claw, to securely work with all of the devices and event history in your Google Home ecosystem,” Taylor Lehman, group product manager at Google Home & Nest, said in a blog post.

According to Lehman, Home MCP integration will connect your AI agent of choice to real-world events, enabling a host of new capabilities. From things like cross-camera analysis — so you could ask your agent what your kid did when they got home from school — to using device state history to figure out how many loads of laundry you did last week or how long the lights were left on. It will also allow your agent to interact with you via voice, for example, by sending an audio message over your Google Home speaker when it has finished a task. You can also have your agent create a custom dashboard to control your Google Home.

Google Home smart speakers will still be controlled by Gemini for Home, but with MCP enabled third-party AI agents will be able to send voice messages to you through them. Photo: Jennifer Patison Tuohy / The Verge

This doesn’t replace Google’s new Gemini for Home assistant, which remains Google’s interface for interacting with Google Home through the Home app and Google Nest smart speakers, following the demise of Google Assistant. Instead, MCP integration adds another layer of control, allowing third-party AI agents to interact directly with devices connected to Google Home through their own interfaces.

If this week wasn’t dominated by headlines about how AI will kill us all, I’d be really excited about this

At launch, availability is limited to Google Home Premium Advanced users in the US ($20/month or $200/year), with access rolling out in the coming weeks. Setup requires creating a Google Cloud project and configuring it to use the Home MCP.

Giving an AI agent access to real-world devices like smart locks, thermostats, and core infrastructure like HVAC systems and appliances raises obvious questions about security, privacy, and safety. Google says Home MCP enforces rate limits and safety protections; for example, it won’t allow an agent to unlock doors. However, depending on your agent, “connecting it to Home MCP can result in unexpected or even undesired behavior,” said Lehman, who recommends reviewing Google’s developer policies and terms of service.

Home Assistant, an open-source smart home platform, has implemented a similar MCP integration that shows what you can do when you give an agent access to your smart home system. I tested this last year to use Claude to vibe-code my smart home, and it easily handled some of the more complex tasks that most interfaces — and users, for that matter — struggle with, including troubleshooting, creating automations, designing a dashboard, and setting up more advanced configurations, all using natural language.

The biggest change here isn’t that Google Home can now turn your lights on and off through your Claude app; it’s that Claude — or your agent of choice — has access to the underlying data and control layer of your home. It’s a step toward building a whole home computer for your smart home that can understand what’s happening in it, reason across its history, and take action on your behalf. And if this last week wasn’t dominated by headlines about how AI will kill us all, I’d be really excited.

A system that can troubleshoot, suggest improvements, and identify patterns across your home is more useful than one that says “I’m sorry, I can’t do that”

Still, there are real advantages to giving an AI agent access to your smart home. It can reason across the data your home generates and act on it in ways traditional smart home systems generally can’t, moving the smart home from command and control toward something more contextual and proactive, closer to actual intelligence. A system that can troubleshoot a device, suggest improvements to automations, and track and identify patterns across your home is much more useful than one that just says “I’m sorry, I can’t do that.” With Home MCP integration, Google is bringing these capabilities into Google Home.

Claude created this dashboard for me in Home Assistant using MCP. With Google Home MCP enabled, it should be able to do something similar for my Google Home. Screenshots by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

While consumer-facing tools like Claude will be useful for smart home tinkerers, the bigger picture here is Google’s developer play. Over the last couple of years, Google has increasingly positioned itself as the smart home’s infrastructure layer. It launched API access to its smart home in 2024 and more recently made Gemini for Home a full-stack AI offering. All of this points toward a more B2B2C strategy: Google can provide the AI and smart home infrastructure while other companies build consumer-facing services and products on top.

With this week’s announcement, Google has also opened a path for developers to use its agentic Antigravity coding tool to build custom AI agents for the smart home that tap into Google Home device data and control layer. But even if developers use a different agent, as long as they’re using Google Home, it’s a win for Google. This way, Google becomes the smart home infrastructure layer, in much the same way AWS became infrastructure for internet and software businesses.

Whether smart home developers will buy into Google’s promises here is a big question. Based on the number of smart home platforms the company has launched and let die over the years — Android @ Home, Weave, Project Brillo, Works with Nest, Google Assistant — developers will have to decide whether Google has finally settled on a smart home platform it intends to stick with.

Tech.title: Claude comes for Gemini with its own take on Docs and Slides
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Claude is getting a pair of new tools today: Docs and Slides. They’ll let you create documents and presentations through Claude chats, which you can export, edit, and share with other users.

As part of the announcement, Anthropic is also simplifying how Claude chats work, merging regular chats and Cowork into “one Claude,” with all of its AI productivity tools available from any chat. Artifacts and Claude Design capabilities will be available through the new single interface as well. According to Anthropic, Claude “can now figure out what a task needs, so what Cowork and Design can do is available from any conversation, with the context, skills, and connectors you already have.”
